## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** Evaluation paper on a working machine: "In this paper we discuss the design of the J-Machine and evaluate the effectiveness of the mechanisms incorporated into the MDP. We measure the performance of the communication and synchronization mechanisms directly and investigate the behavior of four complete applications" (abstract, p. 1); micro-benchmarks (Section 3, p. 3–6), macro-benchmarks (Section 4, p. 6–10), critique (Section 5, p. 11–12).
- **Context:** Argues that "highly-evolved sequential mechanisms are not adequate to support most parallel models of computation", so synchronization, communication and global naming "must be implemented largely in software with prohibitive overhead" (p. 1). Builds on the MDP design paper [5] (Dally et al., IEEE Micro 1992) (p. 1, 12). Compared with nCUBE/2, CM-5, Intel DELTA and Active Messages [17] (Table 1, p. 4), and EM4, KSR, iPSC/860, Delta (Table 3, p. 6).
- **Correctness:** Measurements on a 512-node, 8x8x8 machine at 12.5 MHz (p. 2). The authors caution that speedup curves are "strongly affected by the deﬁnitions of speedup used and the base case" and are "primarily useful in directing attention to interesting trends rather than being of signiﬁcance in themselves" (p. 7–8). The figures for other machines come from published sources whose content is not always clear: "sufﬁcient detail to determine what is being included is rarely provided" (p. 6). The J compiler "currently produces inefﬁcient code", so critical sequences were hand-tuned "to reﬂect the expected future behavior of the compiler" (p. 7).
- **Contributions:** (1) Measured message overhead, latency vs distance and load, terminal bandwidth, producer-consumer and barrier synchronization costs of the MDP (p. 3–6, Tables 1–3, Figures 2–4); (2) profiles of four applications (LCS, Radix Sort, N-Queens, TSP) up to 512 nodes (p. 7–10, Figures 5–6, Tables 4–5); (3) a critique of the mechanisms with proposed fixes: statistics hardware, faster external memory, TLB-based naming, "return-to-sender" flow control, more registers (p. 11–12).
- **Clarity:** Clear and well structured. The PDF's text layer garbles the figures and some table layouts; the page images are legible. No printed page numbers on the preprint.

## Concepts
| Concept | What the paper says | Page |
|---|---|---|
| Message-Driven Processor (MDP) | The J-Machine node chip whose "primitive mechanisms for communication, synchronization, and naming" support "threads with 50 to 150 instructions which exchange small data objects frequently with low-latency and synchronize quickly". | p. 1 |
| Task creation upon message arrival (hardware dispatch) | "When a message arrives at the head of the queue, a task is dispatched to handle it in four processor cycles"; the instruction pointer comes from the message header. | p. 2 |
| Message priorities | Two priorities with separate queues; priority one is preferred in arbitration and may interrupt priority zero; a background priority runs when both queues are empty. | p. 2 |
| Presence tags (cfut, fut) | Data tags marking slots "for values that have not yet been computed"; reading one traps and suspends the thread until the value arrives; fut supports first-class futures. | p. 2, 5 |
| Global name translation (enter, xlate) | Hardware table converting virtual addresses to segment descriptors for a global namespace; judged "inadequate to transparently and inexpensively provide a global name space". | p. 2, 11 |
| Fine-grained communication | Small messages are efficient enough that data need not be sent in large blocks: "In machines lacking efﬁcient communication primitives, one would need to collect and send large blocks of data". | p. 5, 9 |
| One-way message overhead (Ts, Tb) | Fixed send+receive overhead per message and injection overhead per byte, excluding network latency. | p. 4 |
| Terminal network bandwidth | Data rate between two nodes for a given message size; "often becomes the limiting factor" for programs that communicate with neighbours. | p. 5–6 |
| Return-to-sender flow control (proposed) | Back-pressure that "refuses messages when the queue is above a certain threshold by returning them to the sending node". | p. 11 |
| Physically fine-grain machines | Small nodes with little memory each, giving "proportionally better cost/performance while retaining the same total memory capacity". | p. 12 |

- **Category:** Position or analytical argument with a retrospective of first-generation microkernels (Mach, Chorus) and a short design description of second-generation ones (Exokernel, L4). - **Contributions:** A diagnosis of why first-generation microkernels were "inefficient and inflexible" (p. 70): IPC cost (pp. 72–74) and "the policy inside the microkernel" (p. 74). Two evaluation criteria, conservative and progressive (pp. 72–73), and a relative-RPC-overhead model (Fig. 3, p. 73). A description of L4's recursive address spaces (grant, map, demap, with mapping done by IPC) and of the user-level memory servers, pagers, drivers and Unix server built on them (pp. 75–76).

David Wentzlaff, Anant Agarwal (2009). *Factored Operating Systems (fos): The Case for a Scalable Operating System for Multicores*. ACM SIGOPS Operating Systems Review 43(2), pp. 76–85. https://doi.org/10.1145/1531793.1531805

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** A position and design paper with motivating measurements. It argues that SMP operating systems cannot scale to "1000+ core systems" (p. 2), measures two Linux scaling problems (p. 3–4), and describes the design of a new message-passing OS (fos) whose prototype is "under active development" (p. 2, p. 8). fos itself is not evaluated.
- **Context:** Microkernels (Mach, L3, L4; p. 2, p. 8), scalable shared-memory kernels (Tornado/K42, Hive, Disco/Cellular Disco, Corey; p. 9), distributed OSes (Amoeba, Sprite, Clouds; p. 9) and distributed Internet services (DNS, BitTorrent, Chord, AFS, GFS; p. 9–10). The authors' own Raw and Tilera on-chip networks are cited for message costs (p. 8).
- **Correctness:** The Linux measurements are on real hardware (p. 3), and the cache study runs in a QEMU-based simulator (p. 4). The case for fos rests on argument, for example "We believe that the shared nothing, message passing only, approach will encourage OS developers to think very carefully about exactly what data is being shared, which will lead to more scalability" (p. 5). The paper names its own open questions in Section 3.4 (p. 8).
- **Contributions:** (1) A measurement showing that the Linux 2.6.24.7 physical page allocator "does not scale beyond 8 cores under heavy load" (p. 2, Fig. 1 p. 3). (2) A simulated measurement of OS/application cache interference on Apache2 (p. 4). (3) Three recommendations: avoid hardware locks, separate OS from application cores, and avoid global cache-coherent shared memory (p. 5). (4) The fos design: a microkernel with mailbox messaging, OS services split into fleets of servers bound to cores, a name server, and space multiplexing instead of time multiplexing (p. 5–7).
- **Clarity:** Well structured and readable. The figure labels in the author PDF use an odd font encoding (the text cannot be extracted), but the rendered figures are legible. The message format is not described.

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** A retrospective by two of the system's designers. It reviews 20 years of design and implementation decisions across the L4 microkernel family, from L3 to seL4, and reports which were "Retained", "Replaced", "Abandoned", "Added" or remain "Unresolved" (pp.133, 136–147). It reports a few measurements (Table 1, p.135; pp.137, 140, 146), but it is not an evaluation paper.
- **Context:** Liedtke's L4 papers [Liedtke 1993a, p.133; 1995, p.136] and the "microkernel minimality principle" (p.136); the early-1990s IPC cost problem [Condict et al. 1994; Chen and Bershad 1993] (p.133); EROS and capabilities (pp.135, 138); seL4 verification [Klein et al. 2009] (p.133) and WCET analysis [Blackham et al. 2011] (p.135); the multikernel [Baumann et al. 2009] (pp.133, 143).
- **Correctness:** The main assumption is that IPC latency counted in cycles can be compared across very different processors. The authors hedge this themselves: "as far as comparisons across vastly different ISAs and micro architectures have any validity" (p.147). Most "lessons" are argued from the authors' own experience rather than measured. The few numbers are partly taken from cited work (Warton 2005, Nourai 2005, Liedtke 1993a; pp.138, 144).
- **Contributions:** (1) A history and family tree of L4 kernels (Fig. 1, p.134; pp.133–135). (2) One-way IPC cost across eleven kernel and processor pairs from 1993 to 2013 (Table 1, p.135) and kernel sizes (Table 2, p.136). (3) A verdict on each original L4 design principle and implementation trick (Sections 3–4, pp.136–146). (4) The conclusion that "the most general principles behind L4, minimality (including running device drivers at user level) and a strong focus on performance, still remain relevant" (p.147).
- **Clarity:** Clearly written. Each subsection ends with a boxed verdict (e.g. "Abandoned: Long IPC.", p.138). The measurement method behind Table 1 is not described.

# SQ1

## Question
Which computer systems provide sending a message (to an object, actor, process or core) as a primitive below the programming language, that is in the operating system kernel, the instruction set or the hardware, and at which of these levels does each system's message semantics hold, and which systems started message-based at a level and later added paths that are not messages?

## Why it matters to the observation
The observation claims message abstractions stop above the operating system and hardware. This question tests that claim against the systems that tried to go lower, and maps how far down each one got.

## Origin
observation

## Kind
kinds, because the observation's claim is tested by how far down each kind of attempt got and which kinds later added paths that are not messages, not by a catalogue of every kernel with an IPC path: one system of a kind places the message send at the same level, by the same mechanism, as the others of that kind. (`research/sls/1-protocol/step.md`, *How much each question needs*)

Census or kinds is my decision at gate 1c; kinds is recommended. Estimate from `sls/2-search/R0.md`: the 160 papers included through I1 all serve this question (counted as the included rows whose decision names I1; P67 left out, its decision changed to exclude at 3c). Grouping them by the system their title or screening reason names gives about 112 distinct systems, with the L4 family and the Mach family counted once each (about 120 if their variants, such as seL4, Fiasco or Real-Time Mach, count apart). Under census: about 110–120 papers to read from round 0 alone, plus one for each new system a later round finds. Under kinds: round 0 shows about 20 kinds across the three levels, so about 30–40 papers, one or two per kind, then 5 in a row with no new kind.

## Unit
A kind of message-based system: the level where the send is a primitive (an instruction, a hardware or microcode mechanism, or the kernel's own means of communication, as in I1), combined with how the mechanism works. Examples: an object-based processor with port send and receive operations; a message-driven multicomputer node; a many-core chip with on-die message buffers and no coherence; a channel processor; a hardware IPC accelerator for a kernel; a communication coprocessor; a synchronous-IPC microkernel; a port-based microkernel; a capability kernel; a multikernel; a message-based distributed operating system. A paper also adds a new unit if it shows a new kind of path, added later, that is not a message.

## Enough when
At least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 5 in a row add nothing new. 10 + 5 rather than 10 + 3: the systems span four decades and three levels, and a run of kernel papers says nothing about processors.

## Reading order
Levels alternating (instruction set, hardware or microcode mechanism, kernel), and within each level different groups and decades; full designs with an evaluation before position papers and short IPC notes. Start with the seeds and the system papers most other papers build on: the Intel 432 (P10, then P75), the Message-Driven Processor and the J-Machine (P12, P65), the multikernel (P8), L4 (P46, P48). Then: the Single-chip Cloud Computer (P21), KeyKOS and EROS (P53, P77), the Transputer (P96), Spring (P51), Chorus (P200), the ELXSI System 6400, which added shared memory later (P42), the M-Machine (P66), Alewife (P274), the Lisp Machine (P73), hardware IPC support (P159, P221), object and Java processors (P58, P59, P63), QNX (P276), fos and Helios (P102, P45), the message coprocessor and Sylvan (P152, P250). After these, any paper describing a system of a kind not yet covered. Several papers on one system count as one reading for this question (e.g. the L4 family: P46, P48, P172, P188, P204, P233, P251): only the strongest is read for it.

# SQ2

observation

kinds, because the observation needs which kinds of escape route below the language remain and why designers kept them; the same few kinds (shared memory, interrupts, traps, privileged instructions, microcode) recur across systems, so listing them per system adds pages, not answers. A kind of mechanism kept below the language that is not a message send (e.g. shared memory, interrupts, traps, privileged instructions, microcode, global registers), together with the reason given for keeping it; or a kind of level found to be written in the system's own objects and messages. # SQ10

## Question
What does the literature report about the equivalence (duality) of message-passing and shared-memory system structures, and can either one be built on top of the other while keeping its properties (encapsulation, freedom from data races, interposition) and its performance?

## Why it matters to the observation
Lauer and Needham (1978/1979, *On the Duality of Operating System Structures*) argue that message-oriented and procedure-oriented systems are duals: a problem solved in one has a dual solution in the other. If the two are equivalent, the observation's gap may be a matter of which layer exposes which model, and putting messages in hardware may add nothing that a layer above cannot give.

## Origin
counter-evidence (added by skeptic)

## Kind
evidence, because the question asks what the literature reports about equivalence and about building one model on the other: findings (proofs, arguments, measurements), not a list of systems. (`research/sls/1-protocol/step.md`, *How much each question needs*)

## Unit
A finding: a result or argument on the equivalence of the two structures, or a report of one model built on the other, with which properties (encapsulation, freedom from data races, interposition) and how much performance it keeps or loses.

## Enough when
At least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 5 in a row add nothing new. 10 + 5 rather than 10 + 3: the evidence comes from unrelated fields (theory of distributed computing, operating systems, distributed shared memory, multiprocessor hardware, parallel programming measurements).

# SQ9

## Question
What evidence and arguments show that narrowing the semantic gap by raising the hardware interface towards the language harms performance, cost, generality or compiler optimisation, and do those arguments apply to a message send as the machine's primitive?

## Why it matters to the observation
The notes treat the semantic gap as a defect to close. The reduced instruction set argument (Patterson and Ditzel, 1980, *The Case for the Reduced Instruction Set Computer*) was made against exactly that goal. If its reasoning carries over to message sends, the observation describes a deliberate trade-off, not an oversight.

# SQ10

## Question
What does the literature report about the equivalence (duality) of message-passing and shared-memory system structures, and can either one be built on top of the other while keeping its properties (encapsulation, freedom from data races, interposition) and its performance?

## Why it matters to the observation
Lauer and Needham (1978/1979, *On the Duality of Operating System Structures*) argue that message-oriented and procedure-oriented systems are duals: a problem solved in one has a dual solution in the other. If the two are equivalent, the observation's gap may be a matter of which layer exposes which model, and putting messages in hardware may add nothing that a layer above cannot give.

# SQ11

## Question
Why do developers of actor or message-passing programs also use shared state, locks or other concurrency mechanisms alongside messages, and what do they report that the pure message model cannot express or costs too much?

## Why it matters to the observation
The observation wants a system with no escape routes from its own rules. # P11

## Reference
David Michael Ungar (1986, dated "February, 1986" on the cover). *The Design and Evaluation of a High Performance Smalltalk System*. PhD dissertation, Computer Science, University of California, Berkeley. Published as UC Berkeley technical report UCB/CSD-86-287 and later as a book by MIT Press (ACM Distinguished Dissertation, 1987). The report number and the MIT Press edition come from the reference line given to me; neither is printed on the scanned pages I read. P11, screened in under I2 (row R0-011). Pages cited below are the printed arabic page numbers of the dissertation scan in `papers/P11.pdf`. Printed p. *n* is PDF page *n* + 18 up to printed p. 152 (e.g. Chapter 1 starts on printed p. 1, PDF p. 19). Printed p. 153 is scanned twice (PDF pp. 171–172), so from there on printed p. *n* is PDF page *n* + 19 (e.g. Appendix A p. 185 is PDF p. 204). The front matter has no printed numbers, so the abstract is cited by its PDF pages (pp. 7–8). This is not the MIT Press edition, whose page numbers will differ.

## Deepest pass
2

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** Design and evaluation of a processor architecture and its run-time software, SOAR ("Smalltalk On A RISC"). It also contains a survey of earlier high-level-language machines (Ch. 2) and a new garbage collector, Generation Scavenging (Ch. 5) (pp. 1–5).
- **Context:** Smalltalk-80 runs poorly on widely available hardware. The only machine that "has demonstrated universally acceptable Smalltalk-80 performance" is the $120,000 ECL Xerox Dorado (p. 11). Earlier language machines (R-2, Burroughs B5700/B6700, Scheme-79, Symbolics 3600, Katana-32) "closely coupled the source language semantics to the hardware" (p. 14). RISC work (IBM 801, RISC I/II, MIPS) and the Deutsch-Schiffman software techniques for the 68010 are the other context (pp. 12–14, 24–28).
- **Correctness:** The premise is that a RISC with a few Smalltalk-specific additions can match microcoded or high-level-instruction machines. It is tested by instruction-level simulation of Xerox's official benchmarks (pp. 61–66). The NMOS chip exists and ran diagnostics, but Smalltalk-80 had not yet run on it (pp. 2, 127). The value of each feature is an omission cost measured in cycles under the current compiler. The author says this neglects cycle-time effects and compiler interaction (pp. 64–65, 67, 72).
- **Contributions:** (1) The SOAR instruction set, with tagged integer arithmetic, register windows, in-line call-target caching, fast shuffle, trap mechanisms and direct object pointers (Ch. 3). (2) A feature-by-feature evaluation that sorts features into "winners", "questionable" and "losers" (Tables 4.4–4.5, pp. 68–69). (3) Generation Scavenging, which reclaims storage with about 3% CPU overhead and no object table (Ch. 5, p. 126). (4) The "architect's trap" lesson (p. 70).
- **Clarity:** Clearly written and organised, with summary tables per chapter. The scan is legible but OCR-noisy, and a few table cells were checked against page images (pp. 66, 71).

## Quality
| Q | Answer | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | yes | The abstract states the two results (PDF pp. 7–8), and p. 2 states the aim: "We have investigated whether a reduced instruction set computer can provide good performance for the Smalltalk-80 system". |
| Q2 | partly | The receiver is named by its type (class) and dispatch uses the class of the first argument, cached in-line (pp. 8, 46–47). The argument register and the cache word after the call are described (p. 46). Delivery and ordering, and what happens when the receiver is busy, are not discussed; a send is a synchronous call (inferred). |
| Q3 | partly | The performance results come from the Daedalus instruction-level simulator (pp. 61–62, 65). A NMOS chip exists and "has correctly run diagnostics" (p. 2, p. 127), but Smalltalk-80 had not been run on it. The 400 ns cycle time is "our measured cycle time" for the chips (p. 65). |
| Q4 | partly | Overall results name real baselines: the Dorado (times from Xerox's newsletter [Bay84]), Xerox PS on 68010/68020, Tek 4404 and BS (Tables 4.2–4.3, pp. 66). Feature values are against hypothetical SOAR-without-feature configurations (Tables 4.4–4.6, pp. 68–71), which count as partly. |
| Q5 | yes | Benchmarks are given with the reason for choosing them (p. 62). The setup is the simulator and toolchain, with 400 ns cycles (Fig. 4.1, pp. 61–62, 65). The procedure is to run once, reset the counters and measure the second iteration (pp. 62, 65). |
| Q6 | partly | Most abstract and conclusion figures are in the body: Dorado parity (Table 4.2 p. 66), 2.5× the 68010 (Table 4.3 p. 66, p. 72), GS 3% vs 9% (p. 14, pp. 101, 109). However, the abstract says the language-specific hardware "doubles its performance over a RISC II with the same cycle time" (PDF p. 8). The body gives "The speed ratio of full SOAR to RISC II, 1.6" (p. 71, Table 4.6: RISC II 62%). |
| Q7 | partly | Each feature's contribution is isolated by an omission-cost calculation in cycles (Tables 4.4–4.5, Appendix A). Other causes are only asserted or hedged, e.g. "Perhaps the optimizations in Deutsch's compiler account for the difference" (p. 71). Another is that GC hardware "probably did not speed up SOAR" because of cycle time (p. 72), which is not measured. |
| Q8 | partly | Limitations are stated in paragraphs, not in a dedicated section. The results "hold only for Smalltalk-80 systems with state-of-the-art compiler technology" (p. 65). They "do not include virtual memory, operating system, and I/O overhead" (p. 70) and ignore cycle-time effects (p. 72). The algorithm "may not accommodate objects that live for a medium amount of time" (p. 109). |
| Q9 | no | The author designed the architecture and its run-time software ("we have analyzed the architecture of and designed and analyzed the software algorithms", p. 2; the toolchain authors are listed in Fig. 4.1, p. 61). |

## Extracted fields
| Field | Value | Page |
|---|---|---|
| Reference | See Reference above. Version: UC Berkeley dissertation scan (technical-report printing, per the reference line), not the MIT Press book. Printed p. = PDF p. − 18 up to printed p. 152, and PDF p. − 19 from printed p. 153 on. Criterion: I2 (a retrospective/evaluation of an architecture directed at a high-level language, Smalltalk-80, reporting measured (simulated) performance and stated reasons for performance). I4 (follow-up pass, gate 3c 2026-10-13): SQ9 (pp. 2, 14, 17, 21, 24, 34–35, 125–126). | p. 1–2, 5, 14, 24; PDF pp. 1, 3 |
| Paper type | design; implementation (chip summary from Pendleton's thesis); evaluation (simulation); plus a historical survey of earlier language machines (Ch. 2) and an analytical chapter on medium-lifetime objects (Ch. 6, not read) | pp. 2–5, 30, 54–59, 61 |
| System | SOAR (Smalltalk On A RISC), designed at UC Berkeley, a project led by David Patterson (p. 129). NMOS chip by J. Pendleton, fabricated by MOSIS; a CMOS chip also exists (pp. 2, 58, 128). Status: silicon that ran diagnostics, "running at 800 ns" (p. 127). Evaluated by simulation; Smalltalk-80 runs on the SOAR simulator, but "Our goal is to run the Smalltalk-80 system on SOAR" (p. 127). Year: chips 1985 (Table 2.2 gives SOAR's year as 1985, p. 12). Also Berkeley Smalltalk (BS), a 68010 interpreter used as test bed (p. 2). | pp. 2, 12, 58–59, 127–129 |
| Levels with message semantics | Language: the paper says "The Smalltalk-80 language has replaced operating on variables with sending messages to objects" (p. 11). It does not discuss other paths at that level. Runtime/VM: SOAR "abandoned the Smalltalk virtual machine instruction set" (bytecodes) and compiles to SOAR code (p. 35). Instruction set: no. There is no send instruction (Table 3.2, p. 37). A send is compiled to a `call` plus an in-line-cache prologue, with lookup in software (pp. 37, 46–47). The thesis itself calls sends "procedure calls" (p. 8; abstract, PDF p. 7) and "calls" (p. 42). Microcode: none ("Since SOAR has no microcode", p. 39). Hardware: no message mechanism described. Kernel: not stated (the operating system is mentioned only for process switches, p. 46). No change over time is stated. | pp. 11, 35, 37, 39, 42, 46–47 |
| Receiving unit and state ownership | The receiver is an object (Smalltalk-80 "objects", p. 50). Dispatch uses "the type of the first argument to choose its target routine" (p. 8). Machine-level access: "all Smalltalk processes share the same address space" (p. 45). Untagged-mode instructions operate on raw 32-bit data, and "the Smalltalk system already relies on the compiler to ensure system integrity" (p. 33). Activation records "can be manipulated like any other objects" (p. 13; p. 53). Whether an object's state can be accessed only by itself is not stated. | pp. 8, 13, 33, 45, 50, 53 |
| Message mechanism | Synchronous call and return (inferred from the call/return instructions, pp. 37, 48). The receiver is passed in a register: "The argument is passed in r6" (Fig. 3.8, p. 46). Dispatch: a lookup on the receiver's type, whose result is cached in the instruction stream, overwriting the call. A prologue checks the cached type and traps on a miss (Figs. 3.8–3.9, pp. 46–47). The call target is the same as last time "95% of the time" (p. 13, citing [DAmb83]). Ordering, buffering and the busy-receiver case: not stated. | pp. 13, 37, 46–48 |
| Non-message primitives | The whole ISA is conventional RISC operations: ALU, load/store, byte insert/extract, skip, jump, call/return, trap (Table 3.2 p. 37). The thesis gives these reasons: (1) Traps to software handlers replace microcode: "Since SOAR has no microcode, unusual situations must be met with a trap to a software handler" (p. 39). (2) Interrupts: vectored, prioritised traps and interrupts, including I/O and page faults; nested interrupts are not supported "because they complicate the architecture" (pp. 40–41). (3) Software interrupt for process switches, enabled by a bit in call/jump, chosen because software semaphores "would be too expensive" (pp. 45–46). (4) Untagged mode, which also lets C and Pascal run (p. 33). (5) Shared address space and paged virtual memory (pp. 45, 54). (6) Pointer-to-register addressing, so on-chip activation records can be accessed as memory (pp. 53–54). | pp. 33, 37, 39–41, 45–46, 53–54 |
| Self-definition | "We have also coded the Smalltalk primitive operations and storage management software in SOAR assembly language" (Fig. 4.1, p. 61), i.e. outside the Smalltalk object model. The bytecode-to-SOAR converter is written in Smalltalk (p. 38). The debugger must be rewritten because bytecodes were abandoned (p. 39). A source-level debugger "would demonstrate that the primitive level of the instruction set can be hidden from the user" (p. 127). - **Discrepancy (Q6):** the abstract (PDF p. 8) says the language-specific hardware "doubles its performance over a RISC II with the same cycle time". Table 4.6 and p. 71 give a ratio of 1.6. Elsewhere the paper says the language-specific features "approximately double performance" (p. 4), and that register windows and tagged integers "nearly double SOAR's performance" (p. 125). These may measure different things. I record them as stated.

The chips' effective cycle is 510 ns, and the chip ran diagnostics at 800 ns actual system cycle time (Table 3.8 p. 59; p. 127). So the "as fast as a Dorado" claim is a prediction: "the 400 ns NMOS SOAR chips that have been fabricated should run just as fast" (p. 73).

P. Deutsch", p. 68). **SQ18 not met (decided at gate 3c, 2026-10-13):** SQ18 asks for independent evaluations of object-based or capability hardware. # P65

## Reference
Noakes, M. D., Wallach, D. A., Dally, W. J. (1993). *The J-Machine Multicomputer: An Architectural Evaluation*. Proceedings of the 20th Annual International Symposium on Computer Architecture (ISCA '93), pp. 224–235. https://doi.org/10.1145/165123.165158. Screened include under I1 (R0-112); the full text also meets I2 (see Notes).

## Deepest pass
3 (every section, table and figure read; each quantitative claim in the critique checked against the body tables and figures; Figures 3 and 5 read off).

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** Evaluation paper on a working machine: "In this paper we discuss the design of the J-Machine and evaluate the effectiveness of the mechanisms incorporated into the MDP. We measure the performance of the communication and synchronization mechanisms directly and investigate the behavior of four complete applications" (abstract, p. 1); micro-benchmarks (Section 3, p. 3–6), macro-benchmarks (Section 4, p. 6–10), critique (Section 5, p. 11–12).
- **Context:** Argues that "highly-evolved sequential mechanisms are not adequate to support most parallel models of computation", so synchronization, communication and global naming "must be implemented largely in software with prohibitive overhead" (p. 1). Builds on the MDP design paper [5] (Dally et al., IEEE Micro 1992) (p. 1, 12). Compared with nCUBE/2, CM-5, Intel DELTA and Active Messages [17] (Table 1, p. 4), and EM4, KSR, iPSC/860, Delta (Table 3, p. 6).
- **Correctness:** Measurements on a 512-node, 8x8x8 machine at 12.5 MHz (p. 2). The authors caution that speedup curves are "strongly affected by the deﬁnitions of speedup used and the base case" and are "primarily useful in directing attention to interesting trends rather than being of signiﬁcance in themselves" (p. 7–8). The figures for other machines come from published sources whose content is not always clear: "sufﬁcient detail to determine what is being included is rarely provided" (p. 6). The J compiler "currently produces inefﬁcient code", so critical sequences were hand-tuned "to reﬂect the expected future behavior of the compiler" (p. 7).
- **Contributions:** (1) Measured message overhead, latency vs distance and load, terminal bandwidth, producer-consumer and barrier synchronization costs of the MDP (p. 3–6, Tables 1–3, Figures 2–4); (2) profiles of four applications (LCS, Radix Sort, N-Queens, TSP) up to 512 nodes (p. 7–10, Figures 5–6, Tables 4–5); (3) a critique of the mechanisms with proposed fixes: statistics hardware, faster external memory, TLB-based naming, "return-to-sender" flow control, more registers (p. 11–12).
- **Clarity:** Clear and well structured. The PDF's text layer garbles the figures and some table layouts; the page images are legible. No printed page numbers on the preprint.

| Concept | What the paper says | Page |

| Task creation upon message arrival (hardware dispatch) | "When a message arrives at the head of the queue, a task is dispatched to handle it in four processor cycles"; the instruction pointer comes from the message header. | p. 2 |
| Message priorities | Two priorities with separate queues; priority one is preferred in arbitration and may interrupt priority zero; a background priority runs when both queues are empty. | p. 2 |
| Presence tags (cfut, fut) | Data tags marking slots "for values that have not yet been computed"; reading one traps and suspends the thread until the value arrives; fut supports first-class futures. | p. 2, 5 |
| Global name translation (enter, xlate) | Hardware table converting virtual addresses to segment descriptors for a global namespace; judged "inadequate to transparently and inexpensively provide a global name space". | p. 2, 11 |
| Fine-grained communication | Small messages are efficient enough that data need not be sent in large blocks: "In machines lacking efﬁcient communication primitives, one would need to collect and send large blocks of data". | p. 5, 9 |
| One-way message overhead (Ts, Tb) | Fixed send+receive overhead per message and injection overhead per byte, excluding network latency. | p. 4 |
| Terminal network bandwidth | Data rate between two nodes for a given message size; "often becomes the limiting factor" for programs that communicate with neighbours. | p. 5–6 |
| Return-to-sender flow control (proposed) | Back-pressure that "refuses messages when the queue is above a certain threshold by returning them to the sending node". | p. 11 |
| Physically fine-grain machines | Small nodes with little memory each, giving "proportionally better cost/performance while retaining the same total memory capacity". | p. 12 |

# SQ1

## Question
Which computer systems provide sending a message (to an object, actor, process or core) as a primitive below the programming language, that is in the operating system kernel, the instruction set or the hardware, and at which of these levels does each system's message semantics hold, and which systems started message-based at a level and later added paths that are not messages?

## Why it matters to the observation
The observation claims message abstractions stop above the operating system and hardware. This question tests that claim against the systems that tried to go lower, and maps how far down each one got.

## Origin
observation

## Kind
kinds, because the observation's claim is tested by how far down each kind of attempt got and which kinds later added paths that are not messages, not by a catalogue of every kernel with an IPC path: one system of a kind places the message send at the same level, by the same mechanism, as the others of that kind. (`research/sls/1-protocol/step.md`, *How much each question needs*)

Census or kinds is my decision at gate 1c; kinds is recommended. Estimate from `sls/2-search/R0.md`: the 160 papers included through I1 all serve this question (counted as the included rows whose decision names I1; P67 left out, its decision changed to exclude at 3c). Grouping them by the system their title or screening reason names gives about 112 distinct systems, with the L4 family and the Mach family counted once each (about 120 if their variants, such as seL4, Fiasco or Real-Time Mach, count apart). Under census: about 110–120 papers to read from round 0 alone, plus one for each new system a later round finds. Under kinds: round 0 shows about 20 kinds across the three levels, so about 30–40 papers, one or two per kind, then 5 in a row with no new kind.

## Unit
A kind of message-based system: the level where the send is a primitive (an instruction, a hardware or microcode mechanism, or the kernel's own means of communication, as in I1), combined with how the mechanism works. Examples: an object-based processor with port send and receive operations; a message-driven multicomputer node; a many-core chip with on-die message buffers and no coherence; a channel processor; a hardware IPC accelerator for a kernel; a communication coprocessor; a synchronous-IPC microkernel; a port-based microkernel; a capability kernel; a multikernel; a message-based distributed operating system. A paper also adds a new unit if it shows a new kind of path, added later, that is not a message.

## Enough when
At least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 5 in a row add nothing new. 10 + 5 rather than 10 + 3: the systems span four decades and three levels, and a run of kernel papers says nothing about processors.

## Reading order
Levels alternating (instruction set, hardware or microcode mechanism, kernel), and within each level different groups and decades; full designs with an evaluation before position papers and short IPC notes. Start with the seeds and the system papers most other papers build on: the Intel 432 (P10, then P75), the Message-Driven Processor and the J-Machine (P12, P65), the multikernel (P8), L4 (P46, P48). Then: the Single-chip Cloud Computer (P21), KeyKOS and EROS (P53, P77), the Transputer (P96), Spring (P51), Chorus (P200), the ELXSI System 6400, which added shared memory later (P42), the M-Machine (P66), Alewife (P274), the Lisp Machine (P73), hardware IPC support (P159, P221), object and Java processors (P58, P59, P63), QNX (P276), fos and Helios (P102, P45), the message coprocessor and Sylvan (P152, P250). After these, any paper describing a system of a kind not yet covered. Several papers on one system count as one reading for this question (e.g. the L4 family: P46, P48, P172, P188, P204, P233, P251): only the strongest is read for it.

# SQ2

## Question
In the systems found by SQ1, which mechanisms that are not message sends remain (for example shared memory, interrupts, traps, privileged instructions, microcode or global registers), and which levels of each system are written in the system's own objects and messages, and what reasons do the designers give for keeping each one?

## Why it matters to the observation
The observation says systems below the language rest on primitives that break their own rules, so they cannot define themselves. This question finds where each attempt kept such escape routes and how far its self-definition reached.

## Origin
observation

## Kind
kinds, because the observation needs which kinds of escape route below the language remain and why designers kept them; the same few kinds (shared memory, interrupts, traps, privileged instructions, microcode) recur across systems, so listing them per system adds pages, not answers. (`research/sls/1-protocol/step.md`, *How much each question needs*)

Census or kinds is my decision at gate 1c; kinds is recommended, and the choice should follow SQ1's: under census this question reads the same papers as SQ1's census. Estimate from `sls/2-search/R0.md`: every one of the 160 papers included through I1 serves it, since it asks about the systems SQ1 finds; 7 of them name it in their screening reason (P42, P48, P152, P156, P178, P207, P249). Under census: about 110–120 papers from round 0 (one per system, the same set as SQ1's census, and more where the escape routes appear only in a later paper on the same system). Under kinds: about 25–35 papers.

## Unit
A kind of mechanism kept below the language that is not a message send (e.g. shared memory, interrupts, traps, privileged instructions, microcode, global registers), together with the reason given for keeping it; or a kind of level found to be written in the system's own objects and messages. A mechanism already recorded counts as new again only with a reason not yet recorded.

## Enough when

# SQ3

## Question
Which message-based systems below the language level let a component (a proxy, monitor, filter or load balancer) be placed between a sender and a receiver without changing either, by what mechanism, and at what cost?

## Why it matters to the observation
The observation notes that networks allow interposition because parts communicate only through messages, while low-level machines expose shared state where no layer can be put in between. This question asks whether earlier attempts below the language kept that property.

## Origin
observation

## Kind
kinds, because the observation needs the mechanisms by which messages below the language let a component be placed between sender and receiver, and what each costs; which systems have them matters only as examples of each mechanism. (`research/sls/1-protocol/step.md`, *How much each question needs*)

Census or kinds is my decision at gate 1c; kinds is recommended. Estimate from `sls/2-search/R0.md`: 3 included papers name this question in their screening reason (P183, P203, P278); about 10 more are capability, port-based or multiserver kernels where such interposition may be described (P43, P46, P48, P49, P51, P52, P53, P77, P199, P200), counted by the kind of system their screening reason names. Census would have to check every system SQ1 finds, because titles and abstracts rarely say whether a component can be placed in between: about 110–120 papers from round 0, the same set as SQ1's census. Under kinds: about 13–15 papers.

## Unit
A kind of interposition mechanism below the language (e.g. a transparent monitor on the IPC path, a recorder that receives every message, a port or capability that can be redirected to a proxy), with its reported cost. A mechanism already recorded counts as new again if a different cost or limit is reported.

## Enough when
At least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 3 in a row add nothing new.

## Reading order
The three papers whose screening reason names interposition first: transparent monitors on synchronous IPC (P203), the Publishing recorder of all messages (P278), adaptive monitoring in microkernels (P183). Then kinds of system alternating: capability kernels (P53, P77), port-based kernels (P43, P200, P199), synchronous-IPC kernels (P46, P48), Spring's doors (P51), multiserver systems (P52, P49), and processors whose messages go through ports or names the hardware resolves (P10, P12); different decades within each.

# SQ4

## Question
How do operating systems and machines built from message-passing parts that share no state provide protection, scheduling, resource allocation and naming, and which of these functions still rely on a central coordinator, or on replicated parts that must agree, and what does each cost?

## Why it matters to the observation
The notes aim for a system with no central coordinator and leave open how it would provide the functions an operating system normally provides (protection, scheduling, resource allocation). Published systems show which of these have been done without shared state, and which have not.

## Origin
notes

## Kind
evidence, because the question asks how each function is provided, whether it relies on a coordinator or on agreement, and what that costs: findings about functions, not a list of systems. (`research/sls/1-protocol/step.md`, *How much each question needs*)

## Unit
A finding: how one of the four functions (protection, scheduling, resource allocation, naming) is provided in a system of message-passing parts that share no state, whether it relies on a central coordinator or on replicated parts that must agree, or what it costs.

## Enough when
At least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 5 in a row add nothing new. 10 + 5 rather than 10 + 3: four functions, and two eras whose systems differ in kind (distributed message-based operating systems of the 1980s and 1990s, multikernels on one chip since 2009).

## Reading order
Functions and eras alternating, designs with measurements first. Start with the multikernel (P8, replicated state kept by agreement), then capability protection in KeyKOS and EROS (P53, P77), load distribution on microkernels (P167, P194), fos (P102), the Cosmos operating system on the J-Machine (P70), naming in the Lego kernel (P238), Helios (P45), RHODOS process migration (P240), distributed process management on multicores (P230), NLTSS and SHOSHIN (P39, P153), Popcorn Linux (P211, P225), PIKA (P175), StarfishOS (P191), Determinator (P50). Round 0 holds about 22 papers that serve it: 4 name it in their screening reason (P167, P194, P230, P240), the others are multikernel, capability-kernel and distributed message-based operating system papers.

# SQ5

## Question
What performance have message-based or object-based processors, instruction sets and operating system kernels reported against conventional baselines, including the cost of one message send and the scaling with the number of cores, and to what causes are the differences attributed, by whom (the designers or a third party), and is each cause inherent to the design or due to its implementation?

## Why it matters to the observation
The notes cite the Intel 432 and SOAR results and hypothesise that the 432's losses were avoidable (H2) and that many cores without shared state change the picture (H3). This question gathers the measured evidence those hypotheses rest on, and the baselines and metrics later steps can reuse.

## Origin
notes

## Kind
evidence, because the question asks what has been measured and to what causes the differences are attributed: findings (measurements and causes), not a list of systems. (`research/sls/1-protocol/step.md`, *How much each question needs*)

## Unit
A finding: a measurement against a conventional baseline (including the cost of one message send or the scaling with the number of cores), or a cause given for a difference, with who gives it (designers or a third party) and whether it is called inherent to the design or due to its implementation.

## Enough when
At least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 5 in a row add nothing new. 10 + 5 rather than 10 + 3: processors and kernels are measured with different baselines and metrics, across five decades, by designers and by third parties.

## Reading order
Processors and kernels alternating, designers and third parties alternating, measured evaluations first. Start with the Intel 432 evaluations (P10, then the independent P29), the SOAR results (P13, P11), the J-Machine evaluation (P65), L4 IPC (P46, P172), then the argument that IPC cost is becoming irrelevant (P209), Active Messages' evaluation of message-driven machines (P33), the cache effects of microkernel structure (P202), measurements of message-based operating systems (P218, P243), the PEACE kernel on MANNA (P88), the Single-chip Cloud Computer (P21, P104), the multikernel's scaling (P8), hardware IPC support (P159, P221), Lisp machines (P15), and the books on high-level-language and object machines (P1, P76). # SQ7

## Question
What do empirical studies report about the number and kinds of concurrency defects, including deadlocks, message-protocol violations and message-order defects, in programs or systems where each piece of state has one owner and is changed only through messages, compared with programs or systems that share memory?

## Why it matters to the observation
The notes motivate the thesis by the share of concurrency bugs caused by shared state, and already name counter-evidence that message passing causes most blocking bugs in Go. This question collects both sides as published evidence.

## Origin

## Kind
evidence, because the question asks what empirical studies report about defect counts and kinds on both sides: findings (counts, proportions, kinds of defect), not a list of studies. (`research/sls/1-protocol/step.md`, *How much each question needs*)

# SQ8

## Question
What empirical evidence shows that the hardware's execution model, rather than the language, libraries, tools or training, determines how programmers design and write programs, and how correct those programs are?

## Why it matters to the observation
The notes' first premise ("the machine model shapes how programs are written") rests only on two Turing Award lectures, which are essays, not measurements. If the evidence says the language or the runtime decides how people write programs, then changing the hardware does not change the programs on top of it, and the motivation needs another basis.

## Origin
counter-evidence (added by skeptic)

## Kind
evidence, because the question asks what the evidence says about whether the hardware model or the language side shapes programs: findings (measurements, claims, counter-arguments). (`research/sls/1-protocol/step.md`, *How much each question needs*)

A finding: a measurement or argument that the hardware's execution model, or the language, libraries, tools or training, shapes how programs are designed or how correct they are.

## Enough when
At least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 3 in a row add nothing new.

## Reading order
Measurements before essays, hardware side and language side alternating: the large studies of language and defects (P147, P148) alternating with the arguments that hardware is shaped by, or shapes, the language's machine model (P4, P2), then the language-side essay (P3) and Ditzel and Patterson's retrospective (P280). # SQ9

## Question
What evidence and arguments show that narrowing the semantic gap by raising the hardware interface towards the language harms performance, cost, generality or compiler optimisation, and do those arguments apply to a message send as the machine's primitive?

## Why it matters to the observation
The notes treat the semantic gap as a defect to close. The reduced instruction set argument (Patterson and Ditzel, 1980, *The Case for the Reduced Instruction Set Computer*) was made against exactly that goal. If its reasoning carries over to message sends, the observation describes a deliberate trade-off, not an oversight.

# SQ10

## Question
What does the literature report about the equivalence (duality) of message-passing and shared-memory system structures, and can either one be built on top of the other while keeping its properties (encapsulation, freedom from data races, interposition) and its performance?

## Why it matters to the observation
Lauer and Needham (1978/1979, *On the Duality of Operating System Structures*) argue that message-oriented and procedure-oriented systems are duals: a problem solved in one has a dual solution in the other. If the two are equivalent, the observation's gap may be a matter of which layer exposes which model, and putting messages in hardware may add nothing that a layer above cannot give.

## Origin
counter-evidence (added by skeptic)

evidence, because the question asks what the literature reports about equivalence and about building one model on the other: findings (proofs, arguments, measurements), not a list of systems. (`research/sls/1-protocol/step.md`, *How much each question needs*)

Why do developers of actor or message-passing programs also use shared state, locks or other concurrency mechanisms alongside messages, and what do they report that the pure message model cannot express or costs too much?

The observation wants a system with no escape routes from its own rules. Tasharofi, Dinges and Johnson (2013, *Why Do Scala Developers Mix the Actor Model with other Concurrency Models?*, ECOOP) report that most of the large actor programs they studied mix actors with other concurrency models, partly because of shortcomings of the actor model itself. # P48

## Reference
Kevin Elphinstone, Gernot Heiser (2013). *From L3 to seL4: What Have We Learnt in 20 Years of L4 Microkernels?* Proceedings of the 24th ACM Symposium on Operating Systems Principles (SOSP '13), Farmington, PA, USA, pp. 133–150. https://doi.org/10.1145/2517349.2522720. P48, round-file row R0-065, included at screening under I1.

Version: the proceedings version (ACM copyright block and DOI on p.133), downloaded from sigops.org (`https://www.sigops.org/s/conferences/sosp/2013/papers/p133-elphinstone.pdf`) and saved as `papers/P48.pdf`. Its 18 PDF pages carry the printed proceedings page numbers 133–150, so the offset is 132 (PDF page 1 = p.133). All pages cited below are the printed ones. The body runs pp.133–147 and the references pp.147–150.

## Deepest pass
2

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** A retrospective by two of the system's designers. It reviews 20 years of design and implementation decisions across the L4 microkernel family, from L3 to seL4, and reports which were "Retained", "Replaced", "Abandoned", "Added" or remain "Unresolved" (pp.133, 136–147). It reports a few measurements (Table 1, p.135; pp.137, 140, 146), but it is not an evaluation paper.
- **Context:** Liedtke's L4 papers [Liedtke 1993a, p.133; 1995, p.136] and the "microkernel minimality principle" (p.136); the early-1990s IPC cost problem [Condict et al. 1994; Chen and Bershad 1993] (p.133); EROS and capabilities (pp.135, 138); seL4 verification [Klein et al. 2009] (p.133) and WCET analysis [Blackham et al. 2011] (p.135); the multikernel [Baumann et al. 2009] (pp.133, 143).
- **Correctness:** The main assumption is that IPC latency counted in cycles can be compared across very different processors. The authors hedge this themselves: "as far as comparisons across vastly different ISAs and micro architectures have any validity" (p.147). Most "lessons" are argued from the authors' own experience rather than measured. The few numbers are partly taken from cited work (Warton 2005, Nourai 2005, Liedtke 1993a; pp.138, 144).
- **Contributions:** (1) A history and family tree of L4 kernels (Fig. 1, p.134; pp.133–135). (2) One-way IPC cost across eleven kernel and processor pairs from 1993 to 2013 (Table 1, p.135) and kernel sizes (Table 2, p.136). (3) A verdict on each original L4 design principle and implementation trick (Sections 3–4, pp.136–146). (4) The conclusion that "the most general principles behind L4, minimality (including running device drivers at user level) and a strong focus on performance, still remain relevant" (p.147).
- **Clarity:** Clearly written. Each subsection ends with a boxed verdict (e.g. "Abandoned: Long IPC.", p.138). The measurement method behind Table 1 is not described.

| Microkernel minimality principle (new) | "A concept is tolerated inside the µ-kernel only if moving it outside the kernel, i.e. permitting competing implementations, would prevent the implementation of the system's required functionality" [Liedtke 1995]; "Retained" as the key design principle. | p.136 |
| Synchronous (rendezvous-style) IPC (new) | The original L4's "only communication, synchronisation, and signalling mechanism"; avoids kernel buffering; "Replaced" by synchronous IPC augmented with, or replaced by, asynchronous notification. | pp.136–137 |
| Asynchronous endpoint / notification (new) | A single-word notification field; a send ORs a bit mask into it, and the receiver blocks or polls; "similar to multiple binary semaphores allocated within a single word". | pp.136–137 |
| Virtual message registers (new) | A configurable set of 16–64 message registers, some physical and the rest in a pinned per-thread memory area. | p.137 |
| Long IPC (new) | Multi-buffer messages copied by the kernel through a temporary mapping window; "Abandoned" because of complexity and verification, with shared buffers used instead. | pp.137–138 |
| IPC endpoint (port-like) (new) | A kernel object that holds the queue of pending senders or receivers and is the message destination instead of a thread ID; no buffering. | p.138 |
| Clans and chiefs (new) | Kernel redirection of messages that cross a clan boundary to the clan's chief; supports confinement; "Abandoned". | p.139 |
| User-level device drivers / interrupts as IPC (new) | Drivers are user processes, and interrupts are "IPC messages, which the kernel sends to the driver"; "Retained". | p.139 |
| Recursive page mappings / mapping database (new) | Authority over frames comes from existing mappings, established through IPC (map, grant, unmap); needs a mapping database. | pp.140–141 |
| Untyped memory and retype (seL4 kernel memory model) (new) | All kernel memory is subject to capabilities; "Retyping is the only way to create objects in seL4"; capability derivation tree; called "seL4's main contribution to OS design". | pp.141–142 |
| Event-based (single-stack) kernel (new) | One kernel stack with continuations instead of one stack per thread; "Replaced: Process kernel by event kernel in seL4, OKL4 and NOVA". | p.144 |
| Lazy scheduling / Benno scheduling (new) | Lazy: blocked threads are left in the ready queue. Benno: the ready queue holds all runnable threads except the running one, which gives a bounded WCET. | pp.144–145 |
| Direct process switch (new) | On IPC the kernel switches straight to the partner thread on the caller's time slice; "a form of time-slice donation". | p.145 |
| Clustered multikernel (new) | A big-lock kernel across cores sharing an L2 cache, combined with a restricted multikernel (no memory migration between kernels). | p.143 |
| IPC fast path (new) | Hand-optimised common-case IPC code, once in assembler and in seL4 in C; it achieves 188 cycles on ARM11. | p.146 |

- **Source read:** full text, proceedings version (printed pp.133–150), from `https://www.sigops.org/s/conferences/sosp/2013/papers/p133-elphinstone.pdf`, saved as `papers/P48.pdf`. The ACM DL PDF returned HTTP 403. All of the body (pp.133–147) was read, including Tables 1–3 and Figure 1, plus the start of the reference list. The cited works (Warton 2005, Nourai 2005, Liedtke 1993a/1995, Blackham and Heiser 2012) were not checked. Deepest pass: 2 (every section, table and figure read; no reconstruction or checking of the cited measurements).
- **Criterion:** I1(c) is confirmed. The paper names IPC and message passing as the means by which user code obtains kernel-level system services: "User code obtains a system service by communicating with servers via an inter-process communication (IPC) mechanism, typically message passing" (p.133). The family consists of microkernels (pp.133–135). No exclusion criterion appears to apply: X2 and X3 do not apply because the message mechanism is the kernel's (p.133), and X9 does not apply because the paper is a retrospective with its own measurements and reasons (pp.135, 146). **Possible additional criterion, I4:** the paper gives reasons for using non-message mechanisms inside a message-based system, which may answer an SQ on model mixing (SQ11 per the form's *Serves* column). I could not check this, because the SQ files were not among my inputs. The evidence: shared buffers "are generally preferred for bulk data transfer" over long IPC (p.137); asynchronous notifications were added because synchronous-only IPC "forces a multi-threaded design onto otherwise simple systems" (p.136); NOVA added counting semaphores (p.137); OKL4 channels (p.138). The multicore discussion (p.143) may also bear on SQ13/SQ14. If I4 is added, *Model mixing* should be filled from these pages. **I4 (follow-up pass, gate 3c 2026-10-13): SQ11, SQ15.** SQ11: the paper reports why the builders of a message-based (IPC) system use shared buffers, notifications, semaphores and timers alongside synchronous IPC, and what the pure model could not express or cost (pp.136–139); the evidence is the designers' experience, not a developer study. SQ15: the paper argues which form of scheduling coordination suits which multicore ("a global scheduler makes more sense" on embedded multicores, p.143), what the restricted multikernel gives up ("no memory migration is permitted between kernels", p.143), that exporting scheduling policy from the kernel has failed (p.143), and that thread-ID naming pushed servers towards a bottleneck "gateway thread" (p.138); this is argument, not measurement. Not answered: SQ8, SQ9, SQ10, SQ13, SQ16, SQ18, SQ19 (no relevant content); SQ12 (p.137 attributes IPC cost to "the architectural costs of context switching", but for kernel IPC, not actor or message runtimes); SQ14 (p.143 argues a big lock is acceptable "at least for a small number of cores sharing an L2", with no many-core evidence); SQ17 (para-virtualized Linux, p.133, and IOMMU pass-through, p.139, are mentioned without coverage or cost compared with message interposition).
- **Abstract:** in the PDF text layer, the abstract ("The L4 microkernel has undergone 20 years of use and evolution ...") sits in the right column of p.133. Its only claim is: "We demonstrate that while much has changed, the fundamental principles of minimality and high IPC performance remain the main drivers of design and implementation decisions" (p.133).
- **Table 1 provenance:** the paper does not say whether the authors measured all eleven rows themselves or took them from the original publications. It thanks "Adrian Danis for some last-minute seL4 optimisations and measurements" (p.147), which suggests the 2013 seL4 rows are the authors' own (inferred).
- **Kernel sizes (Table 2, p.136), in kSLOC C/C++ + asm = total:** Original (486) 0 + 6.4 = 6.4; L4/Alpha 0 + 14.2 = 14.2; L4/MIPS 6.0 + 4.5 = 10.5; Hazelnut (x86) 10.0 + 0.8 = 10.8; Pistachio (x86) 22.4 + 1.4 = 23.0; L4-embedded (ARMv5) 7.6 + 1.4 = 9.0; OKL4 3.0 (ARMv6) 15.0 + 0.0 = 15.0; Fiasco.OC (x86) 36.2 + 1.1 = 37.6; seL4 (ARMv6) 9.7 + 0.5 = 10.2.

# P102

## Reference
David Wentzlaff, Anant Agarwal (2009). *Factored Operating Systems (fos): The Case for a Scalable Operating System for Multicores*. ACM SIGOPS Operating Systems Review 43(2), pp. 76–85. https://doi.org/10.1145/1531793.1531805

## Deepest pass
2

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** A position and design paper with motivating measurements. It argues that SMP operating systems cannot scale to "1000+ core systems" (p. 2), measures two Linux scaling problems (p. 3–4), and describes the design of a new message-passing OS (fos) whose prototype is "under active development" (p. 2, p. 8). fos itself is not evaluated.
- **Context:** Microkernels (Mach, L3, L4; p. 2, p. 8), scalable shared-memory kernels (Tornado/K42, Hive, Disco/Cellular Disco, Corey; p. 9), distributed OSes (Amoeba, Sprite, Clouds; p. 9) and distributed Internet services (DNS, BitTorrent, Chord, AFS, GFS; p. 9–10). The authors' own Raw and Tilera on-chip networks are cited for message costs (p. 8).
- **Correctness:** The Linux measurements are on real hardware (p. 3), and the cache study runs in a QEMU-based simulator (p. 4). The case for fos rests on argument, for example "We believe that the shared nothing, message passing only, approach will encourage OS developers to think very carefully about exactly what data is being shared, which will lead to more scalability" (p. 5). The paper names its own open questions in Section 3.4 (p. 8).
- **Contributions:** (1) A measurement showing that the Linux 2.6.24.7 physical page allocator "does not scale beyond 8 cores under heavy load" (p. 2, Fig. 1 p. 3). (2) A simulated measurement of OS/application cache interference on Apache2 (p. 4). (3) Three recommendations: avoid hardware locks, separate OS from application cores, and avoid global cache-coherent shared memory (p. 5). (4) The fos design: a microkernel with mailbox messaging, OS services split into fleets of servers bound to cores, a name server, and space multiplexing instead of time multiplexing (p. 5–7).
- **Clarity:** Well structured and readable. The figure labels in the author PDF use an odd font encoding (the text cannot be extracted), but the rendered figures are legible. The message format is not described.

## Quality
| Q | Answer | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | yes | The abstract and introduction say so in one place: "This work investigates why simply scaling up traditional symmetric multiprocessor operating systems is not sufficient ... and proposes how to build a factored operating system (fos)" (p. 1). |
| Q2 | partly | Receiver naming (symbolic mailbox names, name cache, name server; p. 6), delivery ("reliable messaging layer", p. 6) and busy receiver ("If a receive mailbox is full, the sending client send call returns an error", p. 6) are described. Message format and ordering are not. |
| Q3 | no | The claims about fos rest on design and argument. The prototype is only said to boot (p. 8). The Linux studies used to motivate it are measured on hardware (p. 3) and simulated (p. 4), but they do not evaluate fos. |
| Q4 | partly | The Linux allocator scaling is judged against a hypothetical baseline ("perfect scaling would be bars all the same height", p. 3). The fos claims against Mach, L4 and K42 (p. 8–9) are not measured. |
| Q5 | partly | Workloads and hardware or simulator configurations are given (p. 3, p. 4), and the allocator workload is partly justified (p. 4). The number of runs is not reported. |
| Q6 | yes | The only quantitative claims in the abstract and conclusion are core-count projections ("100's to 1,000's of cores", "double every 18 months"). Body text repeats them as the authors' own extrapolation, with no citation of their own. Only the transistor trend behind them is cited: "The ITRS road-map[1] and the continuation of Moore's Law[16] forecast exponential increases in the number of transistors" (p. 1–2). |
| Q7 | partly | Lock contention is isolated by an oprofile breakdown by function (Fig. 1, p. 3). Interference misses are isolated by simulating separate OS-only and application-only caches (p. 4). The architectural overhead is only "believed to be caused by contention in the hardware memory system" (p. 3). The causes of fos's expected benefits are asserted only (p. 7–9). |
| Q8 | yes | Section 3.4 *Challenges* (p. 8) is dedicated to open questions and costs, such as core-to-core latency, shared structures like the buffer cache, lock servers, and multi-sequence operations. |
| Q9 | no | Both authors design fos (p. 1–2), and the paper does not evaluate fos. The Linux systems measured are third-party, but they are only motivating baselines. |

## Extracted fields
| Field | Value | Page |
|---|---|---|
| Reference | Wentzlaff & Agarwal (2009), ACM SIGOPS OSR 43(2): 76–85 (range from Crossref). P102. Included under I1 (I1(c): kernel services communicate by messages). I4 (follow-up pass, gate 3c 2026-10-13): SQ14 (p. 2–5, 8, 9), SQ15 (p. 5, 8). Version read: the author preprint, marked "To appear in ACM SIGOPS Operating System Review ... April 2009", 11 PDF pages with no page numbers printed. Pages below are PDF pages of `papers/P102.pdf`. The publisher's layout was not seen, so no offset is established (75 is likely (inferred), not verified). | p. 1 |
| Paper type | Position or analytical argument (p. 1–2, p. 5); design (fos, p. 5–7); evaluation of a third-party system (Linux scaling and cache studies, p. 3–4); implementation status only, not described in detail (p. 8) | p. 1–8 |
| System | **fos** (factored operating system). Built at MIT CSAIL by Wentzlaff and Agarwal (p. 1); Charles Gruenwald thanked "for help on fos" (p. 10). Year: under development at writing, 2009 (inferred from the venue date). Status: running kernel, partial prototype: "fos is currently booting on 16 core x86_64 hardware and a QEMU simulation of up to 255 processors ... currently consists of a bootloader, microkernel, messaging layer with capability checking, and name server. We are beginning to implement OS Layer servers." **Linux 2.6.24.7** and **Linux 2.6.18.8** (third-party, deployed) are measured as motivating cases (p. 3, p. 4). | p. 1, 3, 4, 8, 10 |
| Levels with message semantics | **Hardware:** not stated for fos in general. fos "does not require architectures to support intra-machine shared memory" (p. 9). On the x86_64 prototype, no (inferred): the paper says "shared memory is the only means by which a desktop hardware architecture allows core-to-core communication" (p. 4), and messages travel "via on-chip networks or shared memory" (p. 6). **Microcode:** not stated. **Instruction set:** not stated. **Kernel, between cores:** partly. "Servers communicate only via the messaging interface provided by the microkernel layer" and "The OS layer does not internally utilize shared memory" (p. 6). The microkernel and its delegated name and privilege servers "communicate via microkernel messaging" (p. 7). Message-only operations: application-to-OS-service requests, server-to-server and fleet traffic, and microkernel-to-delegated-service traffic (p. 6–7). Other paths: applications may share memory between their own cores "if the underlying hardware supports it" (p. 6), and the message transport itself may use shared memory (p. 6). **Kernel, within a core:** partly. System calls are turned into messages: "A small translation library is used to turn system calls into messages from application to an OS layer server" (p. 6). The send itself is a call into the local microkernel ("The message proxy library calls the fos-microkernel to send the message", p. 6). Traps and interrupts: not stated. **Runtime:** a message proxy library on the application side (p. 6). **Language:** not stated. **Started message-based and later added other paths:** not stated (design-stage paper). | p. 4, 6, 7, 9 |
| Receiving unit and state ownership | The unit is a receive mailbox owned by a "fos client", which is "The code executing on a single core under the fos-microkernel" (p. 6). Each client "can allocate a large number of receive mailboxes" (p. 6). A server is "bound to a core" (p. 5) and "executes solely on a dedicated processor core" (p. 6). State: OS-layer servers do not share memory: "the servers which provide the file system and the virtual memory management do not share memory with each other" (p. 8). Mailbox buffers "live in the receiving client's address space" (p. 8), so the microkernel writes into them (inferred: "The receive microkernel deposits message in the file system server's request mailbox", p. 6). Applications may share memory among their own cores (p. 6). | p. 5, 6, 8 |
| Message mechanism | **Sync/async:** asynchronous. "send routines and receive routines do not need to be synchronized like in the L4 operating system ... The use of large input mailboxes decouples send and receive synchronization" (p. 8). **Naming:** "Clients can attach symbolic names to their receive mailboxes and publish these names"; "fos clients send messages to named mailboxes" (p. 6). The microkernel keeps a name cache and delegates lookups to the name server fleet, which "maintains the canonical mailbox name to physical core and mailbox directory" (p. 6). Names can map one-to-many, with the server instance chosen "based off of physical proximity or load balancing" (p. 6). Namespace "can be protected" (p. 6), and the messaging layer has "capability checking" (p. 8). **Delivery:** "reliable transport and enqueuing" (p. 6); "on-chip communications are considered to be reliable" (p. 6). **Ordering:** not stated. **Buffering:** "large buffers which live in the receiving client's address space" (p. 8). **Busy receiver:** "If a receive mailbox is full, the sending client send call returns an error" (p. 6). **Dispatch:** a server has two inbound mailboxes, one for new requests and one for responses, and "prioritizes responses over requests". It is cooperative and non-preemptive; a long-latency operation stores a continuation, and processing yields to the next transaction (p. 7, Fig. 6). Most servers use "stateless protocols" (p. 7). | p. 6, 7, 8 |
| Non-message primitives | (1) **Application shared memory** at the application level, "if the underlying hardware supports it". Reason: "While coherent shared memory may be inherently unscalable in the large, in a small application, it can be quite useful" (p. 6). (2) **Shared memory as message transport** in the microkernel: "transport the message ... via on-chip networks or shared memory". Reason: not stated (p. 6). (3) **Microkernel name cache** and **read-only privilege cache** inside the microkernel. Reason: "fast name lookups and a large namespace at the same time" (p. 6); privileges cached "in a read only manner" (p. 7). (4) **Static privileges** given to privilege-manager servers by the microkernel, "so that a privilege fixed point can be reached" (p. 7). (5) **Fixed knowledge of physical location** of delegated services in the microkernel, "In order to prevent dependency cycles" (p. 7). (6) **Hardware locking instructions:** not used: "if a lock is absolutely necessary, hardware locking instructions are not used as servers are not preempted" (p. 7). Interrupts, direct memory access, I/O ports: not stated. | p. 6, 7 |
| Self-definition | OS services (naming, privilege, memory allocation, file system, scheduling) are written as servers communicating by microkernel messages (p. 6–7). The microkernel is outside that model. It "is platform dependent, provides protection mechanisms but not protection policy, and implements a fast machine-dependent communication infrastructure" (p. 2), and "controls access to resources (protection), provides a communication API and code spawning API ... and maintains a name cache" (p. 5). Implementation language: not stated. Whether a running program can inspect or change these levels: not stated. Cost of the base: not stated. | p. 2, 5, 6, 7 |
| Interposition | Not stated as such. The name server "allows for redirection of mailboxes if a client changes physical location" and "provides a one-to-many mapping function" (p. 6), which may allow a component to be placed behind a published name without changing the sender (inferred). The translation library sits between the application's system-call interface and OS servers (p. 6). Cost: not stated. | p. 6 |
| Operating system functions | **Protection:** microkernel mechanisms plus a privilege service "implemented as a fleet of servers in the OS layer", cached in the microkernel and invalidated by message (p. 7); namespace protection (p. 6); capability checking (p. 8). Central component: no single component is stated. Whether privilege servers must agree: not stated. **Scheduling:** "a fleet which manages process scheduling and layout" (p. 6); "Scheduling becomes a layout problem not a time multiplexing problem" (p. 5); "spatially aware placement engine/scheduler" (p. 2). Central: not stated. **Resource allocation:** "a fleet which manages physical memory allocation" (p. 6). Devices: the OS layer provides "management of system resources such as cores, memory, and input-output devices" (p. 6), with no mechanism given. Central: not stated. **Naming:** the name server fleet holds "the canonical mailbox name to physical core and mailbox directory", cached per microkernel (p. 6), inspired by "the hierarchical caching in the Internet's DNS system" (p. 9). Central: not stated (a canonical directory over a fleet implies coordination (inferred)). **Failure handling:** "broken servers can be steered away from when a fault is detected"; "fos is primarily focused on scalability and not fault tolerance" (p. 6). **Cost of decentralising:** "Writing fos servers can be more challenging than writing traditional shared memory operating system subsystems" (p. 5); in message passing "the destination of any piece of data must be known when a message is sent" (p. 8); for lock servers, "the cost of software-based lock management may dwarf the performance wins of removing traditional locks" (p. 8); whether shared structures like the buffer cache perform well is an "open question" (p. 8). I4 additions (SQ15): coordination is still needed where atomicity is: "synchronization points are still needed to guarantee exclusive access to certain structures when atomicity is required" (p. 8). It is met by a lock-owning server (one coordinator per lock (inferred)) or by "a core as a object server or transaction server"; "By serializing transactions against a transaction server, fos can take advantage of optimistic concurrency" (p. 8). The authors "believe that the cost of using notional locks will affect the design of fos's servers such that notional locks will only be used in rare circumstances" (p. 8). Whether every multi-sequence operation can avoid local locks: "it is not certain that all cases can be handled" (p. 8). | p. 2, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 |
| Cost of message primitives | Not measured for fos. The paper cites figures from other systems: "Typical context switch times are in the 100 cycle to 300 cycle range on modern processors" (no source given), and on Raw and Tilera "the cost of core-to-core dynamic messages is on the order of 15 - 45 cycles depending on distance" ([21, 24, 25]). Tag: design figure (cited, not measured in this paper). | p. 8 |

| fleet (new) | The set of servers of one type that together provide one OS function, e.g. physical memory allocation, file system, scheduling | p. 6 |
| fos client (new) | "The code executing on a single core under the fos-microkernel"; applications and OS servers "act as peers" | p. 6 |
| receive mailbox (new) | A named, protected endpoint owned by a client, with a large buffer in the receiver's address space; a send to a full mailbox returns an error | p. 6, 8 |
| message proxy library / translation library (new) | Turns a traditional system call into a message to an OS-layer server and unpacks the reply | p. 6–7 |
| microkernel to OS layer delegation (new) | The microkernel delegates naming and privilege to OS-layer fleets, caches their answers, and avoids cycles by knowing the delegates' locations and granting static privileges ("privilege fixed point") | p. 7 |
| stateless, transaction-oriented server with continuations (new) | A server processes each transaction to completion without preemption, stores a continuation for long-latency operations, and needs no local locking | p. 7 |
| notional lock / lock server (new) | A lock held by a server and acquired by message; "the cost of software-based lock management may dwarf the performance wins of removing traditional locks" | p. 8 |
| OS-application and OS-OS locality aliasing (new) | OS and application working sets competing for implicitly shared caches and TLBs on one core, including "anti-locality cache collisions" | p. 4 |
| best-effort OS interfaces (new) | Interfaces that return information "which may be slightly out of date" for higher performance, with an accurate but slower alternative | p. 2 |
