=== SQ1.md
## Question
Which computer systems provide sending a message (to an object, actor, process or core) as a primitive below the programming language, that is in the operating system kernel, the instruction set or the hardware, and at which of these levels does each system's message semantics hold, and which systems started message-based at a level and later added paths that are not messages?

## Unit
A kind of message-based system: the level where the send is a primitive (an instruction, a hardware or microcode mechanism, or the kernel's own means of communication, as in I1), combined with how the mechanism works. Examples: an object-based processor with port send and receive operations; a message-driven multicomputer node; a many-core chip with on-die message buffers and no coherence; a channel processor; a hardware IPC accelerator for a kernel; a communication coprocessor; a synchronous-IPC microkernel; a port-based microkernel; a capability kernel; a multikernel; a message-based distributed operating system. A paper also adds a new unit if it shows a new kind of path, added later, that is not a message.

## Enough when
At least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 5 in a row add nothing new. 10 + 5 rather than 10 + 3: the systems span four decades and three levels, and a run of kernel papers says nothing about processors.

## Reading order
Levels alternating (instruction set, hardware or microcode mechanism, kernel), and within each level different groups and decades; full designs with an evaluation before position papers and short IPC notes. Start with the seeds and the system papers most other papers build on: the Intel 432 (P10, then P75), the Message-Driven Processor and the J-Machine (P12, P65), the multikernel (P8), L4 (P46, P48). Then: the Single-chip Cloud Computer (P21), KeyKOS and EROS (P53, P77), the Transputer (P96), Spring (P51), Chorus (P200), the ELXSI System 6400, which added shared memory later (P42), the M-Machine (P66), Alewife (P274), the Lisp Machine (P73), hardware IPC support (P159, P221), object and Java processors (P58, P59, P63), QNX (P276), fos and Helios (P102, P45), the message coprocessor and Sylvan (P152, P250). After these, any paper describing a system of a kind not yet covered. Several papers on one system count as one reading for this question (e.g. the L4 family: P46, P48, P172, P188, P204, P233, P251): only the strongest is read for it.

=== SQ2.md
## Question
In the systems found by SQ1, which mechanisms that are not message sends remain (for example shared memory, interrupts, traps, privileged instructions, microcode or global registers), and which levels of each system are written in the system's own objects and messages, and what reasons do the designers give for keeping each one?

## Unit
A kind of mechanism kept below the language that is not a message send (e.g. shared memory, interrupts, traps, privileged instructions, microcode, global registers), together with the reason given for keeping it; or a kind of level found to be written in the system's own objects and messages. A mechanism already recorded counts as new again only with a reason not yet recorded.

## Enough when
At least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 5 in a row add nothing new. 10 + 5 rather than 10 + 3: as for SQ1, the systems span four decades and three levels, and the escape routes of a processor differ from those of a kernel.

## Reading order
Papers whose screening reason names an escape route first: the ELXSI System 6400 adding shared memory (P42), shared queues between host and message coprocessor (P152), messaging and interrupt mechanisms of a microkernel (P156), in-kernel synchronisation in a scalable microkernel (P178), signals and shared memory between cores (P207), servers moved into the Mach kernel (P249), and twenty years of L4 lessons (P48). Then processors (P10, P12 or P65, P21 or P104, P66, P73) alternating with kernels (P8, P53, P77, P51, P200), across decades. Design retrospectives and lessons-learned papers before papers on a single mechanism.

=== SQ3.md
## Question
Which message-based systems below the language level let a component (a proxy, monitor, filter or load balancer) be placed between a sender and a receiver without changing either, by what mechanism, and at what cost?

## Unit
A kind of interposition mechanism below the language (e.g. a transparent monitor on the IPC path, a recorder that receives every message, a port or capability that can be redirected to a proxy), with its reported cost. A mechanism already recorded counts as new again if a different cost or limit is reported.

## Enough when
At least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 3 in a row add nothing new.

## Reading order
The three papers whose screening reason names interposition first: transparent monitors on synchronous IPC (P203), the Publishing recorder of all messages (P278), adaptive monitoring in microkernels (P183). Then kinds of system alternating: capability kernels (P53, P77), port-based kernels (P43, P200, P199), synchronous-IPC kernels (P46, P48), Spring's doors (P51), multiserver systems (P52, P49), and processors whose messages go through ports or names the hardware resolves (P10, P12); different decades within each.

=== SQ4.md
## Question
How do operating systems and machines built from message-passing parts that share no state provide protection, scheduling, resource allocation and naming, and which of these functions still rely on a central coordinator, or on replicated parts that must agree, and what does each cost?

## Unit
A finding: how one of the four functions (protection, scheduling, resource allocation, naming) is provided in a system of message-passing parts that share no state, whether it relies on a central coordinator or on replicated parts that must agree, or what it costs.

## Enough when
At least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 5 in a row add nothing new. 10 + 5 rather than 10 + 3: four functions, and two eras whose systems differ in kind (distributed message-based operating systems of the 1980s and 1990s, multikernels on one chip since 2009).

## Reading order
Functions and eras alternating, designs with measurements first. Start with the multikernel (P8, replicated state kept by agreement), then capability protection in KeyKOS and EROS (P53, P77), load distribution on microkernels (P167, P194), fos (P102), the Cosmos operating system on the J-Machine (P70), naming in the Lego kernel (P238), Helios (P45), RHODOS process migration (P240), distributed process management on multicores (P230), NLTSS and SHOSHIN (P39, P153), Popcorn Linux (P211, P225), PIKA (P175), StarfishOS (P191), Determinator (P50). Round 0 holds about 22 papers that serve it: 4 name it in their screening reason (P167, P194, P230, P240), the others are multikernel, capability-kernel and distributed message-based operating system papers.

=== SQ5.md
## Question
What performance have message-based or object-based processors, instruction sets and operating system kernels reported against conventional baselines, including the cost of one message send and the scaling with the number of cores, and to what causes are the differences attributed, by whom (the designers or a third party), and is each cause inherent to the design or due to its implementation?

## Unit
A finding: a measurement against a conventional baseline (including the cost of one message send or the scaling with the number of cores), or a cause given for a difference, with who gives it (designers or a third party) and whether it is called inherent to the design or due to its implementation.

## Enough when
At least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 5 in a row add nothing new. 10 + 5 rather than 10 + 3: processors and kernels are measured with different baselines and metrics, across five decades, by designers and by third parties.

## Reading order
Processors and kernels alternating, designers and third parties alternating, measured evaluations first. Start with the Intel 432 evaluations (P10, then the independent P29), the SOAR results (P13, P11), the J-Machine evaluation (P65), L4 IPC (P46, P172), then the argument that IPC cost is becoming irrelevant (P209), Active Messages' evaluation of message-driven machines (P33), the cache effects of microkernel structure (P202), measurements of message-based operating systems (P218, P243), the PEACE kernel on MANNA (P88), the Single-chip Cloud Computer (P21, P104), the multikernel's scaling (P8), hardware IPC support (P159, P221), Lisp machines (P15), and the books on high-level-language and object machines (P1, P76). Round 0 holds about 45 papers that serve it: the 13 included through I2, and about 30 processor and kernel papers whose screening reason names measured IPC or message cost or this question.

=== SQ6.md
## Question
According to their designers and to later evaluations, why were language-directed, object-based and message-based machines abandoned, not adopted, or made unnecessary?

## Unit
A finding: a reason stated for a machine being abandoned, not adopted, or made unnecessary, with who states it (its designers or a later evaluation).

## Enough when
At least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 5 in a row add nothing new. 10 + 5 rather than 10 + 3: each family of machines (capability processors, Lisp machines, Smalltalk processors, message-driven multicomputers) declined for its own reasons, so three papers on one family can add nothing while another family is still unread.

## Reading order
Machine families alternating, designers' retrospectives alternating with later evaluations, strongest first. Start with Ditzel and Patterson's retrospective on high-level-language machines (P280), the Intel 432 (P10, then P29), Lisp machines (P15), SOAR (P13), the compiler techniques that made special hardware unnecessary (P14, P60), message-driven machines (P33, P70), then the books (P1, P76, P72), the history of RISC (P84), the IBM Workplace OS experience (P189) and the ELXSI System 6400 (P42). Round 0 holds about 16 papers that serve it: the 13 included through I2 and the papers named above whose screening reason gives a reason for decline.

=== SQ7.md
## Question
What do empirical studies report about the number and kinds of concurrency defects, including deadlocks, message-protocol violations and message-order defects, in programs or systems where each piece of state has one owner and is changed only through messages, compared with programs or systems that share memory?

## Unit
A finding: a count or proportion of concurrency defects of a kind (e.g. deadlock, message-protocol violation, message-order defect, data race) reported for message-passing or for shared-memory programs, or a comparison between them.

## Enough when
At least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 3 in a row add nothing new.

## Reading order
Both sides alternating: the study that splits the same programs by mechanism first (Go, P9), then the shared-memory baseline (P5), actor bugs (P78), Go channel bugs (P79), then new studies from later rounds, message-passing and shared-memory in turn, different languages and decades. Round 0 holds only these 4 serving papers (the I3 includes), fewer than the 10 the rule needs: all are read, and the question stays open until later rounds bring more.

=== SQ8.md
## Question
What empirical evidence shows that the hardware's execution model, rather than the language, libraries, tools or training, determines how programmers design and write programs, and how correct those programs are?

## Unit
A finding: a measurement or argument that the hardware's execution model, or the language, libraries, tools or training, shapes how programs are designed or how correct they are.

## Enough when
At least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 3 in a row add nothing new.

## Reading order
Measurements before essays, hardware side and language side alternating: the large studies of language and defects (P147, P148) alternating with the arguments that hardware is shaped by, or shapes, the language's machine model (P4, P2), then the language-side essay (P3) and Ditzel and Patterson's retrospective (P280). Round 0 holds only these 6 serving papers, fewer than the 10 the rule needs: all are read, and the question stays open until later rounds bring more.

=== SQ9.md
## Question
What evidence and arguments show that narrowing the semantic gap by raising the hardware interface towards the language harms performance, cost, generality or compiler optimisation, and do those arguments apply to a message send as the machine's primitive?

## Unit
A finding: a measurement or argument that raising the hardware interface towards the language harms, or does not harm, performance, cost, generality or compiler optimisation, or a statement of whether such an argument applies to a message send or method dispatch.

## Enough when
At least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 3 in a row add nothing new.

## Reading order
Both sides alternating, measured comparisons first. Against raising the interface: the RISC case (P17), Hennessy (P85), the VAX-11 and RISC I comparison (P81), the M68000 complex instructions study (P263), instruction-set complexity and memory (P264). For it: the argument for language-directed architectures (P257), the architecture closing the gap to the user interface (P265), hardware support for interpreters (P266), adaptive interpretation (P256), the semantic-gap instruction set thesis (P258). Then the papers closest to a message send or method dispatch: SOAR (P11, P261), SELF's compiler (P14), whether object-oriented languages need special hardware (P60), C and the hardware's machine model (P4), end-to-end arguments (P7), Lisp (P15), and Ditzel and Patterson's retrospective (P280). Round 0 holds 25 papers that serve it (counted as the included rows whose screening reason names this question).

=== SQ10.md
## Question
What does the literature report about the equivalence (duality) of message-passing and shared-memory system structures, and can either one be built on top of the other while keeping its properties (encapsulation, freedom from data races, interposition) and its performance?

## Unit
A finding: a result or argument on the equivalence of the two structures, or a report of one model built on the other, with which properties (encapsulation, freedom from data races, interposition) and how much performance it keeps or loses.

## Enough when
At least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 5 in a row add nothing new. 10 + 5 rather than 10 + 3: the evidence comes from unrelated fields (theory of distributed computing, operating systems, distributed shared memory, multiprocessor hardware, parallel programming measurements).

## Reading order
Theory first, then the two directions alternating, measurements before designs. Lauer and Needham's duality (P18), the partial equivalence under failures (P86); then shared memory built on messages (P279, P269, P271, P275, P267) alternating with messages built on, or beside, shared memory (P274 Alewife, P50 Determinator, P268, P270, P66), the measured comparisons of pure message passing against hybrid models (P90, P219), two views of concurrency in object systems (P255), StarfishOS (P191), COMMOS (P253), Lisp (P15). Round 0 holds 18 papers that serve it (counted as the included rows whose screening reason names this question, plus P275 and P279, whose reasons say only "network" or "library" but whose titles are about shared memory over message passing).

=== SQ13.md
## Question
Which many-core processors were built without hardware shared memory or cache coherence, communicating between cores by messages or channels, how were they programmed, and why were they discontinued or not adopted?

## Unit
One many-core processor built without hardware shared memory or cache coherence whose cores communicate by messages or channels, with how it was programmed and why it was discontinued or not adopted.

## Enough when
Every distinct processor is covered by one read paper, and a search round finds no new one. A processor counts as covered when the papers read for it say how it was programmed and why it was discontinued or not adopted, or when no paper found says so.

## Reading order
One processor at a time, alternating between decades, the paper that best covers programming and fate first: the Single-chip Cloud Computer (P21, then P104 for how it was programmed, P224 and P100 if still needed), the Transputer (P96, P99, P176), the Message-Driven Processor and J-Machine (P65, P70, P64, P12), the M-Machine (P66), RAMP Blue (P97), the processor of P101. Then the argument for message passing on many-core chips (P98) and PIKA (P175), for the reasons they give about such chips.

=== SQ14.md
## Question
What evidence shows that hardware shared memory, cache coherence and shared-memory operating system kernels scale to many cores, and what limits do studies report on the scaling of many-core hardware in general (power, communication, serial fractions)?

## Unit
A finding: a measurement, projection or argument that hardware shared memory, cache coherence or a shared-memory kernel does or does not scale to many cores, or a limit reported on many-core scaling in general (power, communication, serial fractions).

## Enough when
At least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 5 in a row add nothing new. 10 + 5 rather than 10 + 3: the question joins three fields (coherence hardware, operating system kernels, power and parallel-speedup limits), and a run of coherence-protocol papers says nothing about kernels or power.

## Reading order
The three fields alternating, and both sides alternating within each: coherence scales (P22) against the case for message passing on many-core chips (P98); Linux scales to 48 cores (P23) against the multikernel and fos (P8, P102); dark silicon (P24) and the Berkeley view (P111) for general limits; then synchronisation measured across many-core platforms (P103), Tornado (P47), EM2 (P108), the many-core kernel executive (P110), kernels on multicore (P252), and only then the coherence-protocol theses and papers (P105, P106, P107, P109), one at a time, since they resemble each other. Round 0 holds 15 papers that serve it (the included rows whose screening reason names this question; P8 is added because it argues the opposite side).

## Kind
kinds, because the observation's claim is tested by how far down each kind of attempt got and which kinds later added paths that are not messages, not by a catalogue of every kernel with an IPC path: one system of a kind places the message send at the same level, by the same mechanism, as the others of that kind. (`research/sls/1-protocol/step.md`, *How much each question needs*)

Census or kinds is my decision at gate 1c; kinds is recommended. Estimate from `sls/2-search/R0.md`: the 160 papers included through I1 all serve this question (counted as the included rows whose decision names I1; P67 left out, its decision changed to exclude at 3c). A finding: a measurement or argument that raising the hardware interface towards the language harms, or does not harm, performance, cost, generality or compiler optimisation, or a statement of whether such an argument applies to a message send or method dispatch.

## Enough when
At least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 3 in a row add nothing new.

## Reading order
Both sides alternating, measured comparisons first. Against raising the interface: the RISC case (P17), Hennessy (P85), the VAX-11 and RISC I comparison (P81), the M68000 complex instructions study (P263), instruction-set complexity and memory (P264). For it: the argument for language-directed architectures (P257), the architecture closing the gap to the user interface (P265), hardware support for interpreters (P266), adaptive interpretation (P256), the semantic-gap instruction set thesis (P258). Then the papers closest to a message send or method dispatch: SOAR (P11, P261), SELF's compiler (P14), whether object-oriented languages need special hardware (P60), C and the hardware's machine model (P4), end-to-end arguments (P7), Lisp (P15), and Ditzel and Patterson's retrospective (P280). Round 0 holds 25 papers that serve it (counted as the included rows whose screening reason names this question).
=== SQ10
## Question

## Kind
evidence, because the question asks what the literature reports about equivalence and about building one model on the other: findings (proofs, arguments, measurements), not a list of systems. (`research/sls/1-protocol/step.md`, *How much each question needs*)

## Unit
A finding: a result or argument on the equivalence of the two structures, or a report of one model built on the other, with which properties (encapsulation, freedom from data races, interposition) and how much performance it keeps or loses.

## Enough when
At least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 5 in a row add nothing new. 10 + 5 rather than 10 + 3: the evidence comes from unrelated fields (theory of distributed computing, operating systems, distributed shared memory, multiprocessor hardware, parallel programming measurements).

## Reading order
Theory first, then the two directions alternating, measurements before designs. Lauer and Needham's duality (P18), the partial equivalence under failures (P86); then shared memory built on messages (P279, P269, P271, P275, P267) alternating with messages built on, or beside, shared memory (P274 Alewife, P50 Determinator, P268, P270, P66), the measured comparisons of pure message passing against hybrid models (P90, P219), two views of concurrency in object systems (P255), StarfishOS (P191), COMMOS (P253), Lisp (P15). At least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 3 in a row add nothing new.

## Reading order

## Question

census, because the question asks why each such processor was discontinued or not adopted, and those reasons belong to each chip (its maker, its market, its programming model); a chip left out could be the one whose reason still applies to H3. Which computer systems provide sending a message (to an object, actor, process or core) as a primitive below the programming language, that is in the operating system kernel, the instruction set or the hardware, and at which of these levels does each system's message semantics hold, and which systems started message-based at a level and later added paths that are not messages?

## Kind

(`research/sls/1-protocol/step.md`, *How much each question needs*)

Census or kinds is my decision at gate 1c; kinds is recommended. Estimate from `sls/2-search/R0.md`: the 160 papers included through I1 all serve this question (counted as the included rows whose decision names I1; P67 left out, its decision changed to exclude at 3c). Grouping them by the system their title or screening reason names gives about 112 distinct systems, with the L4 family and the Mach family counted once each (about 120 if their variants, such as seL4, Fiasco or Real-Time Mach, count apart). Under census: about 110–120 papers to read from round 0 alone, plus one for each new system a later round finds. Under kinds: round 0 shows about 20 kinds across the three levels, so about 30–40 papers, one or two per kind, then 5 in a row with no new kind.

## Unit
A kind of message-based system: the level where the send is a primitive (an instruction, a hardware or microcode mechanism, or the kernel's own means of communication, as in I1), combined with how the mechanism works. Examples: an object-based processor with port send and receive operations; a message-driven multicomputer node; a many-core chip with on-die message buffers and no coherence; a channel processor; a hardware IPC accelerator for a kernel; a communication coprocessor; a synchronous-IPC microkernel; a port-based microkernel; a capability kernel; a multikernel; a message-based distributed operating system. A paper also adds a new unit if it shows a new kind of path, added later, that is not a message.

## Enough when
At least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 5 in a row add nothing new. 10 + 5 rather than 10 + 3: the systems span four decades and three levels, and a run of kernel papers says nothing about processors.

## Reading order
Levels alternating (instruction set, hardware or microcode mechanism, kernel), and within each level different groups and decades; full designs with an evaluation before position papers and short IPC notes. Start with the seeds and the system papers most other papers build on: the Intel 432 (P10, then P75), the Message-Driven Processor and the J-Machine (P12, P65), the multikernel (P8), L4 (P46, P48). Then: the Single-chip Cloud Computer (P21), KeyKOS and EROS (P53, P77), the Transputer (P96), Spring (P51), Chorus (P200), the ELXSI System 6400, which added shared memory later (P42), the M-Machine (P66), Alewife (P274), the Lisp Machine (P73), hardware IPC support (P159, P221), object and Java processors (P58, P59, P63), QNX (P276), fos and Helios (P102, P45), the message coprocessor and Sylvan (P152, P250). After these, any paper describing a system of a kind not yet covered. Several papers on one system count as one reading for this question (e.g. the L4 family: P46, P48, P172, P188, P204, P233, P251): only the strongest is read for it.

=== SQ1
## Question
Which computer systems provide sending a message (to an object, actor, process or core) as a primitive below the programming language, that is in the operating system kernel, the instruction set or the hardware, and at which of these levels does each system's message semantics hold, and which systems started message-based at a level and later added paths that are not messages?

=== SQ1.md
## Question
Which computer systems provide sending a message (to an object, actor, process or core) as a primitive below the programming language, that is in the operating system kernel, the instruction set or the hardware, and at which of these levels does each system's message semantics hold, and which systems started message-based at a level and later added paths that are not messages?

## Unit
A kind of message-based system: the level where the send is a primitive (an instruction, a hardware or microcode mechanism, or the kernel's own means of communication, as in I1), combined with how the mechanism works. Examples: an object-based processor with port send and receive operations; a message-driven multicomputer node; a many-core chip with on-die message buffers and no coherence; a channel processor; a hardware IPC accelerator for a kernel; a communication coprocessor; a synchronous-IPC microkernel; a port-based microkernel; a capability kernel; a multikernel; a message-based distributed operating system. A paper also adds a new unit if it shows a new kind of path, added later, that is not a message.

## Enough when
At least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 5 in a row add nothing new. 10 + 5 rather than 10 + 3: the systems span four decades and three levels, and a run of kernel papers says nothing about processors.

## Reading order
Levels alternating (instruction set, hardware or microcode mechanism, kernel), and within each level different groups and decades; full designs with an evaluation before position papers and short IPC notes. Start with the seeds and the system papers most other papers build on: the Intel 432 (P10, then P75), the Message-Driven Processor and the J-Machine (P12, P65), the multikernel (P8), L4 (P46, P48). Then: the Single-chip Cloud Computer (P21), KeyKOS and EROS (P53, P77), the Transputer (P96), Spring (P51), Chorus (P200), the ELXSI System 6400, which added shared memory later (P42), the M-Machine (P66), Alewife (P274), the Lisp Machine (P73), hardware IPC support (P159, P221), object and Java processors (P58, P59, P63), QNX (P276), fos and Helios (P102, P45), the message coprocessor and Sylvan (P152, P250). Several papers on one system count as one reading for this question (e.g. the L4 family: P46, P48, P172, P188, P204, P233, P251): only the strongest is read for it.
## Kind
kinds, because the observation's claim is tested by how far down each kind of attempt got and which kinds later added paths that are not messages, not by a catalogue of every kernel with an IPC path:

## Unit
A finding: how one of the four functions (protection, scheduling, resource allocation, naming) is provided in a system of message-passing parts that share no state, whether it relies on a central coordinator or on replicated parts that must agree, or what it costs.

What does the literature report about the equivalence (duality) of message-passing and shared-memory system structures, and can either one be built on top of the other while keeping its properties (encapsulation, freedom from data races, interposition) and its performance?

A finding: a result or argument on the equivalence of the two structures, or a report of one model built on the other, with which properties (encapsulation, freedom from data races, interposition) and how much performance it keeps or loses.

evidence, because the question asks what the literature reports about equivalence and about building one model on the other: findings (proofs, arguments, measurements), not a list of systems. (`research/sls/1-protocol/step.md`, *How much each question needs*)

=== SQ11
Why do developers of actor or message-passing programs also use shared state, locks or other concurrency mechanisms alongside messages, and what do they report that the pure message model cannot express or costs too much?

A finding: a reason developers give or a study reports for using shared state, locks or other mechanisms alongside messages, or a thing the pure message model is reported unable to express or too costly for.

evidence, because the question asks why developers mix models and what they report the pure model cannot do: findings (reasons, limits, costs). (`research/sls/1-protocol/step.md`, *How much each question needs*)

=== SQ12
Where do measured costs and scaling limits come from in actor and message-passing runtimes on conventional hardware, and do their authors identify the hardware's shared-memory model as the limiting factor, or report software techniques that remove it?

A finding: a measured cost or scaling limit of an actor or message-passing runtime on conventional hardware, with the cause its authors give (the hardware's shared-memory model or something else), or a software technique reported to remove it.

evidence, because the question asks where measured costs come from and to what their authors attribute them: findings (measurements and attributed causes). (`research/sls/1-protocol/step.md`, *How much each question needs*)

=== SQ13
Which many-core processors were built without hardware shared memory or cache coherence, communicating between cores by messages or channels, how were they programmed, and why were they discontinued or not adopted?

One many-core processor built without hardware shared memory or cache coherence whose cores communicate by messages or channels, with how it was programmed and why it was discontinued or not adopted.

census, because the question asks why each such processor was discontinued or not adopted, and those reasons belong to each chip (its maker, its market, its programming model); a chip left out could be the one whose reason still applies to H3. The population is small, so covering every chip costs no more than saturating on kinds. (`research/sls/1-protocol/step.md`, *How much each question needs*)

=== SQ14
What evidence shows that hardware shared memory, cache coherence and shared-memory operating system kernels scale to many cores, and what limits do studies report on the scaling of many-core hardware in general (power, communication, serial fractions)?

A finding: a measurement, projection or argument that hardware shared memory, cache coherence or a shared-memory kernel does or does not scale to many cores, or a limit reported on many-core scaling in general (power, communication, serial fractions).

evidence, because the question asks what the evidence shows about scaling and its limits: findings (measurements, projections, arguments), not a list of chips. (`research/sls/1-protocol/step.md`, *How much each question needs*)

=== SQ15
Which system functions (resource allocation, scheduling, naming, protection, failure handling, global consistency) have been shown to require global agreement or to work better with central or logically central coordination, and what do decentralised versions cost or give up?

A finding: a proof, measurement or argument that a system function needs global agreement or works better with central or logically central coordination, or what a decentralised version of it costs or gives up.

evidence, because the question asks which functions have been shown to need agreement or central coordination and what decentralised versions cost: findings (proofs, measurements, arguments), with the function named in each. (`research/sls/1-protocol/step.md`, *How much each question needs*)

=== SQ16
What do studies of reflective and metacircular systems report about whether a system can be defined entirely in its own terms, what must remain outside it as a base (primitives, a level that is not reflected), and what that base costs or prevents?

A finding: a report of what a reflective or metacircular system could define in its own terms, what had to stay outside as a base, or what that base costs or prevents.

evidence, because the question asks what studies report about self-definition and the base it needs: findings (claims, constructions, limits). (`research/sls/1-protocol/step.md`, *How much each question needs*)

=== SQ17
Which mechanisms let a layer be put between a program and conventional shared-memory hardware or kernels without changing either (virtual memory, trap-and-emulate virtualisation, system call interposition, input/output memory management), and how do their coverage and cost compare with interposition on messages?

A kind of mechanism that puts a layer between a program and conventional shared-memory hardware or kernels without changing either, with its coverage (what it can and cannot intercept) and its cost. A kind already recorded counts as new again if a different coverage limit or cost is reported.

kinds, because the question names kinds of mechanism (virtual memory, trap-and-emulate virtualisation, system call interposition, input/output memory management) and compares their coverage and cost with interposition on messages; one well-measured example of each kind answers it, while the monitors and hypervisors that use them are far too many to list. (`research/sls/1-protocol/step.md`, *How much each question needs*)

=== SQ18
What costs of object-based and capability-based hardware do independent evaluations attribute to object orientation, fine-grained protection or object addressing themselves, rather than to compilers or implementation, and how large are those costs?

A finding: a cost of object-based or capability-based hardware, its size, and whether the evaluation attributes it to object orientation, fine-grained protection or object addressing themselves or to compilers or implementation, with whether the evaluator is independent of the designers.

evidence, because the question asks what costs evaluations attribute to object orientation, fine-grained protection or object addressing, and how large they are: findings (measured costs and their attribution). (`research/sls/1-protocol/step.md`, *How much each question needs*)

=== SQ19
Since the end of Dennard scaling, which kinds of specialised architectures have been adopted and which have failed, and what factors (software compatibility, ecosystem, programmability, economics, kind of workload) do analyses give for the difference?

A kind of specialised architecture with its outcome (adopted or failed), or a factor an analysis gives for the difference (software compatibility, ecosystem, programmability, economics, kind of workload).

kinds, because the question itself asks which kinds of specialised architecture were adopted or failed, and the factors analyses give; a census of every specialised chip is outside its wording and would not change the answer H1 needs. Census is not offered for that reason; it stays my decision at gate 1c if I want it. (`research/sls/1-protocol/step.md`, *How much each question needs*)

## Question

## Kind
kinds, because the observation's claim is tested by how far down each kind of attempt got and which kinds later added paths that are not messages, not by a catalogue of every kernel with an IPC path: 
## Unit
A kind of message-based system: the level where the send is a primitive (an instruction, a hardware or microcode mechanism, or the kernel's own means of communication, as in I1), combined with how the mechanism works. Examples: an object-based processor with port send and receive operations; a message-driven multicomputer node; a many-core chip with on-die message buffers and no coherence; a channel processor; a hardware IPC accelerator for a kernel; a communication coprocessor; a synchronous-IPC microkernel; a port-based microkernel; a capability kernel; a multikernel; a message-based distributed operating system. ## Reading order
Levels alternating (instruction set, hardware or microcode mechanism, kernel), and within each level different groups and decades; full designs with an evaluation before position papers and short IPC notes. Nevertheless, there are limitations and potential criticisms of this
work. First, this paper does not perform detailed architectural simulations with specific benchmarks or consider difficult-to-model
queuing impacts due to cache and interconnect contention. We instead show that coherence’s per-miss traffic is independent of the
miss pattern and number of cores. Although less precise than detailed simulation, our results are actually more robust as they are
not limited to the specific benchmarks studied. Furthermore, we
describe our protocol as an existence proof of a scalable coherence
protocol, but we do not claim it to be the best. To this more modest
end, less precision is required.
Second, we did not compare against multicore chips without
caches or without a shared address space. Although these latter
approaches have been successful in high-performance computing,
etc., they have not been common in mainstream multicore systems.
Given that coherence’s costs can be kept low and that we already
have operating systems that use hardware coherence to scale to
many cores [2, 3], there does not appear to be a need to abandon
coherence. Thus, we anticipate that alternatives to cache-coherent
shared memory will continue to exist and thrive in certain domains,
but that on-chip coherence will continue to dominate mainstream
multicore chips. Furthermore, coherent systems can support legacy
algorithms from these other domains, because any program that
works for scratchpad systems (e.g., Cell processor) or message
passing systems (e.g., MPI cluster) can easily map to a shared
memory system with caches.

and stay small, e.g., 2% of total cache size for even 512 cores. We
find negligible energy overhead and zero latency penalty for cache
misses to data that are not actively shared, and our analysis suggests the relative miss penalty and energy overheads of accessing
shared data do not increase appreciably with increasing core count.
Consequently, we predict that on-chip coherence is here to stay.
Computer systems tend not to abandon compatibility to eliminate
small costs, such as the costs we find for scaling coherence. In particular, systems will not likely wish to replace conventional operating systems now that they have been shown to scale using cache
coherence [2, 3]. Boyd-Wickizer et al. [2] concur: “there is no
scalability reason to give up on traditional operating system organizations just yet.”
Some might object to retaining coherence, because many applications do not yet scale well with coherence. True, but is the root
cause the algorithm, program implementation, or coherence? If, for
example, frequent updates must be communicated to many readers,
coherence and most alternatives will do poorly. At least with hardware coherence, programmers can concentrate on choreographing
independent work rather than handling low-level mechanics.
Our claim for the continued viability of on-chip cache coherence
does not imply that other communication paradigms will disappear.
There will continue to be applications for which message passing
is appropriate (e.g., scale out high performance computing) or for
which incoherent scratchpad memories are appropriate (e.g., realtime systems), and we believe those communication paradigms will
persist. However, we predict that they are likely to continue to
coexist with on-chip cache-coherent shared memory.

The Problem of Signals

The most difficult part of the KeyNIX implementation, was support for the signal(2) mechanism. One of
the deliberate design decisions of KeyKOS is that domains are single threaded. A domain is either
waiting for a message, waiting for a reply to a message, or processing a message. There is no mechanism
for stacking messages. This decision increases the reliability of the KeyKOS system, but occasionally
requires that queuing domains be inserted into an otherwise straightforward remote procedure call.

UNIX signals are asynchronous with respect to the receiving process. As a result, the implementation of
the signal mechanism is one of the more complicated and pervasive (not to say perverse) aspects of the
UNIX kernel.3

To ensure that the UNIX Keeper is always able to receive signal notifications promptly, trivial queuing
domains are required where an operation might block or complete slowly. The purpose of these domains
is to queue messages to devices such as ttys and pipes that might otherwise delay the receipt of signals by
the UNIX Keeper. The UNIX Keeper delivers these messages through the queue domain, and waits
asynchronously for the queue domain to send a message indicating completion of the requested service.

# P69

## Reference
William J. Dally, Linda Chao, Andrew Chien, Soha Hassoun, Waldemar Horwat, Jon Kaplan, Paul Song, Brian Totty, Scott Wills (1987). *Architecture of a Message-Driven Processor*. Proc. 14th International Symposium on Computer Architecture (ISCA '87), ACM, pp. 189–196. https://doi.org/10.1145/30350.30372. P69, round-file row R0-121, included under I1. Version read: the ACM publisher PDF (scanned, with an OCR text layer), 8 pages. Pages cited below are the printed pages 189–196 (PDF page = printed page − 188).

## Deepest pass
2

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** An architecture proposal (design) for one processing node of a message-passing MIMD computer. It is evaluated only with instruction-level and register-transfer-level simulators (abstract; pp. 189, 195).
- **Context:** Message-passing computers built from conventional microprocessors (Cosmic Cube, Intel iPSC, S-NET), with about 300 µs software overhead per message. Single-chip nodes: N-CUBE, Mosaic and the Transputer. Multiple register sets in the Z-80 and the Xerox Alto. Actors [1] and the authors' own network work [5, 6] (pp. 190, 196).
- **Correctness:** The premise is that network latency has fallen to "a few microseconds making software overhead a major concern" (p. 190). The comparison baseline (300 µs, p. 190) is stated with no source or configuration. The proposed node's own times are simulated cycle counts, and the clock period is only expected ("We expect the clock period of our prototype to be 100ns", p. 195).
- **Contributions:** Messages are executed directly by a message unit (MU) that buffers or dispatches them in hardware, with one primitive message, EXECUTE (p. 191). A memory-based instruction set with two priority register sets gives fast context switches (pp. 189, 196). On-chip memory with both indexed and associative access is used for object-ID translation and method lookup (pp. 189, 193). Tags support futures and uniform local/remote access (p. 194).
- **Clarity:** Short and clearly organised: user architecture, micro-architecture, execution model, performance (p. 190). The performance section is a single table of simulated cycle counts (p. 195). The scan's OCR layer is noisy, so Table 1 was checked against the rendered page image.

## Quality
| Q | Answer | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | yes | The abstract states "We propose a machine architecture for a high-performance processing node", and §1.1 states the goal (support for fine-grain concurrent programs) and the three means to it (p. 189). |
| Q2 | partly | Three of the four are given: message format (EXECUTE <priority> <opcode> <arg>…, p. 191); naming (physical opcode address, global object identifiers, pp. 189, 191–192); busy receiver (buffered until idle or lower priority, p. 191; queue-overflow trap, p. 192). Ordering and delivery guarantees are not stated. |
| Q3 | partly | The evidence is from "instruction-level and a register-transfer (RT) level simulators" (p. 195). The chip is a prototype still to be built ("will have", p. 193). |
| Q4 | partly | The order-of-magnitude claim names baseline machines (Cosmic Cube, iPSC, S-NET at "about 300µs", p. 190) but gives no version or configuration. Table 1 has no baseline (p. 195). |
| Q5 | partly | The simulators and the expected 100 ns clock are given (p. 195). There are no workloads beyond "a number of simple operations", no reason for choosing them, and no run counts (p. 195). |
| Q6 | partly | "Less than ten clock cycles per message" is backed by Table 1 only for the fixed-length messages (5–8 cycles); READ, WRITE, DEREFERENCE and FORWARD grow with W and N (p. 195). The order-of-magnitude reduction rests on Table 1 and the 300 µs figure (p. 190). "Access … 2^28 words … in less than 10µs" and "an order of magnitude more concurrency" (stated as a conjecture) have no supporting data (pp. 195–196). |
| Q7 | no | The causes are only asserted, e.g. "The MDP achieves much of its performance by using a message-driven control mechanism" (p. 195). No breakdown or ablation is given. |
| Q8 | partly | One objection (memory "unbalanced" for a 4 MIP processor) is answered in passing (p. 196), and benchmarks are deferred to "the near future" (p. 195). There is no limitations section. |
| Q9 | no | All authors propose and design the architecture ("We propose…", p. 189). That all are designers is inferred from the first-person authorship. |

## Extracted fields
| Field | Value | Page |
|---|---|---|
| Reference | See Reference above. I1: (a) the instruction set has "Transmit a message word" and "Suspend execution of a method" instructions; (b) a hardware message unit buffers and dispatches messages ("By performing these functions in hardware (not microcode)"). Publisher version, pp. 189–196, offset 188. | pp. 191–192 |
| Paper type | design (with simulated performance estimates) | pp. 189, 195 |
| System | Message-Driven Processor (MDP), a processing node of 36-bit words for a message-passing concurrent computer. Designed by the MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory and Laboratory for Computer Science and funded by DARPA, 1987. Status: simulated (instruction-level and RT-level simulators). A 1K-word prototype chip is planned ("will have only 1K words of RWM"; about 40 MΛ², about 6.5 mm a side in 2 µm CMOS, design figure). | pp. 189–190, 193–195 |
| Levels with message semantics | Hardware, between nodes: yes (inferred). The only inter-node mechanism described is the message, and a non-local access "a message send results". Hardware, within a node: partly. "The MDP controller is driven by the incoming message stream", and starting execution of a code sequence on message arrival is message-only. The instruction unit also changes state through ordinary instructions and traps (type, overflow, translation miss, illegal instruction, queue overflow), and the status register has "an interrupt enable bit". | pp. 191, 192, 194 |
| Levels with message semantics | Microcode: not stated whether a microcode level exists. Message reception is "in hardware (not microcode)", and complex messages are deliberately not put in microcode. | p. 192 |
| Levels with message semantics | Instruction set: partly. Instructions transmit a message word and suspend a method, alongside "the usual data movement, arithmetic, logical, and control instructions" on local memory. | p. 192 |
| Levels with message semantics | Message set (ROM routines in macrocode): yes. A single primitive message, EXECUTE, is hard-wired. READ, WRITE, READ-FIELD, WRITE-FIELD, DEREFERENCE, NEW, CALL, SEND, REPLY, FORWARD, COMBINE and GC are ROM code that is invoked by message. | pp. 191–192 |
| Levels with message semantics | Kernel: not stated. "operating system code" is mentioned, but its structure is not described. | p. 189 |
| Levels with message semantics | Language (intended, not built): partly. It is an object-oriented concurrent system where "programs operate by sending messages to objects", but a local instance-variable access compiles to "a simple memory reference", and only a non-local one becomes a message send. Whether non-message paths were added later: not stated. | pp. 190, 194, 196 |
| Receiving unit and state ownership | Hardware: the node (MDP), whose MU decides whether to queue or execute. Programming model: the object ("When an object receives a message it looks up and executes the corresponding method"). The state is not exclusively owned. The ROM messages READ and WRITE "read and write blocks of physical memory", and READ-FIELD and WRITE-FIELD "read and write a field of a named object", so any sender can change node memory or an object's fields without running the object's methods. Code running on the node reaches memory through base/limit address registers. | pp. 189–192 |
| Message mechanism | Asynchronous: the MDP supports "a dynamic asynchronous model based on actors". Replies come back through REPLY messages and futures. | pp. 190, 194–195 |
| Message mechanism | Naming: the message opcode "is a physical address to the routine". READ and WRITE use physical node addresses (<reply-node>). Other messages use global object identifiers, "translated at run time to find the node on which the object resides and the address within this node". | pp. 189, 191–192 |
| Message mechanism | Ordering and delivery guarantees: not stated. | — |
| Message mechanism | Buffering: two receive queues, one per priority level, held in on-chip memory and delimited by base/limit and head/tail registers. A word is enqueued in one cycle "by stealing memory cycles", using a dedicated queue row buffer. A send queue is deliberately omitted, so network congestion acts "as a governor on objects producing messages". If a method faults, its message is copied from the queue to the heap. | pp. 191, 193, 194 |
| Message mechanism | Busy receiver: "it is buffered until the node is either idle or executing code at lower priority level". A priority-1 message preempts priority 0 without saving state, because it uses the other register set. Queue overflow causes a trap. | pp. 189, 191, 192 |
| Message mechanism | Dispatch: the control unit vectors the instruction unit to the <opcode> address. CALL names the method directly. SEND forms a key from the receiver's class and the selector and looks it up in the translation table. Misses go to a trap routine that fetches the method from a global data structure. | pp. 191, 194 |
| Non-message primitives | Ordinary instructions on local memory (memory-based ISA, one memory operand per instruction). Reason: fast context switches, because on-chip memory is single-cycle. | pp. 189, 191, 192 |
| Non-message primitives | Traps on type errors, arithmetic overflow, translation miss, illegal instruction and message queue overflow. Reason (for type traps): support for dynamically typed languages and uniform handling of local and non-local data. | pp. 192, 194 |
| Non-message primitives | Interrupt enable bit in the status register. Reason not stated. | p. 191 |
| Non-message primitives | Associative translation table (a key/data lookup and an enter instruction). Reason: a global address space and method lookup in one cycle. | pp. 189, 192, 196 |
| Non-message primitives | Tags (including futures). Reason: dynamically typed languages and futures. | pp. 190, 194 |
| Non-message primitives | Shared or global memory: none in hardware. The paper claims a "single global name space" like a shared-memory machine, provided by messages and translation. | p. 196 |
| Self-definition | Message reception, buffering and dispatch are in hardware. Every message type above EXECUTE is ROM code in the machine's own macro instruction set and "lies in the same address space as the RWM, so it is very easy for the user to redefine these messages simply by specifying a different start address". The translation mechanism "is made visible to the programmer". What remains as a base is the MU hardware and the single EXECUTE message. What this base costs or prevents is not discussed. | pp. 191–192, 196 |
| Interposition | Not stated. The nearest mechanisms are user-redefinable message routines, chosen by the sender's opcode, and relocation-transparent object identifiers ("will work even if their target is relocated to another memory address, or another node"). Neither is presented as placing a third component between unchanged parties. | p. 192 |
| Operating system functions | Protection: base/limit address registers checked by the address arithmetic unit, and type-checked instructions. Any sender's READ and WRITE messages reach physical memory. A central component: not stated. | pp. 190, 192, 193 |
| Operating system functions | Scheduling: per-node hardware. The MU decides to buffer or execute by two priority levels, and SUSPEND passes control to the next message. No central component is described. | pp. 191, 194 |
| Operating system functions | Resource allocation: NEW creates objects, GC messages support garbage collection, and a method may create a context object. A central component: not stated. | pp. 192, 194 |
| Operating system functions | Naming: global object identifiers, translated per node by the associative table. Methods are fetched on cache misses "from a single distributed copy of the program". Whether a central component is involved: not stated. | p. 189 |

+Every review question this paper serves, and what it contributes to that question's answer.

+| SQ1 | Kind: a many-core chip with per-tile on-die message buffers (16 KB MPB) and no hardware cache coherency; the message semantics hold at the library level ("one-sided 'put and get' primitives", p. 176) over loads and stores to "on-die shared memory" (p. 174), with hardware support (MPMT cache-line type, INVDMB instruction, p. 174) but no send instruction; on-die agents talk by mesh packets, and voltage commands go as mesh messages to the VRC (pp. 176, 178). Later non-message paths: not stated. | 173–178 |

+| SQ2 | Kinds kept that are not message sends, with the designers' reasons: on-die shared memory (MPB), "used to increase performance of a message passing programming model whereby cores communicate through local shared memory" (p. 174); cache management (INVDMB, MPMT bit set by the OS) "used to support software managed coherency" (p. 174); off-chip DDR3 memory reached through a LUT (p. 175). No level is written in the system's own objects or messages (not stated). | 174–176 |

+| SQ5 | Findings (designers): messages under 16 KB "see a 15x latency improvement when passed through the MPB, rather than sent through main memory", larger ones "lose this performance edge" (p. 177; Fig. 7(b), p. 178; measured or simulated not stated), cause given as the 16 KB MPB size; NAS LU and BT speedup "effectively linear" up to 32 and 36 cores on the same chip, no external baseline (p. 179; Fig. 11, p. 180); router latency 4 cycles (design figure, pp. 175–176); cost of one send in cycles not stated. | 175–180 |

+| SQ10 | Finding: message passing built as a software protocol on non-coherent on-die shared memory ("a novel message passing based software protocol used to maintain data consistency in shared memory", p. 173); keeps a 15x latency gain over messages through DDR3 for messages under 16 KB (p. 177); encapsulation and freedom from data races not stated, the MPB being shared memory open to loads and stores (p. 174, inferred) and consistency resting on software invalidating MPMT lines (p. 177); no comparison with coherent shared memory. | 173–178 |

+| SQ13 | Instance: the Intel 48-core IA-32 prototype ("Rock-Creek", p. 181; "Single-Chip Cloud Computer", p. 182), 24 tiles on a 6×4 mesh, no hardware cache coherency (p. 173); programmed with one-sided put/get over the MPB, the OS setting the MPMT page-table bit, "independent OS threads" on all 48 cores, and NAS LU and BT "ported ... with minimal effort" (pp. 174, 176, 179); programmer's view deferred to [11]; why it was discontinued or not adopted: not stated (presented as "The prototype processor", p. 173). | 173–181 |

+| SQ14 | Findings, argued by designers without measurement: "the computational value gained through additional cores will at some point be exceeded by the protocol overhead needed to maintain cache coherency among the cores" (p. 173); power density as a general many-core limit, "the exponential surge in power density" (p. 173); measured at low power, memory controllers become "the major power consumer, largely because the analog I/O voltages cannot be scaled due to the DDR3 spec" (p. 180). | 173, 180 |

Every review question this paper serves, and what it contributes to that question's answer.
| SQ | What it contributes | Page |
|---|---|---|
| SQ1 | Kind: capability kernel where the send is the kernel's only means of invoking objects ("total reliance on capabilities without any other mechanisms"; key invocation by call, fork, return, copy semantics, no kernel buffering), with exceptions also delivered as messages to keepers; on conventional System/370, 680x0 and 88x00 processors, so kernel level only (inferred); added non-message path in the UNIX built on it: KeyNIX UNIX Keepers share process and open-file tables in a shared segment. | p. 3, 7, 9, 11 |
| SQ2 | Kinds kept below the messages, with the paper's reasons: privileged in-kernel low-level device drivers ("Except where performance compels otherwise, KeyKOS applications implement the actual device drivers"); shared address-space segments, in KeyNIX for "State that must be shared between multiple UNIX keepers"; direct loads and stores on mapped pages, called "isomorphic to read and write messages on the page key"; page faults "fielded exclusively by the nanokernel" (no reason given); the trap instruction for system calls, kept for binary compatibility. Kernel itself written in C and assembly, not in its own objects and messages. | p. 4-5, 9-11 |
| SQ3 | Kind: interposition by an intervening domain on a key's path ("Message buffering can be implemented transparently by an intervening domain if needed") and by keepers receiving exceptions of unmodified programs (KeyNIX runs unmodified BSD binaries); stated cost, designer-attributed: queue domains impose "considerable context switch overhead" (pipe bandwidth 0.56 of MACH 2.5), and routing every trap to the keeper "severely penalizes all trivial system calls". | p. 7, 9-10, 12, 14, 16 |
| SQ4 | Findings on functions in a capability-message kernel: naming "intrinsically decentralized" because capabilities are the only naming; protection by keys only the nanokernel can create; scheduling through meters subdivided from a single kernel "prime meter", policy in meter keepers; resource allocation through space banks under a master space bank (multiple masters possible); no measured cost of any of these. Not a no-shared-state system throughout (shared segments, p. 7, 11). | p. 3-6 |
| SQ5 | Findings, measured by the designers against Omron MACH 2.5 in "A limited performance comparison": getpid 0.4, open/close 0.26, fork/exit 6.4, exec 11.6, sbrk 14, pipe 0.56, disk access 6.5; one message send "less than 500 cycles" on the 88x00, 90 instructions on System/370 (how obtained not stated); causes stated by the designers: context switches from domain-per-inode (implementation, "we were mistaken"), queue domains (pipe), I/O design ("a direct result of the underlying KeyKOS I/O design", inherent to design). | p. 7, 13-16 |
| SQ10 | Finding: a UNIX (shared-kernel, system-call interface) built on a pure message kernel, binary-compatible, keeping per-process failure isolation but at a cost for trivial calls (getpid 0.4, open/close 0.26 of MACH 2.5); the builders still used a shared segment for UNIX tables and propose replacing it with a domain. Also message buffering built from unbuffered messages by an intervening domain. | p. 7, 10-11, 14-15, 17 |
| SQ11 | Finding: in KeyNIX, a program built of message-passing domains, the developers used a shared segment alongside messages for "State that must be shared between multiple UNIX keepers, including the process table and open file table", and name it "the primary impediment to distribution". Developers here are the kernel's own designers, not users of an actor language. | p. 11, 17 |
| SQ15 | Findings: failure handling by a system-wide checkpoint in which "all processes are briefly suspended" (central); scheduling from one kernel "prime meter" and storage from a master space bank (central, though "multiple master space banks" are possible); naming decentralised; the shared (central) KeyNIX tables are what block distribution. No measurement of a decentralised version's cost. | p. 4, 6, 8, 17 |

'''

EOF

## Reference
Shapiro, J. S., Smith, J. M., Farber, D. J. (1999). *EROS: a fast capability system*. Proceedings of the 17th ACM Symposium on Operating Systems Principles (SOSP '99), Kiawah Island, SC, pp. 170–185. https://doi.org/10.1145/319151.319163. Included under I1 (kernel IPC by capability invocation, I1(c), p. 173–174).

## Deepest pass
3 (sections 3, 4 and 6 read in detail for the message mechanism, the non-message paths and the measurements; the related-work section read for the other systems it compares)

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** Design, implementation and microbenchmark evaluation of a capability-based microkernel with a single-level persistent store (EROS) on a commodity processor, the Pentium (p. 170–171, 180).
- **Context:** The belief that "the desirable features of transparent persistence and capability-based protection are widely believed to have prohibitive performance", which the paper says "is largely justified by experience" with the i432, Mach and the AS/400 (p. 170–171). It builds on GNOSIS/KeyKOS (TymShare) as "a clean-room reimplementation of the GNOSIS architecture in C++" (p. 170), on L3/L4 IPC design (p. 181–182) and on the authors' earlier IPC and state-caching papers [44], [45] (p. 171, 173, 176).
- **Correctness:** Assumes that lmbench-inspired microbenchmarks with "semantically similar" EROS operations are a fair comparison with Linux 2.2.5 (p. 180); the paper itself states that "the microbenchmarks currently available for EROS do not support general conclusions about application performance" (p. 171) and that "A full validation of our performance claim requires application-level benchmarks" (p. 183). The claim that microbenchmarks "approximately predict real system performance" rests on KeyKOS experience [5, 16], not on EROS measurements (p. 183).
- **Contributions:** (1) The EROS kernel architecture: a few primitive capability types (numbers, nodes, pages, processes, entry and resume capabilities) and capability invocation as the only system call (p. 172–174); (2) software caching of nodes and pages into machine-specific forms (process table as a cache, page tables as a read-only cache, producer and product chains) (p. 175–178); (3) user-level storage allocation (space bank), virtual copy and process construction (p. 179–180); (4) microbenchmarks showing EROS "performs favorably on 6 out of 7 benchmarks" against Linux on the same machine (p. 182).
- **Clarity:** Well structured and readable. Figure 11 uses the large-to-small context switch (1.19 µs) as the EROS value, while the text gives 1.60 µs for the large-space case, which is slower than Linux's 1.26 µs (p. 181); the "6 out of 7" count (p. 182) depends on that choice (my observation; the paper does not discuss it).

| capability | "an unforgeable pair made up of an object identifier and a set of authorized operations (an interface) on that object". | p. 171 |
| protection domain | "the set of capabilities accessible to a subsystem"; in EROS "each process is a protection domain". | p. 171, 173 |

No exclusion criterion found. The paper cites the authors' earlier EROS papers on IPC [44] and state caching [45] (p. 185); if those enter the review, X8 should be checked (they report earlier results that this paper only cites).

Tanenbaum, A. S., Herder, J. N., Bos, H. (2006). *Can We Make Operating Systems Reliable and Secure?*. IEEE Computer 39(5) (May 2006), pp. 44–51, cover feature. https://doi.org/10.1109/mc.2006.156. ## Deepest pass
2 (whole text read, every section, figure caption and reference; the authors' claims were not checked against the cited design papers, so not a third pass)

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** A magazine argument comparing "four different approaches that researchers are using to make future operating systems more reliable and secure, proceeding from the least radical to the most radical solution" (p. 45): Nooks, paravirtual machines on L4, multiserver operating systems (Minix 3), and language-based protection (Singularity). It is a position or analytical argument with a design description of the authors' own Minix 3 (pp. 47–49), not a primary research paper.
- **Context:** Operating systems are "huge" and have "very poor fault isolation" (p. 44); bug density figures from cited studies [1, 2, 3] are used to estimate kernel bug counts (p. 44). Builds on Nooks [4, 5], L4 and L4Linux [7, 8, 9], Minix 3 [10], Singularity (no citation given) and the Burroughs B5000 (p. 49).
- **Correctness:** The bug estimates assume bug count scales with lines of code, at "a conservative estimate of six bugs per 1,000 lines" taken from other code bases (pp. 44, 48); this is an assumption, not a measurement of these kernels. Performance claims for Minix 3 are given in one paragraph without baseline version or run counts (p. 49); the paravirtualization overhead "about 3 to 8 percent" is attributed to "performance measurements" with no citation or setup (p. 47).
- **Contributions:** (1) a side-by-side description of four approaches to OS reliability (pp. 45–50); (2) the observation that three of the four "use microkernels" and that microkernels "might be making a comeback due to their potentially higher reliability" (p. 50); (3) a description of Minix 3's message-passing IPC, its integration of interrupts with message passing, and its reincarnation server (pp. 47–49).
- **Clarity:** Clear and well organised by approach; written for a general audience, so mechanisms are described only at the level of principle.

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** An architecture proposal (design) for one processing node of a message-passing MIMD computer. It is evaluated only with instruction-level and register-transfer-level simulators (abstract; pp. 189, 195).
- **Context:** Message-passing computers built from conventional microprocessors (Cosmic Cube, Intel iPSC, S-NET), with about 300 µs software overhead per message. Single-chip nodes: N-CUBE, Mosaic and the Transputer. Multiple register sets in the Z-80 and the Xerox Alto. Actors [1] and the authors' own network work [5, 6] (pp. 190, 196).
- **Correctness:** The premise is that network latency has fallen to "a few microseconds making software overhead a major concern" (p. 190). The comparison baseline (300 µs, p. 190) is stated with no source or configuration. The proposed node's own times are simulated cycle counts, and the clock period is only expected ("We expect the clock period of our prototype to be 100ns", p. 195).
- **Contributions:** Messages are executed directly by a message unit (MU) that buffers or dispatches them in hardware, with one primitive message, EXECUTE (p. 191). A memory-based instruction set with two priority register sets gives fast context switches (pp. 189, 196). On-chip memory with both indexed and associative access is used for object-ID translation and method lookup (pp. 189, 193). Tags support futures and uniform local/remote access (p. 194).
- **Clarity:** Short and clearly organised: user architecture, micro-architecture, execution model, performance (p. 190). The performance section is a single table of simulated cycle counts (p. 195). The scan's OCR layer is noisy, so Table 1 was checked against the rendered page image.

| new: message unit / instruction unit split | The MU receives, buffers and vectors. The IU "simply executes instructions". | pp. 189, 192, 195 |
| new: memory-based architecture for fast context switches | Instructions read or write on-chip memory in one cycle. With four general registers, a context saves or restores in under 10 cycles. | pp. 189, 191, 196 |
| new: priority register sets | Two register sets, one per priority level, so a low-priority message is preempted "without saving state". | pp. 189, 191 |

| new: futures via tags | A reply target is tagged "context future". Use before the reply suspends the context. | pp. 190, 194–195 |

| new: congestion as governor (no send queue) | With no send queue, network congestion blocks producing objects. | p. 191 |

# P11

## Reference
David Michael Ungar (1986, dated "February, 1986" on the cover). *The Design and Evaluation of a High Performance Smalltalk System*. PhD dissertation, Computer Science, University of California, Berkeley. Published as UC Berkeley technical report UCB/CSD-86-287 and later as a book by MIT Press (ACM Distinguished Dissertation, 1987). The report number and the MIT Press edition come from the reference line given to me; neither is printed on the scanned pages I read. P11, screened in under I2 (row R0-011). Pages cited below are the printed arabic page numbers of the dissertation scan in `papers/P11.pdf`. Printed p. *n* is PDF page *n* + 18 up to printed p. 152 (e.g. Chapter 1 starts on printed p. 1, PDF p. 19). Printed p. 153 is scanned twice (PDF pp. 171–172), so from there on printed p. *n* is PDF page *n* + 19 (e.g. Appendix A p. 185 is PDF p. 204). The front matter has no printed numbers, so the abstract is cited by its PDF pages (pp. 7–8). This is not the MIT Press edition, whose page numbers will differ.

## Deepest pass
2

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** Design and evaluation of a processor architecture and its run-time software, SOAR ("Smalltalk On A RISC"). It also contains a survey of earlier high-level-language machines (Ch. 2) and a new garbage collector, Generation Scavenging (Ch. 5) (pp. 1–5).
- **Context:** Smalltalk-80 runs poorly on widely available hardware. The only machine that "has demonstrated universally acceptable Smalltalk-80 performance" is the $120,000 ECL Xerox Dorado (p. 11). Earlier language machines (R-2, Burroughs B5700/B6700, Scheme-79, Symbolics 3600, Katana-32) "closely coupled the source language semantics to the hardware" (p. 14). RISC work (IBM 801, RISC I/II, MIPS) and the Deutsch-Schiffman software techniques for the 68010 are the other context (pp. 12–14, 24–28).
- **Correctness:** The premise is that a RISC with a few Smalltalk-specific additions can match microcoded or high-level-instruction machines. It is tested by instruction-level simulation of Xerox's official benchmarks (pp. 61–66). The NMOS chip exists and ran diagnostics, but Smalltalk-80 had not yet run on it (pp. 2, 127). The value of each feature is an omission cost measured in cycles under the current compiler. The author says this neglects cycle-time effects and compiler interaction (pp. 64–65, 67, 72).
- **Contributions:** (1) The SOAR instruction set, with tagged integer arithmetic, register windows, in-line call-target caching, fast shuffle, trap mechanisms and direct object pointers (Ch. 3). (2) A feature-by-feature evaluation that sorts features into "winners", "questionable" and "losers" (Tables 4.4–4.5, pp. 68–69). (3) Generation Scavenging, which reclaims storage with about 3% CPU overhead and no object table (Ch. 5, p. 126). (4) The "architect's trap" lesson (p. 70).
- **Clarity:** Clearly written and organised, with summary tables per chapter. The scan is legible but OCR-noisy, and a few table cells were checked against page images (pp. 66, 71).

## Quality
| Q | Answer | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | yes | The abstract states the two results (PDF pp. 7–8), and p. 2 states the aim: "We have investigated whether a reduced instruction set computer can provide good performance for the Smalltalk-80 system". |
| Q2 | partly | The receiver is named by its type (class) and dispatch uses the class of the first argument, cached in-line (pp. 8, 46–47). The argument register and the cache word after the call are described (p. 46). Delivery and ordering, and what happens when the receiver is busy, are not discussed; a send is a synchronous call (inferred). |
| Q3 | partly | The performance results come from the Daedalus instruction-level simulator (pp. 61–62, 65). A NMOS chip exists and "has correctly run diagnostics" (p. 2, p. 127), but Smalltalk-80 had not been run on it. The 400 ns cycle time is "our measured cycle time" for the chips (p. 65). |
| Q4 | partly | Overall results name real baselines: the Dorado (times from Xerox's newsletter [Bay84]), Xerox PS on 68010/68020, Tek 4404 and BS (Tables 4.2–4.3, pp. 66). Feature values are against hypothetical SOAR-without-feature configurations (Tables 4.4–4.6, pp. 68–71), which count as partly. |
| Q5 | yes | Benchmarks are given with the reason for choosing them (p. 62). The setup is the simulator and toolchain, with 400 ns cycles (Fig. 4.1, pp. 61–62, 65). The procedure is to run once, reset the counters and measure the second iteration (pp. 62, 65). |
| Q6 | partly | Most abstract and conclusion figures are in the body: Dorado parity (Table 4.2 p. 66), 2.5× the 68010 (Table 4.3 p. 66, p. 72), GS 3% vs 9% (p. 14, pp. 101, 109). However, the abstract says the language-specific hardware "doubles its performance over a RISC II with the same cycle time" (PDF p. 8). The body gives "The speed ratio of full SOAR to RISC II, 1.6" (p. 71, Table 4.6: RISC II 62%). |
| Q7 | partly | Each feature's contribution is isolated by an omission-cost calculation in cycles (Tables 4.4–4.5, Appendix A). Other causes are only asserted or hedged, e.g. "Perhaps the optimizations in Deutsch's compiler account for the difference" (p. 71). Another is that GC hardware "probably did not speed up SOAR" because of cycle time (p. 72), which is not measured. |
| Q8 | partly | Limitations are stated in paragraphs, not in a dedicated section. The results "hold only for Smalltalk-80 systems with state-of-the-art compiler technology" (p. 65). The algorithm "may not accommodate objects that live for a medium amount of time" (p. 109). |
| Q9 | no | The author designed the architecture and its run-time software ("we have analyzed the architecture of and designed and analyzed the software algorithms", p. 2; the toolchain authors are listed in Fig. 4.1, p. 61). |

Elsewhere the paper says the language-specific features "approximately double performance" (p. 4), and that register windows and tagged integers "nearly double SOAR's performance" (p. 125). These may measure different things. I record them as stated.
- **Evidence status:** most performance figures are cycle counts from simulation multiplied by 400 ns. The chips' effective cycle is 510 ns, and the chip ran diagnostics at 800 ns actual system cycle time (Table 3.8 p. 59; p. 127). So the "as fast as a Dorado" claim is a prediction: "the 400 ns NMOS SOAR chips that have been fabricated should run just as fast" (p. 73).
- **Process model:** process switches are deferred to safe calls and jumps through a software interrupt. All Smalltalk processes share one address space (pp. 45–46). This is relevant to SQ2 as a non-message, shared-memory base beneath the object model.

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** Implementation and evaluation report (a master's thesis issued as a technical report). It covers a language (Concurrent Smalltalk, CST), its compiler (Optimist II) and an operating system (Cosmos) for the Message-Driven Processor (MDP) and J-Machine. Measurements were taken on a simulator (pp. 108, 127).
- **Context:** The J-Machine and MDP [14, 16] (p. 2), built by Dally's group (p. ii). JOSS, Totty's earlier kernel, is the source of the BRAT and the object-migration protocol (p. 5). The first Optimist compiler [21] (p. 22). Related work: Smalltalk-80 and optimised Smalltalk (TS), Yokote and Tokoro's CONCURRENTSMALLTALK, and the actor languages Cantor and Acore (pp. 10–13).
- **Correctness:** Premise: "the routing time for a message sent from one end of even a large J-Machine to another is on the order of several microseconds. Operating system overhead on processing and dispatching that message of more than a few microseconds is not acceptable" (p. 2). Instruction counts are given as "rough estimates" (p. 102). They are cross-checked against runs on 4- and 16-node simulated J-Machines in MDPSim (pp. 108–109). The network-saturation limit is a first-order analytical model (p. 110).
- **Contributions:** Listed on p. 4: a redesign of CST; Optimist II (compiler and interpreter); Cosmos; CST runtime libraries; changes to MDPSim; "Modifications to the MDP architecture that make it more suitable for Concurrent Smalltalk." Measured results: a grain size of about 60 instructions, about 100–120 instructions per function call, and about 2 (internal memory) or about 4 (external DRAM) cycles per instruction (pp. 114, 127–128).
- **Clarity:** Clear and well structured, with message-format figures and per-routine instruction-count tables (Figs. 4-10 to 4-21, Tables 7-1 to 7-6). The scan is image-only, with no text layer. Appendix E (the compiler listing) was removed for space (p. 184).
