Which mechanisms let a layer be put between a program and conventional shared-memory hardware or kernels without changing either (virtual memory, trap-and-emulate virtualisation, system call interposition, input/output memory management), and how do their coverage and cost compare with interposition on messages?

## Why it matters to the observation
The observation says that at the low level "layers cannot be put in between the way the network allows". Virtualisation is such a layer: Popek and Goldberg (1974, *Formal Requirements for Virtualizable Third Generation Architectures*, CACM) give the conditions under which a monitor can intercept every sensitive instruction. SQ3 only looks at message-based systems, so it cannot find this counter-evidence.

## Origin
counter-evidence (added by skeptic)

## Kind
kinds, because the question names kinds of mechanism (virtual memory, trap-and-emulate virtualisation, system call interposition, input/output memory management) and compares their coverage and cost with interposition on messages; one well-measured example of each kind answers it, while the monitors and hypervisors that use them are far too many to list. (`research/sls/1-protocol/step.md`, *How much each question needs*)

Census or kinds is my decision at gate 1c; kinds is recommended, but in round 0 the two are close. Estimate from `sls/2-search/R0.md`: 15 included papers serve it (P28, P49, P129–P141; 14 name it in their screening reason, and P49 had it added at 3c). Under census: all 15 in round 0, then every new monitor, hypervisor or interposition system each later round finds, in a field with a very large literature. Under kinds: about 13 papers (10 + 3), since round 0 already shows about 6 kinds (trap-and-emulate, paravirtualisation, hardware-assisted virtualisation, system call interposition, device and input/output virtualisation, isolation kernels).

## Unit
A kind of mechanism that puts a layer between a program and conventional shared-memory hardware or kernels without changing either, with its coverage (what it can and cannot intercept) and its cost. A kind already recorded counts as new again if a different coverage limit or cost is reported.

## Question

A finding: a cost of object-based or capability-based hardware, its size, and whether the evaluation attributes it to object orientation, fine-grained protection or object addressing themselves or to compilers or implementation, with whether the evaluator is independent of the designers.

H1 says the end of free single-processor speedups reopens room for specialised machines. === SQ1
## Question
Which computer systems provide sending a message (to an object, actor, process or core) as a primitive below the programming language, that is in the operating system kernel, the instruction set or the hardware, and at which of these levels does each system's message semantics hold, and which systems started message-based at a level and later added paths that are not messages?
## Unit
A kind of message-based system: the level where the send is a primitive (an instruction, a hardware or microcode mechanism, or the kernel's own means of communication, as in I1), combined with how the mechanism works. Examples: an object-based processor with port send and receive operations; a message-driven multicomputer node; a many-core chip with on-die message buffers and no coherence; a channel processor; a hardware IPC accelerator for a kernel; a communication coprocessor; a synchronous-IPC microkernel; a port-based microkernel; a capability kernel; a multikernel; a message-based distributed operating system. A paper also adds a new unit if it shows a new kind of path, added later, that is not a message.
## Enough when
At least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 5 in a row add nothing new. 10 + 5 rather than 10 + 3: the systems span four decades and three levels, and a run of kernel papers says nothing about processors.
## Reading order
Levels alternating (instruction set, hardware or microcode mechanism, kernel), and within each level different groups and decades; full designs with an evaluation before position papers and short IPC notes. Start with the seeds and the system papers most other papers build on: the Intel 432 (P10, then P75), the Message-Driven Processor and the J-Machine (P12, P65), the multikernel (P8), L4 (P46, P48). Then: the Single-chip Cloud Computer (P21), KeyKOS and EROS (P53, P77), the Transputer (P96), Spring (P51), Chorus (P200), the ELXSI System 6400, which added shared memory later (P42), the M-Machine (P66), Alewife (P274), the Lisp Machine (P73), hardware IPC support (P159, P221), object and Java processors (P58, P59, P63), QNX (P276), fos and Helios (P102, P45), the message coprocessor and Sylvan (P152, P250). After these, any paper describing a system of a kind not yet covered. Several papers on one system count as one reading for this question (e.g. the L4 family: P46, P48, P172, P188, P204, P233, P251): only the strongest is read for it.
=== SQ2
## Question
In the systems found by SQ1, which mechanisms that are not message sends remain (for example shared memory, interrupts, traps, privileged instructions, microcode or global registers), and which levels of each system are written in the system's own objects and messages, and what reasons do the designers give for keeping each one?
## Unit
A kind of mechanism kept below the language that is not a message send (e.g. shared memory, interrupts, traps, privileged instructions, microcode, global registers), together with the reason given for keeping it; or a kind of level found to be written in the system's own objects and messages. A mechanism already recorded counts as new again only with a reason not yet recorded.
## Enough when
At least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 5 in a row add nothing new. 10 + 5 rather than 10 + 3: as for SQ1, the systems span four decades and three levels, and the escape routes of a processor differ from those of a kernel.
## Reading order
Papers whose screening reason names an escape route first: the ELXSI System 6400 adding shared memory (P42), shared queues between host and message coprocessor (P152), messaging and interrupt mechanisms of a microkernel (P156), in-kernel synchronisation in a scalable microkernel (P178), signals and shared memory between cores (P207), servers moved into the Mach kernel (P249), and twenty years of L4 lessons (P48). Then processors (P10, P12 or P65, P21 or P104, P66, P73) alternating with kernels (P8, P53, P77, P51, P200), across decades. Design retrospectives and lessons-learned papers before papers on a single mechanism.
=== SQ3
## Question
Which message-based systems below the language level let a component (a proxy, monitor, filter or load balancer) be placed between a sender and a receiver without changing either, by what mechanism, and at what cost?
## Unit
A kind of interposition mechanism below the language (e.g. a transparent monitor on the IPC path, a recorder that receives every message, a port or capability that can be redirected to a proxy), with its reported cost. A mechanism already recorded counts as new again if a different cost or limit is reported.
## Enough when
At least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 3 in a row add nothing new.
## Reading order
The three papers whose screening reason names interposition first: transparent monitors on synchronous IPC (P203), the Publishing recorder of all messages (P278), adaptive monitoring in microkernels (P183). Then kinds of system alternating: capability kernels (P53, P77), port-based kernels (P43, P200, P199), synchronous-IPC kernels (P46, P48), Spring's doors (P51), multiserver systems (P52, P49), and processors whose messages go through ports or names the hardware resolves (P10, P12); different decades within each.
=== SQ4
## Question
How do operating systems and machines built from message-passing parts that share no state provide protection, scheduling, resource allocation and naming, and which of these functions still rely on a central coordinator, or on replicated parts that must agree, and what does each cost?
## Unit
A finding: how one of the four functions (protection, scheduling, resource allocation, naming) is provided in a system of message-passing parts that share no state, whether it relies on a central coordinator or on replicated parts that must agree, or what it costs.

At least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 5 in a row add nothing new. 10 + 5 rather than 10 + 3: four functions, and two eras whose systems differ in kind (distributed message-based operating systems of the 1980s and 1990s, multikernels on one chip since 2009).
## Reading order
Functions and eras alternating, designs with measurements first. ## Question

A finding: a measurement against a conventional baseline (including the cost of one message send or the scaling with the number of cores), or a cause given for a difference, with who gives it (designers or a third party) and whether it is called inherent to the design or due to its implementation.
## Enough when
At least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 5 in a row add nothing new. 10 + 5 rather than 10 + 3: processors and kernels are measured with different baselines and metrics, across five decades, by designers and by third parties.
## Reading order
Processors and kernels alternating, designers and third parties alternating, measured evaluations first. Start with the Intel 432 evaluations (P10, then the independent P29), the SOAR results (P13, P11), the J-Machine evaluation (P65), L4 IPC (P46, P172), then the argument that IPC cost is becoming irrelevant (P209), Active Messages' evaluation of message-driven machines (P33), the cache effects of microkernel structure (P202), measurements of message-based operating systems (P218, P243), the PEACE kernel on MANNA (P88), the Single-chip Cloud Computer (P21, P104), the multikernel's scaling (P8), hardware IPC support (P159, P221), Lisp machines (P15), and the books on high-level-language and object machines (P1, P76). # SQ1

## Question
Which computer systems provide sending a message (to an object, actor, process or core) as a primitive below the programming language, that is in the operating system kernel, the instruction set or the hardware, and at which of these levels does each system's message semantics hold, and which systems started message-based at a level and later added paths that are not messages?

## Why it matters to the observation
The observation claims message abstractions stop above the operating system and hardware. This question tests that claim against the systems that tried to go lower, and maps how far down each one got.

## Origin
observation

## Kind
kinds, because the observation's claim is tested by how far down each kind of attempt got and which kinds later added paths that are not messages, not by a catalogue of every kernel with an IPC path: one system of a kind places the message send at the same level, by the same mechanism, as the others of that kind. (`research/sls/1-protocol/step.md`, *How much each question needs*)

Census or kinds is my decision at gate 1c; kinds is recommended. Estimate from `sls/2-search/R0.md`: the 160 papers included through I1 all serve this question (counted as the included rows whose decision names I1; P67 left out, its decision changed to exclude at 3c). Grouping them by the system their title or screening reason names gives about 112 distinct systems, with the L4 family and the Mach family counted once each (about 120 if their variants, such as seL4, Fiasco or Real-Time Mach, count apart). Under census: about 110–120 papers to read from round 0 alone, plus one for each new system a later round finds. Under kinds: round 0 shows about 20 kinds across the three levels, so about 30–40 papers, one or two per kind, then 5 in a row with no new kind.

## Unit
A kind of message-based system: the level where the send is a primitive (an instruction, a hardware or microcode mechanism, or the kernel's own means of communication, as in I1), combined with how the mechanism works. Examples: an object-based processor with port send and receive operations; a message-driven multicomputer node; a many-core chip with on-die message buffers and no coherence; a channel processor; a hardware IPC accelerator for a kernel; a communication coprocessor; a synchronous-IPC microkernel; a port-based microkernel; a capability kernel; a multikernel; a message-based distributed operating system. A paper also adds a new unit if it shows a new kind of path, added later, that is not a message.

## Enough when
At least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 5 in a row add nothing new. 10 + 5 rather than 10 + 3: the systems span four decades and three levels, and a run of kernel papers says nothing about processors.

## Reading order
Levels alternating (instruction set, hardware or microcode mechanism, kernel), and within each level different groups and decades; full designs with an evaluation before position papers and short IPC notes. Start with the seeds and the system papers most other papers build on: the Intel 432 (P10, then P75), the Message-Driven Processor and the J-Machine (P12, P65), the multikernel (P8), L4 (P46, P48). Then: the Single-chip Cloud Computer (P21), KeyKOS and EROS (P53, P77), the Transputer (P96), Spring (P51), Chorus (P200), the ELXSI System 6400, which added shared memory later (P42), the M-Machine (P66), Alewife (P274), the Lisp Machine (P73), hardware IPC support (P159, P221), object and Java processors (P58, P59, P63), QNX (P276), fos and Helios (P102, P45), the message coprocessor and Sylvan (P152, P250). After these, any paper describing a system of a kind not yet covered. Several papers on one system count as one reading for this question (e.g. the L4 family: P46, P48, P172, P188, P204, P233, P251): only the strongest is read for it.

=== SQ1
## Question
Which computer systems provide sending a message (to an object, actor, process or core) as a primitive below the programming language, that is in the operating system kernel, the instruction set or the hardware, and at which of these levels does each system's message semantics hold, and which systems started message-based at a level and later added paths that are not messages?

## Unit
A kind of message-based system: the level where the send is a primitive (an instruction, a hardware or microcode mechanism, or the kernel's own means of communication, as in I1), combined with how the mechanism works. Examples: an object-based processor with port send and receive operations; a message-driven multicomputer node; a many-core chip with on-die message buffers and no coherence; a channel processor; a hardware IPC accelerator for a kernel; a communication coprocessor; a synchronous-IPC microkernel; a port-based microkernel; a capability kernel; a multikernel; a message-based distributed operating system. A paper also adds a new unit if it shows a new kind of path, added later, that is not a message.

=== SQ2
## Question
In the systems found by SQ1, which mechanisms that are not message sends remain (for example shared memory, interrupts, traps, privileged instructions, microcode or global registers), and which levels of each system are written in the system's own objects and messages, and what reasons do the designers give for keeping each one?

## Unit
A kind of mechanism kept below the language that is not a message send (e.g. shared memory, interrupts, traps, privileged instructions, microcode, global registers), together with the reason given for keeping it; or a kind of level found to be written in the system's own objects and messages. A mechanism already recorded counts as new again only with a reason not yet recorded.

=== SQ3
## Question
Which message-based systems below the language level let a component (a proxy, monitor, filter or load balancer) be placed between a sender and a receiver without changing either, by what mechanism, and at what cost?

## Unit
A kind of interposition mechanism below the language (e.g. a transparent monitor on the IPC path, a recorder that receives every message, a port or capability that can be redirected to a proxy), with its reported cost. A mechanism already recorded counts as new again if a different cost or limit is reported.

=== SQ4
## Question
How do operating systems and machines built from message-passing parts that share no state provide protection, scheduling, resource allocation and naming, and which of these functions still rely on a central coordinator, or on replicated parts that must agree, and what does each cost?

## Unit
A finding: how one of the four functions (protection, scheduling, resource allocation, naming) is provided in a system of message-passing parts that share no state, whether it relies on a central coordinator or on replicated parts that must agree, or what it costs.

=== SQ5
## Question
What performance have message-based or object-based processors, instruction sets and operating system kernels reported against conventional baselines, including the cost of one message send and the scaling with the number of cores, and to what causes are the differences attributed, by whom (the designers or a third party), and is each cause inherent to the design or due to its implementation?

## Unit
A finding: a measurement against a conventional baseline (including the cost of one message send or the scaling with the number of cores), or a cause given for a difference, with who gives it (designers or a third party) and whether it is called inherent to the design or due to its implementation.

=== SQ6
## Question
According to their designers and to later evaluations, why were language-directed, object-based and message-based machines abandoned, not adopted, or made unnecessary?

## Unit
A finding: a reason stated for a machine being abandoned, not adopted, or made unnecessary, with who states it (its designers or a later evaluation).

=== SQ7
## Question
What do empirical studies report about the number and kinds of concurrency defects, including deadlocks, message-protocol violations and message-order defects, in programs or systems where each piece of state has one owner and is changed only through messages, compared with programs or systems that share memory?

## Unit
A finding: a count or proportion of concurrency defects of a kind (e.g. deadlock, message-protocol violation, message-order defect, data race) reported for message-passing or for shared-memory programs, or a comparison between them.

=== SQ8
## Question
What empirical evidence shows that the hardware's execution model, rather than the language, libraries, tools or training, determines how programmers design and write programs, and how correct those programs are?

## Unit
A finding: a measurement or argument that the hardware's execution model, or the language, libraries, tools or training, shapes how programs are designed or how correct they are.

=== SQ9
## Question
What evidence and arguments show that narrowing the semantic gap by raising the hardware interface towards the language harms performance, cost, generality or compiler optimisation, and do those arguments apply to a message send as the machine's primitive?

## Unit
A finding: a measurement or argument that raising the hardware interface towards the language harms, or does not harm, performance, cost, generality or compiler optimisation, or a statement of whether such an argument applies to a message send or method dispatch.

=== SQ10
## Question
What does the literature report about the equivalence (duality) of message-passing and shared-memory system structures, and can either one be built on top of the other while keeping its properties (encapsulation, freedom from data races, interposition) and its performance?

## Unit
A finding: a result or argument on the equivalence of the two structures, or a report of one model built on the other, with which properties (encapsulation, freedom from data races, interposition) and how much performance it keeps or loses.

=== SQ11
## Question
Why do developers of actor or message-passing programs also use shared state, locks or other concurrency mechanisms alongside messages, and what do they report that the pure message model cannot express or costs too much?

## Unit
A finding: a reason developers give or a study reports for using shared state, locks or other mechanisms alongside messages, or a thing the pure message model is reported unable to express or too costly for.

=== SQ12
## Question
Where do measured costs and scaling limits come from in actor and message-passing runtimes on conventional hardware, and do their authors identify the hardware's shared-memory model as the limiting factor, or report software techniques that remove it?

## Unit
A finding: a measured cost or scaling limit of an actor or message-passing runtime on conventional hardware, with the cause its authors give (the hardware's shared-memory model or something else), or a software technique reported to remove it.

=== SQ13
## Question
Which many-core processors were built without hardware shared memory or cache coherence, communicating between cores by messages or channels, how were they programmed, and why were they discontinued or not adopted?

## Unit
One many-core processor built without hardware shared memory or cache coherence whose cores communicate by messages or channels, with how it was programmed and why it was discontinued or not adopted.

=== SQ14
## Question
What evidence shows that hardware shared memory, cache coherence and shared-memory operating system kernels scale to many cores, and what limits do studies report on the scaling of many-core hardware in general (power, communication, serial fractions)?

## Unit
A finding: a measurement, projection or argument that hardware shared memory, cache coherence or a shared-memory kernel does or does not scale to many cores, or a limit reported on many-core scaling in general (power, communication, serial fractions).

=== SQ15
## Question
Which system functions (resource allocation, scheduling, naming, protection, failure handling, global consistency) have been shown to require global agreement or to work better with central or logically central coordination, and what do decentralised versions cost or give up?

## Unit
A finding: a proof, measurement or argument that a system function needs global agreement or works better with central or logically central coordination, or what a decentralised version of it costs or gives up.

=== SQ16
## Question
What do studies of reflective and metacircular systems report about whether a system can be defined entirely in its own terms, what must remain outside it as a base (primitives, a level that is not reflected), and what that base costs or prevents?

## Unit
A finding: a report of what a reflective or metacircular system could define in its own terms, what had to stay outside as a base, or what that base costs or prevents.

=== SQ17
## Question
Which mechanisms let a layer be put between a program and conventional shared-memory hardware or kernels without changing either (virtual memory, trap-and-emulate virtualisation, system call interposition, input/output memory management), and how do their coverage and cost compare with interposition on messages?

## Unit
A kind of mechanism that puts a layer between a program and conventional shared-memory hardware or kernels without changing either, with its coverage (what it can and cannot intercept) and its cost. A kind already recorded counts as new again if a different coverage limit or cost is reported.

=== SQ18
## Question
What costs of object-based and capability-based hardware do independent evaluations attribute to object orientation, fine-grained protection or object addressing themselves, rather than to compilers or implementation, and how large are those costs?

## Unit
A finding: a cost of object-based or capability-based hardware, its size, and whether the evaluation attributes it to object orientation, fine-grained protection or object addressing themselves or to compilers or implementation, with whether the evaluator is independent of the designers.

=== SQ19
## Question
Since the end of Dennard scaling, which kinds of specialised architectures have been adopted and which have failed, and what factors (software compatibility, ecosystem, programmability, economics, kind of workload) do analyses give for the difference?

## Unit
A kind of specialised architecture with its outcome (adopted or failed), or a factor an analysis gives for the difference (software compatibility, ecosystem, programmability, economics, kind of workload).

# Selection criteria

A paper is included if it meets at least one inclusion criterion and no exclusion criterion. Each verdict names the criterion that decided it. There is no restriction on publication date. "Message-based" in these criteria means: meets I1.

Terms used in the criteria and the SQs:
- **Below the programming language:** in the operating system kernel, the instruction set, microcode or hardware; not in a language runtime, library or virtual machine hosted on a conventional kernel (as in X2).
- **Written in its own objects and messages:** the level's code is objects receiving messages in the system's own model, not a lower language, microcode or hardware outside that model.
- **Without changing either:** neither the sender's nor the receiver's code, nor how they name each other, is modified to place the component between them.

| ID | Inclusion criterion |
|---|---|
| I1 | A paper is included if it describes, implements, simulates or evaluates a processor, instruction set, microarchitecture, multicomputer node or operating system kernel in which sending a message, invoking a method on an object, or delivering a message to an actor is a primitive of that level, i.e. one of: (a) an instruction of the instruction set; (b) a hardware or microcode mechanism; (c) for a kernel, the stated means by which the kernel and its system services, or the kernel's own parts, communicate (as in microkernels, multikernels, or operating systems written in an object or actor language that run without an underlying conventional kernel). The paper must name the mechanism with at least one of these terms: message, message passing, send, mailbox, actor, active message, inter-process communication (IPC), method invocation. (SQ1–SQ5) |
| I2 | A paper is included if it is a retrospective, evaluation or historical account of at least one computer architecture that its authors describe as directed at a high-level language, object-based, object-oriented or message-driven, and it reports either measured performance of that architecture or a stated reason for its performance, adoption, abandonment, or becoming unnecessary. (SQ5, SQ6) |
| I3 | A paper is included if it is an empirical study of concurrency defects (bugs) in real programs or systems (not only examples written by the authors) and it reports counts or proportions of defects either split by communication mechanism (shared memory versus message passing) or for programs or systems built on message passing only, or for programs or systems built on shared memory only, as the comparison baseline for SQ7. Programs whose defects are reported as accesses to shared variables count as shared-memory programs even if the paper does not use that term. (SQ7) |
| I4 | A paper is included if it reports evidence or an argument that directly answers one of SQ8–SQ19, whether or not it mentions messages or objects. (SQ8–SQ19) |

| ID | Exclusion criterion |
|---|---|
| X1 | A paper is excluded if it meets none of I1, I2, I3, I4. |
| X2 | A paper included only through I1 is excluded if message passing appears only at the application, library, language runtime, virtual machine or network-protocol level, running on a processor whose instruction set and hardware have no message mechanism and on a kernel that fails I1(c) (e.g. an actor library, the Erlang virtual machine, a Message Passing Interface library, a Smalltalk virtual machine hosted on Unix or Windows). Does not apply to papers that meet I2 or I3. |
| X3 | A paper is excluded if the system is a cluster or network of separate computers, each with a processor whose instruction set and hardware have no message mechanism and a kernel that fails I1(c), and the message mechanism lies only in the network interface or interconnect between them. |
| X4 | A paper is excluded if the hardware it presents is stated to serve only a fixed function or domain (e.g. neural-network inference, signal processing, packet switching, graphics) and is not stated to run general programs. Does not apply to papers included through I4. |
| X5 | A paper is excluded if it is not one of: journal article; conference or workshop paper longer than 2 pages; book or book chapter; doctoral or master's thesis; technical report of a university, company research laboratory or standards body; magazine article of a professional society (Association for Computing Machinery, Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, USENIX); architecture or system reference manual published by the system's manufacturer. Patents, slides, posters, extended abstracts of 2 pages or fewer, blog posts, forum posts, encyclopaedia entries and product brochures are excluded. |
| X6 | A paper is excluded if its full text is in neither English nor Spanish. |
| X7 | A paper is excluded if its full text cannot be obtained from the publisher, an author's or institution's web page, arXiv, Semantic Scholar, the Internet Archive, or the university library. The sources tried are recorded with the verdict. |
| X8 | A paper is excluded if it reports the same system and the same results as another included paper. The one with more pages is kept; the other is excluded unless it reports at least one measurement, design element or stated reason absent from the kept one. |
| X9 | A paper is excluded if its title or abstract presents it as a survey, review, overview or taxonomy of other work and it reports no measurement and states no reason under I2 of its own. Its reference list is still used for snowballing. |

P261 (Bush, Samples, Ungar and Hilfinger, 1987, *Compiling Smalltalk-80 to a RISC*) serves two review questions, SQ5 and SQ9. I added a *Serves* section before *Concepts* in /home/garro/dev/faculty/Thesis/research/sls/3-reading/P261.md and set `status: proposed`; nothing else in the record changed. I checked the key quotes and their pages against /home/garro/dev/faculty/Thesis/research/papers/P261.pdf (printed page = PDF page − 6).

**SQs served:**
- **SQ5** (finding, through criterion I2):
  - SOAR "runs Smalltalk roughly 2.5 times as fast as a Motorola 68010 with a similar cycle time" and is about as fast as the Dorado (p. 1). The workload is not stated, and the figure is cited from Ungar's dissertation [4].
  - The designers credit "register windows, integer tags and traps, and in-line method caches" (p. 10). The removal figures are 46% for windows (p. 3), an estimated 26% for tags (p. 6) and an estimated 33% for the cache (p. 8), all cited from [4] or [8].
  - The paper gives no cost for a single send.
- **SQ9** (finding, through criterion I4):
  - The paper says "Several features supported by the SOAR hardware could easily be performed by the compiler at marginal increased time and space costs" (p. 10). Generation tags would cost about 1% and 2%, and pointer to register 3% (p. 7). Software tag tests, by contrast, would cost an estimated 26% in speed and 15% in image size (pp. 6–7).
  - The hardware "in the main simplified" the compiler (p. 6). Limits on optimisation are blamed on the language and its bytecodes, not the hardware (pp. 3, 7).
  - The argument applies to a message send only partly. Windows speed up the call that implements a send (p. 3), and tag traps lead into method lookup (p. 6), but SOAR has no send instruction.

**Not served:**
- **SQ1 and SQ2:** SOAR does not meet I1, since the paper describes no send primitive (pp. 3, 6, 8).
- **SQ6:** the paper does not say what became of SOAR.
- **SQ16 and SQ18:** the earlier follow-up pass already found they are not met, as recorded in the record's Notes.
- **All other SQs:** nothing in the text bears on them.

**Open issues:** none new. The overlap and duplicate question already in the record's Notes still stands: the results come from Ungar (P11) or Bush (1986).

'''

I added a *Serves* section to /home/garro/dev/faculty/Thesis/research/sls/3-reading/P49.md, placed before *Concepts* as the template does, and set `status: proposed` (it was `changed`). Nothing else in the record was changed. Source was research/papers/P49.pdf, the publisher version, pp. 44–51 (printed page = PDF page + 43). I checked the key quotes against the PDF text with pdftotext and the record's pages matched.

The paper serves 7 of the 19 SQs:
- **SQ1 (kinds):** two kernel-level kinds.
  - Minix 3 is a multiserver OS whose servers and drivers talk only by synchronous "rendezvous" fixed-length messages, and its interrupts are turned into messages (pp. 47–48).
  - Singularity is a microkernel protected by its language, with one shared address space and "strongly typed messages" over typed channels (pp. 49–50). The paper describes it second-hand.
  - The paper gives no history of non-message paths added later; it presents Singularity's shared heap as a design exception (p. 50).
- **SQ2 (kinds):** non-message mechanisms the systems keep, with the reasons given.
  - Minix 3 "kernel calls" for privileged operations and I/O ports (pp. 47–48).
  - The clock driver runs in the microkernel's address space; no reason given (p. 47).
  - Singularity's "shared object heap", because sending everything over channels "would be very slow" (p. 50).
  - Singularity uses mutexes; no reason given (p. 49).
  - Singularity is written "almost entirely in Sing#", apart from trusted code in C#, C++ or assembler (p. 49).
- **SQ3:** serves only by its criterion (I1). The paper describes no component placed between a message sender and its receiver. Minix 3's bitmaps that block sends are filtering, not interposition (inferred) (p. 48).
- **SQ4 (findings):** Minix 3 runs protection, scheduling, naming and resource allocation centrally: kernel process-table bitmaps, the microkernel, the data store, and the process manager. That resource allocation is central is my inference. Singularity names through a root name server and protects through language safety. No cost is stated (pp. 47–50).
- **SQ5 (findings):** all are Minix 3 designers' figures unless marked.
  - Measurements: Minix 3 drivers in user mode lose "less than 10 percent" against "in-kernel drivers", with no named baseline. The system builds itself in "less than 6 seconds" on a 2.2-GHz Athlon, with no baseline (p. 49).
  - Causes: microkernels are "slightly lower performance" by design (p. 47); Minix 3 is not optimised, an implementation cause (p. 49).
  - Singularity's single address space removes kernel traps and context switches. That is a third-party claim and the paper does not measure it (p. 49).
  - The paper gives no cost for one message send and no scaling.
- **SQ6 (finding):** microkernels were "long discarded ... because of their lower performance", and "In the 1980s, performance counted for everything". This comes from Minix 3's designers and is about microkernels, not machines (pp. 47, 50). Whether it fits SQ6's scope is your call.
- **SQ17 (kinds, under I4):** two mechanisms.
  - Nooks puts wrappers between kernel and driver, using the virtual memory page map. It catches "99 percent of the fatal driver errors and 55 percent of the nonfatal ones"; the paper names the gaps; it needed 455 hand-written wrappers (pp. 45–46).
  - Drivers can run unchanged in paravirtualized Linux virtual machines on L4. The guest kernel had to be changed because the Pentium "is not fully virtualizable", at about 3,000 + 5,000 lines of code and "about 3 to 8 percent" overhead (pp. 46–47).
  - The paper does not compare either with interposition on messages.

**Not served:** SQ7–SQ16, SQ18 and SQ19. This matches what was decided at gate 3c and recorded in the record's Notes: SQ11, SQ8 and SQ9 were checked and do not meet I4. On SQ15, the paper only describes central components and gives no argument that any function needs to be central.

I added its *Serves* section to /home/garro/dev/faculty/Thesis/research/sls/3-reading/P72.md, placed just before *Concepts*, and set `status: proposed`. Nothing else in the record changed. The rows reuse the record's existing extraction. I checked the key quotes and pages against research/papers/P72.pdf: printed page = PDF page + 158, pp. 159, 162, 166, 168, 171–173, 180, 183–186.

**SQs served, one line each:**
- **SQ1 (a kind):** an object-based processor with instructions that "send messages to and receive messages from port objects". Interprocess communication is "in hardware and microcode". Message semantics hold only for interprocess communication; scalar operations, CALL/RETURN and faults are not messages. No non-message path is described as added later. It is the same kind as P10 and P75 (pp. 159, 162, 171).
- **SQ2 (kinds kept, with reasons):**
  - Mechanisms kept: shared system memory and I/O through attached processors (no reason given for either), hardware branching to fault handlers, and CALL/RETURN.
  - Reasons given: contexts are preallocated because allocating one per call "was time-consuming"; local stack storage areas exist because garbage collection "is prohibitive for short-lived objects".
  - Level written in its own objects: type managers are split between hardware and OS software, with "no special privileges" (pp. 159–160, 168–169, 172–173, 180, 184–185).
- **SQ5 (finding):** CALL went from 300 µs to under 100 µs, with no workload given. Levy, a third party, attributes the gain to implementation changes. The initial version had performance problems. There is no SEND/RECEIVE cost and no conventional baseline (pp. 185–186).
- **SQ6 (finding, third party):** not a commercial success, "probably due in part to premature (and somewhat overzealous) marketing", plus initial performance problems (p. 186).
- **SQ9 (finding, argument):** costs of raising the hardware interface:
  - up to four memory references per byte access;
  - 64K-byte segments that force special compiler code;
  - explicit loading of capabilities;
  - variable instruction size.

  None of these is said to apply to the message send (pp. 166, 184–186).
- **SQ16 (finding):** user-defined type managers use the same mechanisms as the OS's, but hardware-defined operations remain as a base whose cost is not stated. Its relevance is marked `(inferred)`, because the 432 is not presented as reflective (pp. 173, 184–185).
- **SQ18 (finding):** object addressing "potentially" needs four memory references per byte, called "comparable" to conventional virtual memory and reduced by caches, with no measured size. That Levy is independent of the designers, and that the cost comes from the addressing design itself, are both marked `(inferred)` (pp. 166, 185–186).

**Open issues (yours to confirm):**
- **SQs left out:**
  - SQ3: no interposition on the message path is described. The object-descriptor indirection (pp. 163–164) is for relocation.
  - SQ4 and SQ13: the 432 shares memory (p. 159), so it is outside both.
  - SQ15: the single Object Table Directory (pp. 164–165) is a design fact, not evidence that central coordination is better.
  - SQ7, 8, 10–12, 14, 17 and 19 do not apply.
- **Borderline inclusions:** SQ16 and SQ18 could be dropped if you read their scope strictly.
- **Earlier notes still stand:** the existing record already notes that P72 also appears to meet I2 (pp. 185–186), and points to Cox et al. (1983) as a possible snowball lead for SQ1 (p. 186).

**SQs served (7):**
- **SQ1:** adds a kind, a message-driven multicomputer node (the MDP, a 1987 design that was only simulated). Sending is an instruction, and a hardware message unit receives, buffers and dispatches messages. Only one message, EXECUTE, is hard-wired. The paper reports no non-message path added later (pp. 189, 191–192, 194).
- **SQ2:** names the non-message mechanisms the design keeps, with the stated reasons:
  - memory-based instructions, for fast context switches;
  - traps;
  - an interrupt enable bit, for which no reason is given;
  - an associative translation table.

  It also contributes a level written in the system's own terms: every message above EXECUTE is user-redefinable ROM macrocode (pp. 189, 191–192, 194, 196).
- **SQ4:** a design finding, not a measured one. Each node handles its own protection (base/limit registers and type checks, though READ and WRITE messages from any sender still reach physical memory), its own scheduling (two priority levels) and its own naming (object-ID translation). No central component is described, and costs are not stated (pp. 189–194).
- **SQ5:** a simulated finding from the designers. Table 1 gives cycle counts per message type, "less than ten clock cycles per message", compared with "about 300µs" on Cosmic Cube, iPSC and S-NET, for which no source is given. The designers attribute the gain to features inherent in the design, and none is isolated (pp. 190, 195–196).
- **SQ9:** an argument by the designers, not a measurement. Executing messages directly cuts overhead, and messages built on EXECUTE run "almost as efficiently ... as they could if they were hard-wired" (pp. 189, 191).
- **SQ10:** a claim without measurement. A "single global name space" is provided over messages, and the MDP "provides many of the advantages of both message-passing multicomputers and shared-memory multiprocessors" (p. 196).
- **SQ13:** a partial instance. The paper says the MDP is meant to run object-oriented programs by message sending and can also emulate other programming models. Why it was discontinued or not adopted is not stated, because the prototype was still planned. It belongs to the same machine line as P12, P64 and P65 (pp. 190, 193, 196).

**Left out on purpose:**
- **SQ3:** the record finds no interposition mechanism (p. 192).
- **SQ6:** the machine's fate is not stated.
- **SQ14:** the only limit named is about message-passing machines: the limiting factor has moved from message latency to processor overhead (p. 196). That is not evidence on whether shared memory scales.
- **SQ16:** the MDP is not a reflective or metacircular system, so its self-definition point went under SQ2 instead.
- **SQ18:** the paper is the designers' own and attributes no costs.

It is the same kind as P10 and P75 (pp. 159, 162, 171).
- **SQ2 (kinds kept, with reasons):**
  - Mechanisms kept: shared system memory and I/O through attached processors (no reason given for either), hardware branching to fault handlers, and CALL/RETURN.
  - Reasons given: contexts are preallocated because allocating one per call "was time-consuming"; local stack storage areas exist because garbage collection "is prohibitive for short-lived objects".
  - Level written in its own objects: type managers are split between hardware and OS software, with "no special privileges" (pp. 159–160, 168–169, 172–173, 180, 184–185).
- **SQ5 (finding):** CALL went from 300 µs to under 100 µs, with no workload given. Levy, a third party, attributes the gain to implementation changes. The initial version had performance problems. There is no SEND/RECEIVE cost and no conventional baseline (pp. 185–186).
- **SQ6 (finding, third party):** not a commercial success, "probably due in part to premature (and somewhat overzealous) marketing", plus initial performance problems (p. 186).
- **SQ9 (finding, argument):** costs of raising the hardware interface:
  - up to four memory references per byte access;
  - 64K-byte segments that force special compiler code;
  - explicit loading of capabilities;
  - variable instruction size.

  None of these is said to apply to the message send (pp. 166, 184–186).
- **SQ16 (finding):** user-defined type managers use the same mechanisms as the OS's, but hardware-defined operations remain as a base whose cost is not stated. Its relevance is marked `(inferred)`, because the 432 is not presented as reflective (pp. 173, 184–185).
- **SQ18 (finding):** object addressing "potentially" needs four memory references per byte, called "comparable" to conventional virtual memory and reduced by caches, with no measured size. **Open issues (yours to confirm):**
- **SQs left out:**
  - SQ3: no interposition on the message path is described. The object-descriptor indirection (pp. 163–164) is for relocation.
  - SQ4 and SQ13: the 432 shares memory (p. 159), so it is outside both.
  - SQ15: the single Object Table Directory (pp. 164–165) is a design fact, not evidence that central coordination is better.
  - SQ7, 8, 10–12, 14, 17 and 19 do not apply.
- **Borderline inclusions:** SQ16 and SQ18 could be dropped if you read their scope strictly.
- **Earlier notes still stand:** the existing record already notes that P72 also appears to meet I2 (pp. 185–186), and points to Cox et al. (1983) as a possible snowball lead for SQ1 (p. 186).

I added a *Serves* section to P77 (EROS, Shapiro, Smith, Farber, SOSP '99). It sits before *Concepts* as the template places it, and I set `status: proposed` (it was `changed`). Nothing else in the record changed. I used the existing extraction and checked the key quotes and their pages against `research/papers/P77.pdf`.

The paper serves 11 SQs:
- **SQ1 (kind):** a capability kernel on a commodity processor, where "capability invocation is the only 'system call' implemented by the kernel" (p. 173–174). It also reports that Mach started with a single mach_msg system call and later added others "for performance" (p. 182).
- **SQ2 (kind plus reason):** these mechanisms are kept outside messages:
  - Per-trap kernel entry, because the Pentium saves state in an "irregular" format (p. 178).
  - Device drivers and the persistent store kept in the kernel "To simplify security assurance" (p. 170).
  - A per-process switch that turns off capability calls "For emulation of other operating systems" (p. 173 fn. 3).
  - Direct memory access and shared address spaces, for which no reason is given (p. 173).

  Storage allocation, virtual copy and process construction are written in the system's own processes (p. 179–180).
- **SQ3 (kind plus cost):** a filter process or the kernel's indirector object can be "transparently interposed in front of most objects", because all capabilities take the same arguments (p. 174). The cost is 1.6 µs for a trivial call against 0.7 µs for Linux getppid; the paper says "function was favored over performance" (p. 180).
- **SQ4 (finding):** protection is by capabilities plus a user-level reference monitor (KeySafe), and storage comes from one central space bank (p. 172–174, 179). Caveat: EROS processes can share an address space (p. 173), so it is not strictly a system of parts that share no state (inferred).
- **SQ5 (finding):** it is faster than Linux 2.2.5 on 6 of 7 microbenchmarks, on the same uniprocessor 400 MHz Pentium II. One round-trip message costs 2.38–3.21 µs. The designers give the causes, and only the page-table fast-path speedup is isolated. The paper itself says these microbenchmarks "do not support general conclusions" (p. 171, 180–183).
- **SQ6 (weak finding):** KeyKOS "Development ceased in 1991 when the company closed", and KeyKOS is a kernel, not a machine (p. 170). It also says the i432's "performance suffers dramatically" from its complexity, citing [7]; the paper does not say this is why the i432 was abandoned (p. 183).
- **SQ9 (finding):**
  - "capability systems can perform well without resorting to specialized hardware assists" (p. 182).
  - On the CAP computer, capabilities at the language's grain cause more capability lookups "than the hardware can effectively support" (p. 182).
  - The i432, "designed as a high level language machine", loses performance to its complexity (p. 183).
  - EROS credits part of its speed to a minimal "semantic gap" between kernel and hardware (p. 183).
- **SQ10 (weak finding):** memory load/store "may be modeled as an efficiently cached capability invocation" (p. 173). The paper measures nothing about what this keeps or loses.
- **SQ15 (finding):** failure handling is one global, consistency-checked snapshot taken while "all processes are halted", in under 50 ms for 256 MB (p. 174). Storage goes through a single space-bank process (p. 179). The paper does not say what a decentralised version would cost.
- **SQ16 (weak finding):** the paper does not present EROS as a reflective system. Its services are defined in its own processes, while the kernel and "the hand-constructed initial system image" stay outside as the base (p. 179–180).
- **SQ18 (third-party finding, no sizes given):** the i432 and CAP costs are attributed to their design, not to compilers (p. 182–183). These are the paper's statements about other teams' machines; it gives no sizes.

The paper does not serve SQ7, 8, 11, 12, 13, 14, 17 or 19. The only remark relevant to SQ14 is a footnote on SMP locality (p. 173 fn. 2), and I judged it too slight to list.

Open issues for you at gate 3c: whether to keep the four weak entries (SQ6, SQ10, SQ16, SQ18) and SQ4 with its caveat. Each one is hedged in its row. No criterion change was found, and there are no decision cards.

Nothing else in the record was changed.

The paper serves seven SQs:
- **SQ1 (kind):** a microcoded language machine. A message send is an ordinary call of the receiving instance, and the microcode does the dispatch: it "binds self to the object, binds the instance variables ... and calls a dtp-select-method" (p. 309). The manual itself says "no new features are added to Lisp for message sending" (p. 285). I found no separate send instruction (inferred). Whether paths that are not messages were added later is not stated.
- **SQ2 (kinds kept, with reasons):**
  - Shared memory between processes, "Unlike other systems which have special restricted mechanisms for inter-process communication" (p. 429).
  - Locking primitives, and sequence breaks, described as "a kind of interrupt" (p. 429).
  - Subprimitives hand-coded in microcode (p. 172).
  - Unrestricted access to internal state, because it is "an interactive system" with "no strong distinction between the 'system' programs and the 'user' programs" (p. 282).
- **SQ3 (kind):** two ways to redirect without changing sender or receiver. Encapsulations made by trace or advise wrap a function and survive its redefinition (p. 153); methods can be wrapped the same way (inferred from p. 309). At the memory level, structure-forward redirects references to another object through invisible pointers (p. 175). Cost is not stated.
- **SQ5 (finding):** causes given by the designers, with no measured baseline:
  - Run time is often "determined by paging rather than by CPU run time" (p. 484).
  - Generic instructions have "data dependencies" that strongly affect speed (p. 484).
  - Call cost is "somewhat higher than it should be", and fixing it "might require incompatible system architecture changes" (p. 485), i.e. tied to the design (inferred).
  - The figures are estimates that "may vary ... by as much as a factor of two" (p. 484).
- **SQ10 (finding):** messages are a calling convention inside one shared address space, and messages between processes "can be implemented as lists or arrays" (p. 429). Encapsulation is intentionally not enforced (p. 282). Effect on performance is not stated.
- **SQ11 (finding):** the designers' reasons for shared state alongside messages are communication "in arbitrary ways through shared Lisp objects" (p. 429) and the need to "examine and alter internal state interactively" (p. 282).
- **SQ16 (finding):** "Everything on the Lisp Machine is written in Lisp" (p. 1), but the base below that is microcode subprimitives, which "cannot do full checking" and can "destroy the environment" (p. 172).

I judged that it does not serve the other twelve:
- **SQ4:** processes share one address space (p. 429), so this is not a system of parts that share no state.
- **SQ6:** the manual does not state the machine's fate.
- **SQ15:** it has a single central scheduler (p. 429), but it does not argue that central scheduling is needed or works better.
- **SQ7–9, SQ12–14, SQ17–19:** nothing in the sections read bears on them.

It also adds processor support for user-level handlers, but only as a design (p. 438–439). The paper's own Active Messages layer is a user-level layer over a network interface, not a primitive below the language.
- **SQ2 (kinds kept, with reasons):**
  - interrupts, "the only way to signal an asynchronous event" (p. 439)
  - polling on the CM-5, because interrupts cost too much (p. 433–434)
  - kernel traps, because there is no user-level access to the network (p. 433)
  - DMA (p. 432) and memory-mapped FIFOs (p. 433)
  - local memory and busy-wait flags (p. 434, p. 436)
  - on the J-Machine, software copies about 1/3 of messages out of the hardware queue (p. 437)
- **SQ4 (findings):** on the nCUBE/2, the kernel checks each send for protection; on the CM-5, the kernel time-shares the network interface. Scheduling is only "primitive" (handlers run to completion), resources are allocated in advance, and Split-C "does not address naming issues". Nothing is said about a central coordinator (p. 433–435, p. 438).
- **SQ5 (findings):** start-up cost per send is 30 µs against the vendor's 160 µs on the nCUBE/2, and 23 µs against 86 µs on the CM-5, where the vendor library is "not yet fully optimized". The designers blame buffer management, which is an implementation cause. The poor performance of message-driven processors is blamed on "lack of locality" and presented as inherent to the design, but this is argued, not measured (p. 432–437).
- **SQ6 (findings):** message-driven prototypes "could not utilize traditional processor design know-how", and the support was "partly counter-productive" (p. 435). The J-Machine "does not actually support the message driven programming model fully", and Monsoon pays for it with "a large amount of high-speed memory" (p. 437). These are stated by the designers of Active Messages; Culler co-designed Monsoon.
- **SQ9 (findings, directly about a message send as the primitive):** the hardware support is "partly counter-productive" (p. 435). Software handlers "can exploit and optimize special cases" (p. 437). One fast primitive is "more versatile" than special hardware (p. 431). Hardware support gets handling down to "a handful of instructions, but not to one" (p. 439).
- **SQ10 (findings):** Active Messages are "more primitive" than send/receive and shared memory, and implement both (p. 431). Send/receive built on them beats the vendor library on the CM-5 (p. 434). Split-C gives a shared-memory style on messages (p. 434), and TAM simulates the message-driven model (p. 437). Which properties are kept or lost is not discussed.
- **SQ12 (finding):** the cost of message libraries comes from buffer management and protocols, "a mismatch between the programming model and the hardware functionality". A software technique, Active Messages, removes most of it (p. 432–433). These are distributed-memory machines, so the hardware's shared-memory model is not in question.
- **SQ13 (partial instance):** the J-Machine's Message-Driven Processor. Its programming model is given (handlers as methods, SEND and SUSPEND, a two-priority hardware queue), and so is a hardware limit (p. 436–438). Why it was discontinued is not stated.

# P5

## Reference
Shan Lu, Soyeon Park, Eunsoo Seo, Yuanyuan Zhou (2008). *Learning from Mistakes: A Comprehensive Study on Real World Concurrency Bug Characteristics*. Proceedings of the 13th International Conference on Architectural Support for Programming Languages and Operating Systems (ASPLOS '08), Seattle, pp. 329–339 (page range from Crossref; the PDF prints no page numbers). https://doi.org/10.1145/1346281.1346323

## Deepest pass
2

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** Empirical defect study: a manual characteristic study of 105 real concurrency bugs taken from the bug databases of four open-source applications (P5, p. 329, p. 330).
- **Context:** Builds on general bug-characteristic studies (IBM defect types [38], operating system errors [8]) and on the single prior concurrency bug-pattern study [11], which used bugs written on purpose by students (P5, p. 330, p. 338); targets data race, atomicity-violation and deadlock detectors, interleaving testing and transactional memory (P5, p. 329–330).
- **Correctness:** The assumptions are stated: the four C/C++ applications represent server and client programs; fixed, reported bugs matter more than unreported ones; the authors know the code from earlier work (P5, p. 332). The paper says it does not claim generality beyond these applications and languages (P5, p. 330, p. 332).
- **Contributions:** 13 findings on bug pattern (atomicity and order violation), manifestation (threads, variables, accesses), fix strategy and avoidance by transactional memory, each with an implication for detection, testing or language design (P5, Table 1, p. 331).
- **Clarity:** Well structured: definitions in Table 2, per-application tables for every finding, worked code examples (Figures 1–9) (P5, p. 332–337). Some table layouts are dense but every number in the abstract can be traced to a table.

## Quality
| Q | Answer | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | yes | Contributions stated in one place, §1.2 and Table 1 (P5, p. 330–331). |
| Q2 | partly | Studied programs named with language (C/C++) and threads; they communicate through shared variables and locks (P5, p. 331–333), but ordering, delivery and blocking behaviour of that mechanism are not described. |
| Q3 | yes | Bugs randomly sampled from the bug databases of MySQL, Apache, Mozilla, OpenOffice (P5, p. 331). |
| Q4 | partly | Defect counts have no comparison baseline; only the transactional-memory avoidance claim names its reference point, "basic TM designs [2, 16, 25, 26]" (P5, p. 337). |
| Q5 | partly | Programs and why chosen (P5, p. 331) and sample size (about 500 reports screened, 105 kept, P5, p. 331) are reported; no hardware setup, because nothing is executed. |
| Q6 | yes | Every percentage in the abstract and Table 1 matches a table in the body (Tables 4–10, P5, p. 333–337); checked by recomputing, e.g. 24/74 = 32 %, 97/105 = 92 %. |
| Q7 | no | Causes such as "programmers think sequentially" (P5, p. 333) or "most threads do not closely interact with many others" (P5, p. 334) are asserted, not isolated by a measurement. |
| Q8 | yes | Dedicated §2.3 "Threats to validity" (P5, p. 332), repeated in §5.3 (P5, p. 337). |
| Q9 | no | Literal rubric: the paper evaluates no system. The authors did not build the studied applications; they only modified and used them in earlier work (P5, p. 332). |

| System | No system is built or evaluated. Studied programs: MySQL (database server), Apache (web server), Mozilla (browser suite), OpenOffice (office suite); 9–13 years of development history, 1–4 million lines of code, C/C++; status: deployed (mature open-source applications) | p. 331, p. 332 |
| Levels with message semantics | Not applicable: the paper describes no hardware, instruction set, kernel or runtime | p. 329 |
| Receiving unit and state ownership | Not applicable as a system. In the studied programs, threads read and write shared variables directly; correctness depends on locks, flags or ordering the programmer adds (e.g. Figure 1, Figure 6) | p. 333, p. 335 |
| Message mechanism | Not stated for the studied programs, except one Mozilla bug (#131447) fixed by changing "a message handling and queueing algorithm" so it tolerates a reply message arriving before its callback is ready | p. 336 |
| Non-message primitives | In the studied programs (application level): shared variables, locks and mutexes, read-write locks, while-flags, I/O and system calls inside critical regions; the paper gives no reason for their use, as it studies defects, not design | p. 331, p. 333, p. 336, p. 338 |
| Self-definition | Not applicable: no system described | p. 329 |
| Interposition | Not applicable: no system described | p. 329 |

| Cost of message primitives | Not applicable: nothing is executed or timed | p. 331 |
| Performance results | None measured. The paper states, without measurement, that fix strategies other than adding locks "usually have better performance than corresponding lock-based fixes, if existing", that one consistency-check fix (Figure 8) "has better performance than corresponding lock-based fixes", and that adding locks "may hurt the performance" | p. 336 |
| Scaling | None measured. Server applications run "hundreds or thousands of threads"; 101 of 105 bugs need no more than two threads to manifest (Table 5) | p. 331, p. 334 |

All stated by the authors (third party to the applications), about defects not performance. The paper frames (a) as how programmers think, (b) as an omission by programmers, and (d) as a limit of locks and basic TM together ("cannot be easily enforced by the basic TM design or locks"); it calls none of them inherent. No measurement isolates any of them | p. 329, p. 333, p. 334, p. 336, p. 338 |

Evidence: qualitative reading of bug reports, patches and discussions, with counts | p. 329, p. 333, p. 334, p. 336, p. 338 |
| Hardware–language trade-off | Only on transactional memory: hardware TM may not handle regions with very large memory footprint (whole garbage collection); I/O is hard to roll back; long transactions "can be addressed by combining software and hardware TMs". Does not concern message send as a primitive | p. 338 |
| Model equivalence | Not addressed | p. 329 |
| Model mixing | Not addressed as a measure; one example of a message handling and queueing algorithm inside threaded Mozilla code (bug #131447), with no frequency or reason | p. 336 |
| Runtime limits | Not addressed | p. 329 |
| Many-core scaling | Not addressed; multi-core hardware is the motivation only ("made concurrent programs pervasive") | p. 329 |
| Adoption factors | Not addressed for architectures; transactional memory called "a promising language feature" with listed concerns (I/O rollback, long regions, code nature) | p. 331, p. 338 |
| Quality | See Quality table above | p. 330–338 |
| Notes | See Notes | — |

## Concepts
| Concept | What the paper says | Page |
|---|---|---|
| new: atomicity violation | "The desired serializability among multiple memory accesses is violated": a region meant to be atomic is not enforced; 51 of 74 non-deadlock bugs | p. 332, p. 333 |
| new: order violation | "The desired order between two (groups of) memory accesses is flipped"; 24 of 74 non-deadlock bugs; "many" are missed by existing race and atomicity detectors; some can be fixed with coarser-grained locking, others cannot be fixed by locks | p. 332, p. 334, p. 336 |
| new: manifestation condition | "A specific execution order among a smallest set (S) of memory accesses" that guarantees the bug manifests, measured in threads, variables and accesses | p. 332 |
| new: multi-variable concurrency bug | Unsynchronized accesses to correlated variables leave inconsistent state; 25 of 74 non-deadlock bugs; missed by single-variable detectors | p. 335 |
| new: data race (not a bug pattern) | Two conflicting accesses to one shared variable without proper synchronization; excluded as a category because races can be benign and "data-race free does not mean concurrency bug free" | p. 329, p. 332 |
| new: deadlock | "Two or more operations circularly wait for each other to release the acquired resource"; 7 of 31 involve one thread acquiring a resource it already holds | p. 329, p. 334 |
| new: order intention | A programmer's expectation that A precedes B (or that A runs before B or not at all); "cannot be easily enforced by the basic TM design or locks"; the "before B or not at all" sub-type occurs in 7 bugs; 20 of 105 bugs cannot benefit from basic TM, their violated intentions being "such as order intentions" | p. 338 |

## Notes
- **Source:** full text, author-hosted PDF https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~shanlu/paper/asplos122-lu.pdf (identical file also at cs.columbia.edu), 11 pages, ASPLOS '08 camera-ready with the ACM copyright block; saved as `research/papers/P5.pdf`. Page numbers cited are the proceedings pages 329–339 (from Crossref); PDF page k is proceedings page 328 + k.
- **Text extraction:** pdftotext merges the abstract with the first introduction column (the "Abstract" heading prints empty); the abstract content was read from that merged text (P5, p. 329).
- **I3 fit:** the paper reports counts for programs that communicate through shared variables and locks (P5, p. 332–336) but never calls them "shared-memory" programs, and gives no split by communication mechanism. Its own example of a message-queue bug in Mozilla (P5, p. 336) shows that at least one studied program also uses messages internally. So the "shared memory only" label in R0-005 is an inference by the reader, not something the paper states.
- **SQ7 relevance:** the only message-related defect is Mozilla #131447, which the paper counts in the "Design" fix category (P5, p. 336). Using this paper as a shared-memory baseline needs that caveat.
- **Generality:** the authors limit their findings to C/C++ server and client applications. Scientific programs, operating systems and Java are explicitly not covered (P5, p. 332).

| new: replicated (not shared) state | Potentially shared state is accessed as a local replica, with consistency kept by messages and agreement protocols. | pp. 6–7 |
| new: split-phase operation | An operation sends a request and continues, and the reply arrives later. | p. 6 |
| new: late binding of protocol and transport | The protocol and transport are chosen at runtime to fit the hardware or workload. | p. 6 |
| new: pipelining and batching of messages | Several requests in flight, or several requests in one message, give more throughput per core. | pp. 2, 6 |

# P9

## Reference
Tu, T., Liu, X., Song, L., Zhang, Y. (2019). *Understanding Real-World Concurrency Bugs in Go*. Proceedings of the 24th International Conference on Architectural Support for Programming Languages and Operating Systems (ASPLOS '19), ACM, pp. 865–878. https://doi.org/10.1145/3297858.3304069. P ID: P9 (row R0-009). Included under I3.

## Deepest pass
2

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** Empirical study of real-world concurrency bugs: "the first systematic study on concurrency bugs in real Go programs", 171 bugs from six applications (P9, p. 1).
- **Context:** Builds on earlier real-world bug studies, mainly of C, C++ and Java (Lu et al. ASPLOS '08 [45], TaxDC [40], Node.js [57]), and on deadlock and race detection work (P9, pp. 1, 5, 12). It sets out to test Go's claim that "explicit message passing is less error-prone" than shared memory (P9, p. 2). It cites earlier static checkers for Go channels (Lange et al. [38, 39], Ng and Yoshida [49]) (P9, p. 12).
- **Correctness:** The assumptions are mostly sound, but the sampling is under-reported. Bugs were found by searching commit logs for keywords (3211 matching commits), then randomly sampling those commits and studying them by hand (P9, p. 5). The paper does not say how many commits were sampled. It does not say who classified each bug, and it gives no agreement figure between classifiers. Only bugs that were fixed and well documented were kept (P9, p. 6). One claim, that message passing is "even more likely" to cause blocking bugs, divides bug counts by static counts of primitive use (Table 4). It does not measure how often each primitive is exercised at run time (P9, pp. 4, 6).
- **Contributions:** (1) The first empirical study of Go concurrency bugs, in six production applications. (2) Nine observations and eight implications about bug causes, fixes and detection. (3) A taxonomy along two orthogonal dimensions: behaviour (blocking or non-blocking) and cause (shared memory or message passing). Study data is published at github.com/system-pclub/go-concurrency-bugs (P9, p. 2).
- **Clarity:** Clear and well organised. Each section ends with numbered Observations and Implications, and counts are in Tables 5–12 (P9, pp. 5–11). The numbers in the tables match the numbers in the text.

|---|---|---|
| Q1 | yes | The aim and a three-item contribution list are stated in the introduction (P9, pp. 1–2). |
| Q2 | partly | The channel mechanism is described for the studied programs. It covers behaviour when the receiver is busy (unbuffered channels block, buffered channels block only when full) and ordering in `select` (random choice). Naming is not described. Message format is not described (P9, p. 3). |
| Q3 | yes | Defects come from the GitHub commit histories and linked bug reports of six real applications (P9, p. 5). |
| Q4 | partly | The defect comparisons name their baseline. Shared-memory bugs are the baseline in the same applications, and gRPC-C is the baseline for goroutine use (P9, pp. 4, 6). The fix results are compared only qualitatively with traditional deadlock fixes and an earlier C/C++ study (P9, pp. 8, 11); the detector results give no baseline (P9, pp. 8, 11). |
| Q5 | partly | The paper gives the programs and why they were chosen (P9, p. 3), and sample sizes and run counts (171 bugs; 41 reproduced; each race test run 100 times) (P9, pp. 5–6, 11). It gives no hardware configuration for the gRPC runs or the detector runs. |
| Q6 | yes | The abstract's 171 bugs are in Table 5 (P9, p. 5). Its "more than half … Go-specific" can be derived from Tables 6 and 9 (P9, pp. 6, 9), but the paper never adds it up. The conclusions' claims are in Tables 6 and 9 (P9, p. 12). |
| Q7 | no | Causes are asserted, not isolated. Examples: "we suspect Go's new programming model" (P9, p. 7); the detector failures are put down to design goals (P9, p. 9); "possible reasons" for the race detector's misses (P9, p. 12); "we suspect" that programmers see channels as safer (P9, p. 11). |
| Q8 | yes | A dedicated "Threats to validity" paragraph (P9, p. 6). |
| Q9 | yes | The evaluated systems are Go's built-in deadlock detector and race detector (P9, pp. 8, 11). No author is listed as a designer of Go or of these detectors. Whether Q9 applies to I3 studies at all is open (see Notes). |

# SQ10

## Question
What does the literature report about the equivalence (duality) of message-passing and shared-memory system structures, and can either one be built on top of the other while keeping its properties (encapsulation, freedom from data races, interposition) and its performance?

## Why it matters to the observation
Lauer and Needham (1978/1979, *On the Duality of Operating System Structures*) argue that message-oriented and procedure-oriented systems are duals: a problem solved in one has a dual solution in the other. If the two are equivalent, the observation's gap may be a matter of which layer exposes which model, and putting messages in hardware may add nothing that a layer above cannot give.

## Origin
counter-evidence (added by skeptic)

## Kind
evidence, because the question asks what the literature reports about equivalence and about building one model on the other: findings (proofs, arguments, measurements), not a list of systems. (`research/sls/1-protocol/step.md`, *How much each question needs*)

## Unit
A finding: a result or argument on the equivalence of the two structures, or a report of one model built on the other, with which properties (encapsulation, freedom from data races, interposition) and how much performance it keeps or loses.

## Enough when
At least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 5 in a row add nothing new. 10 + 5 rather than 10 + 3: the evidence comes from unrelated fields (theory of distributed computing, operating systems, distributed shared memory, multiprocessor hardware, parallel programming measurements).

## Reading order
Theory first, then the two directions alternating, measurements before designs. Lauer and Needham's duality (P18), the partial equivalence under failures (P86); then shared memory built on messages (P279, P269, P271, P275, P267) alternating with messages built on, or beside, shared memory (P274 Alewife, P50 Determinator, P268, P270, P66), the measured comparisons of pure message passing against hybrid models (P90, P219), two views of concurrency in object systems (P255), StarfishOS (P191), COMMOS (P253), Lisp (P15). Round 0 holds 18 papers that serve it (counted as the included rows whose screening reason names this question, plus P275 and P279, whose reasons say only "network" or "library" but whose titles are about shared memory over message passing).

# SQ11

## Question
Why do developers of actor or message-passing programs also use shared state, locks or other concurrency mechanisms alongside messages, and what do they report that the pure message model cannot express or costs too much?

## Why it matters to the observation
The observation wants a system with no escape routes from its own rules. Tasharofi, Dinges and Johnson (2013, *Why Do Scala Developers Mix the Actor Model with other Concurrency Models?*, ECOOP) report that most of the large actor programs they studied mix actors with other concurrency models, partly because of shortcomings of the actor model itself. If programmers keep building escape routes where they have the choice, a machine that removes them may be unusable rather than cleaner.

## Origin
counter-evidence (added by skeptic)

## Kind
evidence, because the question asks why developers mix models and what they report the pure model cannot do: findings (reasons, limits, costs). (`research/sls/1-protocol/step.md`, *How much each question needs*)

## Unit
A finding: a reason developers give or a study reports for using shared state, locks or other mechanisms alongside messages, or a thing the pure message model is reported unable to express or too costly for.

## Enough when
At least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 3 in a row add nothing new.

## Reading order
Empirical studies of real programs first (P19), then designs that add shared state to actors, each stating what the pure model lacked (P93, P92), transactional memory in actors (P55, P56), the type system for race-free messages on shared-memory runtimes (P254), and the L4 lessons (P48). Round 0 holds only these 7 serving papers, fewer than the 10 the rule needs: all are read, and the question stays open until later rounds bring more.

# SQ13

## Question
Which many-core processors were built without hardware shared memory or cache coherence, communicating between cores by messages or channels, how were they programmed, and why were they discontinued or not adopted?

## Why it matters to the observation
Hypothesis H3 says this design is different because it targets many cores with no shared state. That target has been built before: the Inmos Transputer with occam channels, and Intel's 48-core Single-chip Cloud Computer, a message-passing processor without cache coherence (Howard et al., 2010, ISSCC). If such chips were dropped for reasons that still apply, H3 does not separate this work from earlier failures.

## Origin
counter-evidence (added by skeptic)

## Kind
census, because the question asks why each such processor was discontinued or not adopted, and those reasons belong to each chip (its maker, its market, its programming model); a chip left out could be the one whose reason still applies to H3. The population is small, so covering every chip costs no more than saturating on kinds. (`research/sls/1-protocol/step.md`, *How much each question needs*)

Census or kinds is my decision at gate 1c; census is recommended. Estimate from `sls/2-search/R0.md`: 9 included papers name this question in their screening reason (P21, P70, P96, P97, P98, P100, P104, P175, P224); 7 more describe the same or similar processors (P12, P64, P65, P66, P99, P101, P176), counted from the processors their screening reasons name. Together they cover about 5 or 6 distinct processors: the Single-chip Cloud Computer, the Transputer, the Message-Driven Processor of the J-Machine, the M-Machine, the RAMP Blue emulation and the many-core of P101 (whether the M-Machine and P101 lack hardware shared memory is for the full text to say). Under census: about 8–12 papers from round 0 (one per processor, plus a second where the first does not say how it was programmed or why it ended), plus one per chip a later round finds. Under kinds: the stop rule needs at least 13 papers (10 + 3) for about 3 kinds, so it reads more, not fewer.

## Unit
One many-core processor built without hardware shared memory or cache coherence whose cores communicate by messages or channels, with how it was programmed and why it was discontinued or not adopted.

## Enough when
Every distinct processor is covered by one read paper, and a search round finds no new one. A processor counts as covered when the papers read for it say how it was programmed and why it was discontinued or not adopted, or when no paper found says so.

## Reading order
One processor at a time, alternating between decades, the paper that best covers programming and fate first: the Single-chip Cloud Computer (P21, then P104 for how it was programmed, P224 and P100 if still needed), the Transputer (P96, P99, P176), the Message-Driven Processor and J-Machine (P65, P70, P64, P12), the M-Machine (P66), RAMP Blue (P97), the processor of P101. Then the argument for message passing on many-core chips (P98) and PIKA (P175), for the reasons they give about such chips.
