The authors add that a detector in the runtime scheduler finds complex blocking bugs only with great difficulty without losing performance. No measurement isolates it. | pp. 8–9 |
| Fate and reasons | Not applicable: no system is evaluated for fate. Go was the 9th most popular language on GitHub in 2017; at the time of writing there were 187K Go repositories. | p. 3 |
| Concurrency defects | **Population:** six Go applications; 3211 commits matched keywords, and a random sample of them gave 171 bugs (p. 5). **Categories:** behaviour, either blocking (broader than deadlock: it includes waiting with no circular wait) or non-blocking; cause, either shared memory or message passing (p. 5). **Totals:** 85 blocking, 86 non-blocking; 105 shared memory, 66 message passing (Table 5, p. 5). **Blocking** (Table 6, p. 6): shared memory 36 (Mutex 28, RWMutex 5, Wait 3), about 42%; message passing 49 (Chan 29, Chan with other primitives 16, messaging libraries 4), about 58%. **Non-blocking** (Table 9, p. 9; p. 10): shared memory 69, about 80% (traditional 46, anonymous function 11, WaitGroup 6, library 6); message passing 17, about 20% (channel 16, library 1). Message-order defects: 3 bugs from `select`'s random choice (p. 10). Protocol violations: closing a channel twice, missing send, receive or close (pp. 7, 10). **Fixes:** blocking-bug patches average 6.8 lines, and about 90% adjust synchronization primitives (p. 8). About 69% of non-blocking bugs are fixed by restricting timing (p. 11). Channels also fix shared-memory bugs (Table 11, p. 11). **Detection:** the built-in deadlock detector finds 2 of 21 reproduced blocking bugs (Table 8, p. 8). The race detector finds 10 of 20 non-blocking bugs within 100 runs (Table 12, p. 11). **By construction:** the paper claims no design prevents any of these defects. It tests the belief that message passing is less error-prone and refutes it for blocking bugs (Observation 3, p. 6). It supports the belief for non-blocking bugs "when used correctly" (Implication 6, p. 11). | pp. 5–11 |
| What shapes programs | Language features and libraries shape correctness: anonymous-function goroutines, buffered versus unbuffered channels, `select`'s random choice, the `time`, `context` and `testing` libraries, and Go's RWMutex implementation (pp. 2, 6, 9–10). So does programmers' understanding: "the lack of a clear understanding in new Go features" (p. 9), and channels are only useful if programmers understand them and Go's other synchronization (p. 12). Evidence: manual root-cause analysis of 171 real bugs. | pp. 2, 6, 9–10, 12 |
| Hardware–language trade-off | Not applicable: hardware is not discussed. | — |
| Model equivalence | Not stated as one model built on the other. Freedom from data races is not kept: references passed through channels still race (p. 9). Channels are used to fix shared-memory bugs, and replacing a channel with shared variables is used to fix channel bugs (pp. 8, 11). | pp. 8–9, 11 |
| Model mixing | Shared memory is used more than message passing in every application. Mutex is 45.01–70.34% of primitive uses and `chan` 18.48–42.99% (Table 4). The mix is stable from Feb 2015 to May 2018 (Figs. 2–3). gRPC-Go uses 8 kinds of primitive in 786 places, against lock only in gRPC-C (746 places). 16 blocking bugs involve a channel combined with a lock or wait (Table 6). Reason developers give: none recorded; the authors "suspect" programmers see message passing as "more reliable" or "easier-to-program". | pp. 4, 6, 7, 11 |
| Runtime limits | Not applicable to performance. The runtime's deadlock detector reports only when no goroutine can progress. It does not see goroutines that wait on other systems' resources. Its limits come from its minimal-overhead design goal. | pp. 8–9 |
| Many-core scaling | Not applicable. | — |
| Adoption factors | Not applicable: no specialised architecture is discussed. | — |
| Quality | Q1 yes; Q2 partly; Q3 yes; Q4 partly; Q5 partly; Q6 yes; Q7 no; Q8 yes; Q9 yes (see Quality) | pp. 1–12 |
| Notes | See Notes. | — |

## Serves
Every review question this paper serves, and what it contributes to that question's answer.
| SQ | What it contributes | Page |
|---|---|---|
| SQ7 | Finding: in 171 real bugs from six Go applications, message passing causes 49 of 85 blocking bugs (about 58%) and shared memory 36 (about 42%), while shared memory causes 69 of 86 non-blocking bugs (about 80%) and message passing 17 (about 20%); "Contrary to the common belief", message passing is not less error-prone for blocking bugs, but "When used correctly, message passing can be less prone to non-blocking bugs". Kinds include channel-protocol violations (double close, missing send/receive/close) and 3 message-order bugs from `select`'s random choice. Scope: Go programs that use both models, not systems where each piece of state has one owner. | pp. 5–7, 9–11 |
| SQ8 | Finding (language side, not hardware): bugs are traced to Go's language features and libraries (anonymous functions, buffered vs. unbuffered channels, `select`, `time`/`context`/`testing`, Go's RWMutex implementation) and to "the lack of a clear understanding in new Go features"; manual root-cause analysis, no hardware factor examined. | pp. 2, 6, 9–10, 12 |
| SQ10 | Finding: channels layered on a shared-memory language do not keep freedom from data races: a reference passed across a channel still races (Docker#22985, CockroachDB#6111); channels are used to fix shared-memory bugs and shared variables to fix channel bugs, but no equivalence is argued and no performance is compared. | pp. 8–9, 11 |
| SQ11 | Finding: shared memory is used more than channels in all six applications (Mutex 45.01–70.34% vs. `chan` 18.48–42.99% of primitive uses, stable 2015–2018) and 16 blocking bugs mix a channel with a lock or wait; no developer-given reason is recorded, the authors only "suspect" some programmers "view message passing as a more reliable way or easier-to-program way". | pp. 4, 6–7, 11 |

## Concepts
| Concept | What the paper says | Page |
|---|---|---|
| New: blocking bug | One or more goroutines are unintentionally stuck and cannot move forward. This is broader than deadlock, because it includes waiting with no circular wait for a resource that no other goroutine supplies. | p. 5 |
| New: non-blocking bug | All goroutines finish their tasks, but their behaviour is not the one intended. | p. 5 |
| New: cause dimension (shared memory vs. message passing) | Bugs are classified by how goroutines communicate: by misprotecting shared memory or by misusing message passing. | pp. 2, 5 |
| New: message passing is less error-prone (common belief, refuted for blocking bugs) | "Contrary to the common belief", message passing causes 58% of blocking bugs, while shared-memory primitives are used more. Message passing causes fewer non-blocking bugs. | pp. 2, 6, 10–12 |
| New: mixing message passing with other synchronization | Using channels together with locks, wait, or libraries (`context`, `time`, `Pipe`) gives blocking bugs that are "very hard to detect". | pp. 2, 7, 12 |
| New: channel usage rules | The rules Go enforces on its channels: no use before initialization, no double close, no send on a closed channel, and every send or receive needs a matching partner. Breaking these rules is "one major reason" for concurrency bugs. | pp. 2, 3, 12 |
| New: data race through a message-passed reference | Sending a reference to a shared variable over a channel can cause a data race. | p. 9 |
| New: Go's new implementation of existing primitives | The same primitives as in other languages can cause new bugs because Go implements them differently, for example RWMutex giving writers priority. | p. 6 |

## Notes
- **Source:** the authors' PDF at https://songlh.github.io/paper/go-study.pdf (14 pages; acmart LaTeX, created 2019-03-22). It has the same title, DOI and ASPLOS '19 copyright block as the ACM version. The ACM Digital Library PDF link returned an HTML page and was not used. The authors' PDF is saved as `research/papers/P9.pdf`.
- **Page convention:** page numbers in this record are the PDF's pages 1–14. The proceedings page is 864 plus the PDF page (865–878, per Crossref).
- **Checks:** the counts in Tables 5, 6 and 9 add up to the totals in the text (36 + 69 = 105 shared memory; 49 + 17 = 66 message passing). The 42% and 58% split is 36 and 49 of 85 blocking bugs (pp. 5–6, 9).
- **Q9 for I3:** `quality.md` defines Q9 for evaluating a system. Here the system evaluated is incidental: Go's built-in detectors (pp. 8, 11). Answered yes because no author built them, but an I3 study arguably "does not evaluate a system", which would make it "no".
- **SQ7 relevance:** this is a within-language comparison. Both mechanisms are in the same programs, and channels sit on top of a language that also has shared memory. It is not a system built on message passing only (pp. 2–3).
- **Extra artefact:** the authors built a detector for anonymous-function races that found new bugs, one confirmed by developers (p. 12). It is not evaluated in the paper.

# P10

## Reference
Colwell, R. P., Gehringer, E. F., Jensen, E. D. (1988). *Performance Effects of Architectural Complexity in the Intel 432*. ACM Transactions on Computer Systems 6(3), 296–339. https://doi.org/10.1145/45059.214411. Included under I1 and I2 (Send instruction, I1(a), p. 298).

## Deepest pass
3

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** Evaluation of an existing object-based processor (Intel 432) by cycle-level simulation, with "what if" modelling of design changes; ends with a retrospective verdict (p. 299–300, 328, 337–338).
- **Context:** The RISC versus CISC / "functional migration" controversy: critics claim a complex architecture is inherently less efficient than a simple one with good software (p. 296). Builds on the Berkeley 432 measurements of Hansen et al. [13] (p. 309), Colwell's CMU thesis [5] (p. 304, 325, 328, 338) and Gehringer and Colwell's procedure-call paper [10] (p. 309, 338).
- **Correctness:** Assumes that only incremental changes, checked with the 432's silicon architects, are fair (p. 300); that cycle savings measured per category from simulator logs can be combined after adjusting for overlap (p. 333); that cross-machine comparisons with different languages (Ada vs C/Pascal) and technologies are hard to draw conclusions from (p. 309) and a "rough estimate" (p. 336). The remaining 2–3x gap is attributed to object orientation as a residual, not measured directly (p. 336).
- **Contributions:** (1) A breakdown of the 432's lost cycles by cause (compiler, alignment, literals, caches, registers, buses) (p. 311–328); (2) a "synthetic 432" showing, in the authors' words, that "from 35-45 percent" of cycles were wasted by errors unrelated to object orientation (p. 330), though the table it refers to gives 2.2–93.7 % by benchmark, with only the CFA rows (39.6–44.7 %) near that range (Table XVI, p. 329); (3) an estimate of the inherent cost of the 432's style of object orientation (p. 336–337); (4) the conclusion that the 432's performance was "dominated, in large part, by artifacts and not by concepts" (p. 338).
- **Clarity:** Clear structure and many tables; some numeric ranges in the text do not match the tables or each other (see Notes). The available scan has OCR errors in table labels.

## Quality
| Q | Answer | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | yes | The abstract and Section 2.1 state the aim: measure the performance impact of each migrated function and how large an inherent overhead object orientation is (p. 296, 299–300). |
| Q2 | partly | The procedure-call message object is described (data part plus access part, named by an Access Descriptor, built as a refinement of the calling context) (p. 306–307), but the Send/port IPC mechanism is only named; its delivery, ordering and busy-receiver behaviour are not described (p. 298). The reference list has Cox et al. [6] on 432 IPC (p. 338), but the text never cites it. |
| Q3 | partly | Nearly all results come from Intel's Release 3.0 432 microsimulator plus hand modelling (p. 300); real Release 2.0 432/670 hardware was used only to corroborate the Berkeley numbers (p. 309). |
| Q4 | partly | Every improvement is measured against a named baseline (Release 3.0 432, 6 waitstates, Table VI) (p. 310–311), but cross-machine comparisons give ranges over unspecified OS/compiler/clock configurations (p. 335–336). |
| Q5 | partly | Workloads and the reason for choosing them are given (p. 301, 309) and the simulator setup and waitstates are given (p. 300, 310); the CFA benchmarks are not described, and no run count is given (the simulator is deterministic, but the paper does not say so). |
| Q6 | partly | The abstract gives no percentages, only "speeded up very significantly" and "one-fourth to one times the speed" (p. 296); the conclusions' percentages trace to Tables XVI–XXII (p. 329–336), but the ranges do not all match: "one to four times slower" (p. 337) vs "two and three times" (p. 336) vs "3–4 times slower" (p. 336); "another 35–45 percent" (p. 337) vs 33–59 % in Table XXI (p. 336). |
| Q7 | partly | Implementation causes are isolated per category from the simulator log files (Tables VII–XX, p. 313–335); the "inherent cost of object orientation" is a residual estimate (p. 336), and the claim that object orientation is a minor factor in call cost is deferred to [10] (p. 309). |
| Q8 | yes | Paragraphs are dedicated to the limits of benchmarking (Section 2.2, p. 300), to the limits of the cross-machine comparison (p. 309), to double counting (p. 333) and to the "apples and oranges" limit of the final estimate (p. 336–337). |
| Q9 | yes | None of the three authors appears among the authors of the 432 design papers the paper cites (refs 1, 2, 6, 17–21, 30, p. 338–339); the authors note only Intel's cooperation and consultation with the 432's silicon architects (p. 296, 300). |

## Extracted fields
| Field | Value | Page |
|---|---|---|
| Reference | Colwell, Gehringer, Jensen (1988), ACM TOCS 6(3), pp. 296–339; P10; included under I1 and I2 (Send instruction, I1(a), p. 298; R0-010). | p. 296, 298 |
| Paper type | Evaluation (simulation of an existing processor plus modelled design changes), with a closing retrospective on the system's fate. | p. 299–300, 337–338 |
| System | Intel 432 (iAPX 432), Intel Corporation; conceived 1975; status: silicon, sold commercially (432/670 development system; OS Releases 2.0 and 3.0); year built not stated. Also the "synthetic 432", a hypothetical improved 432 (simulated/modelled only). | p. 297, 299, 309, 328 |
| Levels with message semantics | Instruction set: no; Send is one of over 200 instructions (an "interprocess communication primitive"), next to memory-to-memory data instructions. Microcode/hardware: no; IPC, scheduling, dispatching, virtual memory and I/O are migrated into the architecture, but alongside direct memory references. Kernel: not stated (432 supports "domain-based operating systems"). Language (Ada): no; procedure calls pass parameters in a Message object. Started message-based and later added non-message paths: not stated. | p. 297–299, 306, 316 |
| Receiving unit and state ownership | Objects (instruction segments, data structures, processes, messages); a context (activation record) receives call parameters through a Message object. State is readable or writable by any program holding an Access Descriptor with read/write rights to the object; every reference is checked for rights and bounds by hardware/microcode. The 432 is a shared-memory multiprocessor; the paper notes data shared without an intervening type manager is "extremely rare" in well-modularized code. | p. 297, 303–306, 321 |
| Message mechanism | Procedure call (the mechanism measured): synchronous (inferred from call/return semantics; the paper does not use the word, p. 321); parameters go in the data part of the MSG object and ADs to passed objects in its access part; receiver named by capability (AD); MSG is a refinement of the calling context; the called context must traverse the refinement ("approximately 77 clock cycles" on p. 307, but 148 cycles on p. 323 and p. 326; p. 322 gives 77 for a plain DS-cache miss and 148 for a refinement) and execute enter-environment to use passed ADs. Send/port IPC: named only; ordering, buffering, busy-receiver behaviour and dispatch not described here (the reference list has Cox et al. [6], "Interprocess communication and processor dispatching on the Intel 432", p. 338, which the text never cites). GDPs are "self-dispatching" via on-chip microcode. | p. 297–298, 306–307, 312, 322–324, 326, 338 |
| Non-message primitives | Shared memory: "pure memory-to-memory architecture" on a shared-memory multiprocessor; reasons: chip size (registers would cost base/length registers or microcode), faster process swap with little on-chip state, and "conceptual unity and simplicity" of a memory-to-memory shared-memory machine. Microcode: creates protected pointers (no instruction for it), manipulates object headers and rights checks; reason: pointers must not be forgeable. I/O: done only by the Interface Processor, so the GDPs see "only objects". Garbage-collection marking in copy-AD (9 cycles, cannot be turned off). Global Constants Object read by microcode. Unprotected branch-intersegment(-and-link) instructions exist but the compiler never generated them. Unified fault handler in hardware, microcode and OS. | p. 297, 299, 302, 311, 315–317, 319 |
| Self-definition | Object addressing, rights checks, protected-pointer creation, IPC, scheduling, dispatching, virtual memory and fault handling are implemented in microcode and hardware, outside the object model ("functional migration"). Whether a running program can inspect or change those levels: not stated. Base cost: "Barring microcode bugs ... an errant user program can crash itself but cannot bring down the 432's operating system"; the Instruction Decode Unit fills an entire chip; chip space limited caches and excluded registers. | p. 296, 298–299, 302, 305, 316 |
| Interposition | Not stated. (The proposed AD cache is placed in the addressing path "without violating any of the fundamental principles of object orientation", but it is a hardware cache, not a third component between sender and receiver.) | p. 325 |
| Operating system functions | Protection: capabilities (ADs) with per-reference rights and bounds checks in hardware/microcode, two-level addressing, "need-to-know" contexts; central component: not stated. Scheduling: process scheduling and processor dispatching migrated into the architecture, GDPs self-dispatching; central component: not stated. Resource allocation: virtual memory management in the architecture via Object Table Directory and Object Tables; garbage collection; devices only via Interface Processors; memory must be cleared before reuse by a new context. Naming: two-level addressing (AD selector to AD, to Object Table Directory and Object Table, to physical address). Failure handling: a "distributed fault handler" across hardware, microcode and OS software. Decentralised version cost: not stated. | p. 297, 299, 303–305, 311, 332–333 |
| Cost of message primitives | Procedure call: 982 cycles, 16 memory reads and 24 writes, about 10x a call on MC68010 or VAX-11/780 (in cycles). Return: about 850 cycles, of which about 430 restore three environments (144 per environment). Passing two integers in a recursive call: 148 cycles. DS-cache miss: 77 cycles (148 for a refinement). Enter-environment: 9 memory operations. Moving memory clearing to dedicated hardware would speed a call by about 31 %. Send (IPC) latency: not reported. Platform: Intel Release 3.0 432 microsimulator (Simula on DEC KL10), 6 waitstates default. | p. 300, 308–310, 322, 324, 333 |
| Performance results | (1) Berkeley data [13], time in ms, Search/Sieve/Puzzle/Acker: 432 4 MHz Ada rel. 3 (16-bit) 14.2/3200/165000/260000; VAX-11/780 C 1.4/250/9400/4600; 8086 5 MHz Pascal 7.3/764/44000/11100; 68000 8 MHz C 4.7/740/37100/7800. (2) Rel. 2.0 432 was 10x (Search) to 26x (Acker) slower than the VAX, 2–23x slower than the 8086. (3) Baseline 432 Rel. 3.0, 6 waitstates, total cycles: Acker 394,650,393; Sieve 7,603,486; CFA5 34,916,445; CFA5R 61,137,893; CFA10 48,803,488; Dhrystone 69,036. (4) Synthetic baseline (compiler and alignment/literal fixes) vs original baseline, cycles saved: Acker 2.2 %, Sieve 14.9 %, CFA5 43.6 %, CFA5R 39.6 %, CFA10 44.7 %, Dhrystone 93.7 %. (5) Synthetic plus technology improvements vs original baseline: 35, 65, 68, 66, 68, 58 % saved; real time Sieve 332 ms, Dhrystone 3.59 ms. (6) Dhrystone, others per Weicker [36]: VAX-11/780 540–1,800 µs; 80286/68000 1,000–1,500 µs; 8088 2,400–9,600 µs; so the improved 432 is about 3–4x slower than 16-bit microprocessors. | p. 309–311, 329, 335–336 |
| Scaling | Not measured. The paper analyses uniprocessor performance only and states the 432's multiprocessing support is "not addressed". | p. 318, 328 |
| Attributed causes | (a) Ada compiler code quality (no flow analysis, redundant enter-environments, no common subexpression elimination, value/result parameters, only protected calls) loses 25–35 % of throughput; stated by the authors (third party); implementation; isolated per category by simulator-log breakdown (Tables VII–XI, XVII–XVIII). (b) Bit-aligned instructions and lack of instruction-stream literals lose another 5–10 %; authors; implementation; isolated (Tables XIII–XIV). Lack of literals came from an early Intel study that zero and one would suffice, which "enabled the Instruction Decoder and Execution Unit to be built as separate chips" (George Cox, private communication, p. 318–319; the paper gives Cox no role, but he co-authored 432 design papers [6] and [30], p. 338–339). (c) No data registers, 16-bit buses, 16-bit top of stack, no AD cache, software memory clearing: design/technology limits; isolated (Tables XII, XIX–XX). (d) DS cache flushed on every call, return and enter because protected calls must deny access to objects without an AD; authors say an AD cache could remove much of this without violating object principles, so implementation. (e) Remaining 2–3x vs contemporaries: "our estimate for the inherent cost of the 432's style of object orientation"; inherent to the 432's set of design decisions, not to object-based systems in general; residual estimate, not isolated. (f) Procedure-call cost: object orientation "shown to be only a minor factor" in [10], not here. (g) the cycles wasted ("from 35-45 percent" in the text; 2.2–93.7 % by benchmark in Table XVI, p. 329) are "not spent in pursuit of object orientation", not "the inevitable fallout of a complex instruction set", nor microcode inefficiency. | p. 301, 309, 312–330, 336–337 |
| Fate and reasons | Commercial failure: "not a commercial success" (p. 299); "as a commercial venture ... failed completely" (p. 337). Reasons given: probably "tried to do too many new things all at once (while getting a few old things wrong along the way)"; the target market (high reliability/availability, large software development) "may still not be large enough or defined well enough". Not given as reasons for the failure: "perhaps due to" publicity and high expectations, its disappointing performance made it "the favorite target" of researchers (p. 337); initial performance measurements were "quite discouraging" (p. 297). Judged a research success: it showed that flow of control, modularization, storage hierarchies, virtual memory, message passing and process/processor scheduling can be "subsumed under a unified set of ideas". Stated by the authors (third party, not designers). | p. 297, 299, 337–338 |
| Concurrency defects | Not applicable: the paper reports no defect study. | p. 296 |
| What shapes programs | Not addressed as a finding. The paper notes that the 432's goal of better software productivity could not be evaluated because too few large programming efforts existed. It reports the module connectivity of three large Ada systems (Mercury mail, about 33K lines; Adix kernel, about 20K lines; a Hughes database, about 5K lines): 38 % of Mercury routines call no other package and 12 % call more than three. | p. 299, 320–321 |
| Hardware–language trade-off | Costs of raising the interface: complex instruction set (Instruction Decode Unit fills a chip), little chip space left for registers or caches, slow protected calls (982 cycles). Benefits claimed by designers: compact code, complete/orthogonal instruction set easing compilers, unified fault model; the authors doubt the value of completeness since high-level-language users never see the instruction set, and bit-alignment did not make code much smaller than VAX or 68000 code. Even if IPC and procedure calls took zero time, the 432 would still be slow. Moving intra-module call protection from hardware to the compiler would save up to 20.5 % (Dhrystone). The compiler never used the cheaper instructions the hardware offered. Applies to message send: partly; measured on the procedure call with its Message object, not on Send. | p. 296, 298–299, 301, 305, 309, 315–316, 318 |
| Model equivalence | Messages on shared memory: the 432 is a shared-memory multiprocessor in which messages are objects in memory, and a procedure-call Message object is a refinement (a view) of the caller's context. Encapsulation is kept by capabilities and per-reference checks. The paper does not quantify what is kept or lost against a pure message model. | p. 297, 306–307 |
| Model mixing | Not addressed. | p. 296 |
| Runtime limits | Not addressed (no actor or message runtime is studied). | p. 296 |
| Many-core scaling | Not addressed. The 432 supports "transparent multiprocessing" over a variable number of GDPs on a shared-memory interconnect; the paper notes only that registers would reduce memory contention among GDPs. | p. 297–298, 318 |
| Adoption factors | Intel 432: not adopted (commercial failure). Factors given: too many innovations at once; a target market too small or poorly defined to support special systems (p. 337). Performance gains were "not enough to satisfy either its champions or its critics" (p. 297), but the paper does not name performance or publicity as causes of non-adoption. Software compatibility and ecosystem: not stated. | p. 297, 337 |
| Quality | See the Quality table: Q1 yes, Q2 partly, Q3 partly, Q4 partly, Q5 partly, Q6 partly, Q7 partly, Q8 yes, Q9 yes. | p. 296–339 |
| Notes | The paper argues RISC critiques "find apt targets in the Intel 432" but that published RISC work "does not indicate what the 432 should have done". | p. 337 |

## Serves
Every review question this paper serves, and what it contributes to that question's answer.
| SQ | What it contributes | Page |
|---|---|---|
| SQ1 | Kind: an object-based processor (Intel 432, silicon, sold) whose instruction set has a Send instruction, an "interprocess communication primitive", with IPC, scheduling and dispatching migrated into microcode/hardware; the measured mechanism is the procedure call, whose parameters go in a Message object named by an Access Descriptor. Message semantics at instruction set and microcode, but not exclusive (memory-to-memory data instructions); a later added non-message path is not stated. | p. 297–298, 306–307 |
| SQ2 | Kinds kept that are not message sends, with reasons: shared memory ("pure memory-to-memory architecture", for chip size, faster process swap and "conceptual unity and simplicity"); microcode as the only creator of protected pointers (so pointers cannot be forged); I/O only through the Interface Processor (GDPs see "only objects"); unprotected branch-intersegment instructions (never used by the compiler). | p. 302, 311, 315–317 |
| SQ5 | Findings: Rel. 2.0 432 10x (Search) to 26x (Acker) slower than VAX-11/780 (Berkeley data); a procedure call costs 982 cycles, about 10x MC68010/VAX; compiler code quality loses 25–35 % and bit alignment/no literals another 5–10 % (implementation, isolated per category, third party); remaining 2–3x on Dhrystone given as "our estimate for the inherent cost of the 432's style of object orientation" (residual, not isolated); Send latency not reported; scaling with processors not measured. | p. 301, 309–310, 312–330, 336–337 |
| SQ6 | Finding (authors not among the 432 designers): "as a commercial venture ... failed completely"; probably "tried to do too many new things all at once (while getting a few old things wrong along the way)", and the target market "may still not be large enough or defined well enough". | p. 337 |
| SQ9 | Finding: raising the interface cost chip space (the Instruction Decode Unit fills a chip, leaving no room for data registers or larger caches) and gave slow protected calls; claimed benefits (completeness, compact bit-aligned code) were doubted or small; "Even if the high-level functions of the 432 (interprocess communication, procedure calls) were free, executing in zero time" it would still be slow, so the argument applies only partly to a message send (measured on the procedure call, not on Send). | p. 298–299, 301, 309, 316, 318 |
| SQ10 | Finding: messages built on shared memory: a procedure-call Message object is an object in shared memory and a refinement of the caller's context, with encapsulation kept by capabilities and per-reference checks; the refinement saves the caller a cache miss but costs the callee 148 cycles to traverse. What is kept or lost against a pure message model is not quantified. | p. 297, 306–307, 323 |
| SQ16 | Finding (inferred relevance; the 432 is not described as reflective): object addressing, rights checks, protected-pointer creation, IPC, scheduling and fault handling stay outside the object model, in microcode and hardware; the base costs chip space (decode unit fills a chip, registers excluded); whether programs can inspect or change it is not stated. | p. 298–299, 302, 305, 316 |
| SQ18 | Finding (independent third-party evaluation): the "synthetic 432" shows cycles wasted by compiler and design errors "not spent in pursuit of object orientation" ("from 35-45 percent" in the text, 2.2–93.7 % by benchmark in Table XVI); DS-cache flushing on protected calls is called fixable by an AD cache without violating object principles; the remaining 2–3x on Dhrystone is the authors' "rough estimate" of "the inherent cost of the 432's style of object orientation"; performance "dominated, in large part, by artifacts and not by concepts". | p. 325, 329–330, 336–338 |

## Concepts
| Concept | What the paper says | Page |
|---|---|---|
| new: functional migration | Moving functions that other systems perform in software (OS functions, high-level-language operations, object addressing and checks, fault handling) into microcode and hardware. | p. 296, 298–299 |
| new: object model | The 432's common semantic model supporting both data abstraction and domain-based operating systems; all information is encapsulated in protected objects. | p. 297 |
| new: protected pointer (capability, Access Descriptor) | A pointer the user program cannot manipulate directly; only microcode creates and manipulates it; carries the rights the bearer has to the object. | p. 302–304, 306 |
| new: two-level addressing | AD to Object Table Directory and Object Table to physical address; separates object location, size and type from the rights programs have to them. | p. 304–305 |
| new: entered environment and object qualification | An object must be "entered" and "qualified" (type, length, rights checked, base/length cached) before use; the 432 provides three entered environments per context. | p. 303–304, 308, 320 |
| new: refinement (Message object) | The procedure-call Message object is a refinement of the calling context, which saves the caller a cache miss but makes the callee traverse the refinement. | p. 307, 323 |
| new: transparent multiprocessing | The object model lets the 432 run on a variable number of processors without recompiling software. | p. 297 |
| new: cycle sink | A cause of lost cycles measured from simulator logs (compiler, alignment, literals, caches, registers, buses). | p. 310, 330 |
| new: synthetic 432 | A hypothetical 432 with the design and compiler errors corrected and incrementally better technology, used to isolate the cost of object orientation. | p. 328–329 |
| new: inherent cost of object orientation | The remaining performance gap (2–3x, or 1–4x) of the improved 432 against conventional processors, attributed to the 432's specific set of object-orientation decisions, not to object-based systems in general. | p. 336–337 |
| new: artifacts vs concepts | The 432's performance was "dominated, in large part, by artifacts and not by concepts". | p. 338 |
| new: compiler-protected intra-module call | Protection of intra-module calls left to the compiler, with only inter-module calls protected by the architecture. | p. 315–316 |

## Notes
- **Source:** full text read from the PDF in the Internet Archive item `432_complexity_paper` (file `10.1.1.140.5969.pdf`, a CiteSeerX scan of the published ACM TOCS version, 44 pages = pp. 296–339, with ACM header and page numbers). The ACM Digital Library PDF (the OpenAlex/Semantic Scholar open-access link) returned HTTP 403, and its Wayback Machine capture could not be loaded. Saved as `research/papers/P10.pdf`. Journal page = PDF page + 295. The scan's OCR garbles some labels (e.g. "1966" for 1988 in footers, "A&r" for Acker); values were read from the page text.
- **Pass:** pass 3, meaning every section and table was read and figures were checked across tables and against the abstract and conclusions (see the inconsistencies below). The arguments were not re-derived from the simulator data, which is not available.
- **Internal inconsistencies found (p.):** text says the CFA benchmarks show a "30–40 percent reduction" (p. 329), but Table XVI shows 39.6–44.7 % (p. 329); Table XXI lists Sieve "cycles saved" and "improved cycles" both as 4,489,605 (p. 336), which cannot both be right; the inherent-cost ratio is given as "one-fourth to one times the speed" (p. 296) and "one to four times slower" (p. 337), which say the same thing (1–4x, across all benchmarks), while the Dhrystone-only figures are 3–4x before the technology allowance and 2–3x after it (p. 336).
- **Criteria:** besides I2, the paper describes an instruction set with a Send instruction named an "interprocess communication primitive" (p. 298), which may also satisfy I1(a); R0-010 records I2 only.
- **Related work to snowball:** Cox et al. 1983, "Interprocess communication and processor dispatching on the Intel 432", ACM TOCS 1(1) (ref [6], p. 338), which by its title should describe the Send/port mechanism this paper does not (the text never cites it); Gehringer and Colwell 1986, ISCA (ref [10], p. 338) holds the procedure-call analysis; Colwell's 1985 CMU thesis CMU-CS-85-159 (ref [5], p. 338) holds the details omitted for space (p. 328).

## Reference
David Michael Ungar (1986, dated "February, 1986" on the cover). *The Design and Evaluation of a High Performance Smalltalk System*. PhD dissertation, Computer Science, University of California, Berkeley. Published as UC Berkeley technical report UCB/CSD-86-287 and later as a book by MIT Press (ACM Distinguished Dissertation, 1987). The report number and the MIT Press edition come from the reference line given to me; neither is printed on the scanned pages I read. P11, screened in under I2 (row R0-011). Pages cited below are the printed arabic page numbers of the dissertation scan in `papers/P11.pdf`. Printed p. *n* is PDF page *n* + 18 up to printed p. 152 (e.g. Chapter 1 starts on printed p. 1, PDF p. 19). Printed p. 153 is scanned twice (PDF pp. 171–172), so from there on printed p. *n* is PDF page *n* + 19 (e.g. Appendix A p. 185 is PDF p. 204). The front matter has no printed numbers, so the abstract is cited by its PDF pages (pp. 7–8). This is not the MIT Press edition, whose page numbers will differ.

## Deepest pass
2

## Serves
Every review question this paper serves, and what it contributes to that question's answer.
| SQ | What it contributes | Page |
|---|---|---|
| SQ5 | Findings (designer, simulated at an assumed 400 ns cycle): SOAR runs the Xerox macro-benchmarks at a median 107% of the Dorado and 103% on the compiler benchmark, against 40% for the Xerox PS 68010 compiler (Tables 4.2–4.3, p. 66). Send-related cost: in-line caching takes 23% of SOAR's time (11% probes, 12% misses, pp. 47, 72); `call` 1 cycle, `return` 2 (design figures, p. 37). Causes, by the designer, isolated by omission costs: "Register windows, tagged integer instructions, direct pointers, and generation scavenging account for most of the difference" with the 68010 (p. 72); the 1.6 ratio to RISC II "indicates that the reduced instruction set architecture (including register windows) and the Smalltalk-specific hardware features contribute equally to performance" (p. 71). Implementation causes: the fast-shuffle critical path raised the cycle from 400 to 510 ns (pp. 48, 72); GC hardware "probably did not speed up SOAR" (p. 72, not isolated). SOAR has no message-send instruction (sends compile to `call` plus software lookup, pp. 37, 46–47), so it serves SQ5 as a language-directed (Smalltalk-80) processor under I2, not as a message-based one. | pp. 37, 46–48, 66, 71–72 |
| SQ6 | Findings, stated by the author as a later evaluator of other machines: earlier language machines "closely coupled the source language semantics to the hardware-supported operations and data types. Although memory-efficient, this approach has usually resulted in increased cost and poor performance" (p. 14). Exploratory environments such as Smalltalk-80 "remain largely experimental" because "They suffer from poor cost-performance" (p. 10); the Dorado costs $120,000 (p. 11); "this lack of widely available high-performance implementations has severely curtailed the system's acceptance" (p. 1). Scheme-79 shows "a machine that is specialized for a particular system must also exploit compilation to attain high performance" (p. 17). SOAR's own fate is not reported beyond chips that ran diagnostics at 800 ns (p. 127). | pp. 1, 10–11, 14, 17, 127 |
| SQ9 | Findings (designer; simulated or estimated): compiling to a low-level instruction set instead of Smalltalk bytecodes gives "an approximate doubling in speed" for about 500 KB more memory (p. 35; Table 4.4's ~100% is a "Rough estimate", p. 68), and bytecode decoding "takes either substantial hardware or substantial time" (p. 34). Earlier systems "pushed the source-level semantics into the hardware, sacrificing either simplicity or performance" (p. 2); "the key to good performance is a willingness to migrate functionality from one level of abstraction to another" (p. 126). On the message send: it was not raised into hardware; instantaneous call-lookup hardware would gain at most 23% (Table 4.4, p. 68), and the author suggests further research into computing the call target "could yield substantial savings" (p. 47). Four specialised features were "mistakes" (the architect's trap, p. 70). | pp. 2, 34–35, 47, 68, 70, 126 |

## Reference
William J. Dally, J.A. Stuart Fiske, John S. Keen, Richard A. Lethin, Michael D. Noakes, Peter R. Nuth, Roy E. Davison, Gregory A. Fyler (1992). *The Message-Driven Processor: A Multicomputer Processing Node with Efficient Mechanisms*. IEEE Micro 12(2), 23–39. https://doi.org/10.1109/40.127581. P12, included under I1 (row R0-012). Pages below are those of the authors' 25-page preprint (see Notes), not the IEEE Micro pages.

## Deepest pass
2

## Serves
Every review question this paper serves, and what it contributes to that question's answer.
| SQ | What it contributes | Page |
|---|---|---|
| SQ1 | Kind: a message-driven multicomputer node. SEND instructions are in the ISA, and buffering and dispatch are in hardware, so message arrival creates a task ("There is no receive instruction"). Message semantics hold at the hardware level for task creation only; the ISA is a conventional one extended with SEND (inferred: not message-based at the instruction-set level). At the language level (CST), a non-message path was added: a call whose type is known "is optimized directly to the correct function invocation". | pp. 1, 6, 9, 20 |
| SQ2 | Kinds kept that are not message sends, with the designers' reasons. Presence and type tags with fault handlers ("makes software more efficient and robust", p. 7). Segment descriptors with bounds checks (relocation and protection, pp. 6–7). A translation table written by ENTER (global naming, p. 7). A diagnostic port for a console processor (supervisory commands, pp. 3, 5). Local READ/WRITE, with no reason given (p. 8). No level is said to be written in the system's own objects and messages: handlers are MDP assembly (pp. 10–11, 22). | pp. 3, 5–8, 10–11, 22 |
| SQ3 | Serves only by its criterion (I1): no interposition mechanism is stated. The nearest thing is an XLATE miss or fault, after which COSMOS moves or copies the object, so its location stays transparent to the caller. No cost is given. | pp. 7, 21 |
| SQ4 | Findings for a machine of nodes that share no memory. Protection: per-node segment descriptors and IP status bits, with no central component (pp. 6, 15). Scheduling: per-node hardware dispatch from priority queues, and load balancing and scheduling are "open questions" (pp. 6, 9, 18). Naming: per-node translation tables, with a global namespace from COSMOS (pp. 7, 20). Resource allocation: "buffer memory is automatically allocated on the receiving node" (p. 2). A console processor reaches every node, but run-time use is not stated (pp. 3, 5). No costs are given. | pp. 2–3, 5–7, 9, 15, 18, 20 |
| SQ5 | Finding: message delivery plus task dispatch takes "< 2 µs on the J-Machine, as opposed to 5 ms on an iPSC-1 or 300 µs on an iPSC-2" (configuration not given). The designers attribute it to the design: sequential machines need "hundreds of instructions to create a new process" (p. 2), and hardware dispatch "avoids the overhead otherwise associated with control transfer" (pp. 10–11). Not isolated. The designers attribute a 3–4x area and 2–3x performance loss to the implementation (standard cells, p. 16). | pp. 2, 10–11, 16 |
| SQ6 | Finding from the designers: at the time of writing the MDP is a research chip, not adopted. A commercial product is "very plausible". The designers name no well-established parallel benchmarks, programs biased to their original machines, and a "very conservative" implementation. | pp. 23–24 |
| SQ8 | Finding (designers' assertion, no data): "most parallel programs are very biased by the mechanisms (or lack thereof) of the machines for which they were initially written" (p. 24). Also, fine-grain parallelism is hard to extract from "stock programs written in C or FORTRAN" (p. 18). | pp. 18, 24 |
| SQ9 | Finding (argued, not measured): the MDP provides general mechanisms (SEND plus hardware dispatch, tags, translation) rather than specialising to one model, and is claimed "competitive with processing nodes specialized to a single model of computation such as iWARP" and the Transputer. The argument is about a message send as the primitive. Tags are said to make the no-fault case faster than "test and branch instructions". | pp. 1–2, 7, 23 |
| SQ10 | Finding: shared memory built on messages. "one can build a shared memory model that gives the application programmer a single, shared address space" through name translation. CST and dataflow run on a shared address space. The paper does not say which properties or how much performance are kept or lost. | pp. 5, 7, 23 |
| SQ11 | Finding, at the compiler and not from developers: the CST compiler replaces message sends with a direct function call when the receiver's type is known or declared, as an optimisation. The paper does not state how often this happens or what it costs. | p. 20 |
| SQ18 | Finding (designers, not independent): the 3–4x area and 2–3x performance loss is attributed to the implementation (standard cells), not to tags or object addressing. The costs of tags and XLATE themselves are not measured. | pp. 7, 16 |

## Concepts
| Concept | What the paper says | Page |
|---|---|---|
| message-driven processing (new) | "processing is performed in response to messages (via the dispatch mechanism). There is no receive instruction. A task is created to handle each arriving message." | p. 1 |
| primitive mechanisms vs programming models (new) | Mechanisms are the hardware's primitive operations from which programming abstractions are built. The MDP gives general communication, synchronisation and naming mechanisms instead of specialising for one model. | pp. 1–2 |
| message dispatch as task creation (new) | The header opcode is loaded into the IP and a message segment descriptor goes into A3, creating a task in 3 cycles. | p. 9 |
| presence tags / futures (FUT, CFUT) (new) | Tagged locations are marked empty, and reading one faults and suspends the task until a value is written. Used for synchronisation. | pp. 6–7 |
| name translation (XLATE/ENTER) (new) | A hardware associative table maps arbitrary keys to values (segment descriptors or node numbers) to support a global virtual address space. | p. 7 |
| fine-grain multicomputer / jellybean node (new) | An inexpensive node with small memory, many per system, giving more performance per unit cost. Tasks are about 20 instructions and objects about 8 words. | pp. 1–2, 23 |
| global virtual address space over message passing (new) | The same IDs name local and remote objects. A shared-memory model can be built on the mechanisms. | pp. 3, 5 |
| selector-object dispatch (new) | CST method invocation is a message to the first argument. COSMOS picks the function by class from a selector object; known types bypass it with a direct call. | pp. 20–21 |

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** Evaluation of a built system: a reduced instruction set computer for Smalltalk (SOAR), used to "estimate the performance implications of the Smalltalk-80 programming environment" (P13, abstract). Probably also a retrospective, as R0-015 proposes, but the abstract does not say so.
- **Context:** Exploratory programming environments such as Smalltalk-80 "require such expensive computers that few programmers can afford them"; SOAR ("Smalltalk on a RISC") was built by a research project at the University of California to widen that community (P13, abstract). Related work cited by the paper: not reachable.
- **Correctness:** Not assessable from the abstract. The abstract claims the authors "are now able to estimate" performance implications, which implies measurement on SOAR, but no figures, baselines or setup are given (P13, abstract).
- **Contributions:** (1) a list of "the demands that Smalltalk-80 places on traditional computer systems"; (2) "software and hardware ideas that answer those demands"; (3) an estimate of the performance implications of Smalltalk-80 (P13, abstract).
- **Clarity:** The abstract is clear about the aim and the structure of the article; the body was not read.

## Concepts
| Concept | What the paper says | Page |
|---|---|---|
| new: single-writer, multiple-reader (SWMR) invariant | All coherence protocols ensure that, per block, there is either one core with write permission or any number with read permission. | p. 2 |
| new: scalable coherence | Coherence is "scalable" when its cost "grows (at most) slowly as core count increases". Five costs are examined: traffic, storage, inclusion, latency, energy. | p. 3 |
| new: amortized coherence traffic | A write that invalidates N sharers must follow N read misses, so average traffic per miss is constant in core count. | p. 3 |
| new: exact vs inexact encoding of sharers | Exact encoding uses one bit per core and gives constant traffic. Inexact (coarse-vector, limited-pointer) encoding bounds storage but causes "unnecessary invalidations", up to ~6× traffic at 1024 cores. | pp. 4–5 |
| new: hierarchical inclusive coherence | Cluster caches track their cores and the last-level cache tracks clusters. This gives fan-out invalidation, acknowledgment combining, and storage proportional to √C or ∛C. | pp. 5–6 |
| new: explicit eviction notifications | Private caches notify the shared cache on every eviction, including clean ones, so tracking is exact and recalls become rare. The cost is extra small messages. | p. 3, p. 6 |
| new: recall (back-invalidation) | When an inclusive shared cache evicts a block with sharers, it forces their eviction. This is rare (<0.1%) at a 4× capacity ratio. | p. 3, pp. 6–7 |
| new: direct vs indirect miss | Coherence adds latency only to indirect misses (blocks cached elsewhere), 1.5–2× a non-coherent miss, and the ratio does not depend on core count. | p. 7 |
| new: coherence messages implement shared memory | The coherent shared-memory abstraction is carried by point-to-point request, forward, invalidation, recall and ack messages between cache controllers. | pp. 2–3 |
| new: complexity shifting | Removing hardware coherence "does not remove the complexity, but rather shifts the complexity from hardware to software". | p. 9 |
| new: compatibility as reason for coherence | Coherence dominates for "technical and legacy reasons", and systems "tend not to abandon compatibility to eliminate small costs". | p. 1 |
| new: coexistence of communication paradigms | Message passing and scratchpads persist in HPC and real-time niches but "coexist with" coherent shared memory, which dominates mainstream chips. | p. 1, p. 8 |

| SQ4 | Finding (design, not measured): protection is per node by base/limit address registers and type checks, while READ and WRITE messages from any sender reach physical memory; scheduling is per-node hardware by two priority levels; naming is by global object identifiers translated per node by the associative table. No central component is described for any of them; their cost is not stated. | pp. 189–194 |
| SQ5 | Finding (simulated, designers): Table 1 gives per-message cycle counts on the MDP instruction-level/RT-level simulators (e.g. SEND 8, CALL 5, READ 5+W; expected clock 100 ns), "less than ten clock cycles per message" against "about 300µs" on Cosmic Cube, iPSC and S-NET (no source or configuration), stated as "more than an order of magnitude". The designers attribute the gain to "a message-driven control mechanism", the memory-based ISA with two register sets, and associative memory, all inherent to the design and not isolated. | pp. 190, 195–196 |
| SQ9 | Finding (argument by the designers, not a measured comparison): putting the message send in the machine reduces overhead "by directly executing messages rather than interpreting them with sequences of instructions"; only EXECUTE is hard-wired, and more complex messages "can be implemented as almost as efficiently using the EXECUTE message as they could if they were hard-wired". | pp. 189, 191 |
| SQ10 | Finding (claim, no measurement): a shared-memory-like "single global name space" is provided over messages and object-ID translation, and the paper says the MDP "provides many of the advantages of both message-passing multicomputers and shared-memory multiprocessors". Properties kept or lost and their performance are not reported. | p. 196 |
| SQ13 | Instance (partial): the MDP, the node of a machine without hardware shared memory whose nodes communicate by messages; programmed as an object-oriented concurrent system where "programs operate by sending messages to objects", with ROM message routines, and also seen "as an emulator ... with other programming models". Why it was discontinued or not adopted: not stated (a prototype is planned). Same machine line as P12, P64, P65. | pp. 190, 193, 196 |

## Concepts
| Concept | What the paper says | Page |
|---|---|---|
| new: message-driven processor | A processing node whose "controller is driven by the incoming message stream". Each arrival schedules a code sequence. | pp. 189, 191 |
| new: direct execution of messages | Overhead is reduced "by directly executing messages rather than interpreting them with sequences of instructions". "no instructions are required to receive or buffer the message". | pp. 189, 191 |
| new: single primitive message (EXECUTE) | Only EXECUTE <priority> <opcode> <arg>… is hard-wired. Richer messages are ROM macrocode, and the paper says they run "almost as efficiently" as hard-wired ones. | p. 191 |
| new: message unit / instruction unit split | The MU receives, buffers and vectors. The IU "simply executes instructions". | pp. 189, 192, 195 |
| new: memory-based architecture for fast context switches | Instructions read or write on-chip memory in one cycle. With four general registers, a context saves or restores in under 10 cycles. | pp. 189, 191, 196 |
| new: priority register sets | Two register sets, one per priority level, so a low-priority message is preempted "without saving state". | pp. 189, 191 |
| new: associative (set-associative) memory | The same on-chip memory is accessed by address or by content. It is used to translate object IDs to node and address, and class+selector to a method address (a method cache). | pp. 189, 193 |
| new: global name space / object identifiers | Global object IDs are translated at run time. Code is kept as one distributed copy. Local and non-local objects are handled uniformly through tags and traps. | pp. 189, 194, 196 |
| new: futures via tags | A reply target is tagged "context future". Use before the reply suspends the context. | pp. 190, 194–195 |
| new: fine-grain concurrency (grain size) | The natural grain is "about 20 instruction times". The MDP aims at about 10 instructions, against several hundred on existing machines. | pp. 190, 195 |
| new: congestion as governor (no send queue) | With no send queue, network congestion blocks producing objects. | p. 191 |

## Reference
Waldemar Horwat (1991). *Concurrent Smalltalk on the Message-Driven Processor*. MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, Technical Report 1321 (AITR-1321); also DTIC ADA259417. Second edition, "Updated September 26, 1991", of an S.M. thesis submitted to MIT EECS on May 12, 1989 (title and abstract pages, unnumbered, PDF pp. 3, 5). https://openalex.org/W1564741993, http://hdl.handle.net/1721.1/7090. P70, screened include under I1 (row R0-122). Pages below are the printed page numbers of the scanned report. Printed page = PDF page − 16 (checked at pp. 1, 98, 176).

## Serves
Every review question this paper serves, and what it contributes to that question's answer.
| SQ | What it contributes | Page |
|---|---|---|
| SQ1 | Kind: a message-driven multicomputer node (MDP/J-Machine) with a kernel (Cosmos) and language (CST) on top. The send is an instruction (SEND, SEND2, SENDE, SEND2E, SUSPEND), buffering and dispatch are hardware ("dispatches on the address given in the first word of the message"), and Cosmos's inter-node services are message protocols. Semantics hold between nodes at the hardware and kernel levels; within a node only partly ("almost completely message-driven", p. 176). Non-message path added later, at the language level: Optimist II's "reduction of method calls to function calls" and inlining, "added and found to be highly successful" (p. 4). | pp. 2, 4, 49, 70–76, 176, 179, 183 |
| SQ2 | Kinds kept that are not message sends, with reasons: system calls (CALL) for Cosmos utilities that "would suffer too much overhead if they had to be called via the standard function call mechanism" (p. 54); fixed MDP code for low-level modules "critical to the MDP's operation or because calling them as functions would be inefficient" (p. 52); XLATE/ENTER associative table (fast ID translation and method cache, pp. 60–61, 75); diagnostic port, INTERRUPT fault and background mode (no reason, pp. 57, 74, 180); per-node globals shared "because of flaws in the MDP architecture" (p. 57); CST locks "used to synchronize computation" (p. 54). Self-definition: the CST runtime is written in CST, but Cosmos is "hand-optimized assembly language" (p. 51) and the MDP runtime is assembly because it implements "functionality that cannot be easily expressed in Concurrent Smalltalk" (p. 52). | pp. 51, 52, 54, 57, 60–61, 74, 75, 180 |
| SQ3 | Serves only by its criterion (I1): no interposition mechanism is stated. The nearest are kernel-level: a message to a distributed object's group name is routed by the OS "to a constituent of its choosing" (p. 20), and a message for a migrated object is forwarded by its home node (pp. 70, 79). No cost is isolated. | pp. 20, 70, 79 |
| SQ4 | Findings for nodes that share no memory. Protection: per-node bounds-checked address registers and tags; "Absolute memory addressing is not allowed except by the operating system" (pp. 100, 176). Scheduling: per-node hardware priority queues with pre-emption; Cosmos places invocations via ObjectNode, primitives on random nodes; load management "yet to be adequately addressed" (pp. 5, 57, 73, 120). Resource allocation: a heap manager per MDP, no garbage collection; distributed-object allocation is serialised at one node (pp. 58, 120). Naming: object IDs carrying the home node, a BRAT per node; the home node is a "fanout bottleneck" for popular immutable objects (pp. 63–64, 68, 119). No costs measured. | pp. 5, 57, 58, 63–64, 68, 73, 100, 119, 120, 176 |
| SQ5 | Findings, all simulated (MDPSim, 4 and 16 nodes) or analytical, by the designer. Cost of one call: ~100 instructions analytical, 81–162 simulated; tail-forwarded ~36 (pp. 104–108). Only baseline: factorial of 4 in 725 (cold) / 265 (hot) steps against 431 for Spertus's dataflow on the same J-Machine; "faster than dataflow, but not by much" (p. 110), not a conventional processor. Grain size about 60 instructions (pp. 109, 114); CPI 1.87 (internal) and 3.48 (external RAM) on sort (p. 113). Causes (designer, implementation): "operating system overhead time overwhelms the execution time" (p. 50), ~70% of active time in the OS (p. 104), context save and restore "especially in the CFUT fault handler" (p. 114). Scaling: no speed-up curve; analytical network limit at 343 nodes (p. 110). | pp. 50, 104–110, 113, 114 |
| SQ6 | Finding (designer, 1991): no reason for non-adoption is stated. The system is "still an evolving research and demonstration vehicle, and many issues still have to be addressed before it becomes a truly general-purpose system" (p. 115); development had little "feedback from applications because until very recently it was not possible to run any applications on even a simulated J-Machine" (p. 128). | pp. 1, 115, 128 |
| SQ8 | Finding (designer's statement, about the language and a coding rule, not measured on programmers): target costs shaped CST's design ("some actions which are cheap in one language are expensive in the other, which affects the language design", p. 12), and the MDP's queues impose a rule on programs: "user Concurrent Smalltalk methods are not allowed to loop without a message send somewhere to break the loop to prevent the incoming message queues on an MDP from overflowing" (p. 12, footnote). | p. 12 |
| SQ9 | Findings (designer's arguments, not measured; no conventional-processor baseline). Does not harm compiler optimisation: hardware tags free the compiler from type analysis, "even if Optimist II cannot determine the type of some expression, performance does not suffer too much" (p. 11). Costs: fixed hardware limits (queues of 1024 words, 512 XLATE bindings, 16 tags; p. 125), FIP-after-fault and shared-register flaws (pp. 57, 125), and the message-based call path costing "between 100 and 140" instructions per call (p. 114). Generality: floating point via RAP chips reached by messages, where "the message overheads would make this approach inefficient" for mainly symbolic work (pp. 117–118). The last two apply to a message send as the primitive. | pp. 11, 57, 114, 117–118, 125 |
| SQ11 | Finding (from the language design, not from developers): CST provides simple-locks and queueing-locks alongside messages; "Locks are used to synchronize computation" (p. 54), to make atomic transactions (p. 11). No developer reports. | pp. 11, 19–20, 54 |
| SQ13 | Instance: the J-Machine, a "65536-processor, message-passing, MIMD, parallel computer" of MDPs connected in a 3-D mesh, each with its own memory and data structures "replicated on every MDP" (pp. 2, 56); programmed in CST compiled by Optimist II, on the Cosmos kernel, and in MDP assembly (pp. 4, 51). Why discontinued or not adopted: not stated; CST came to run on J-Machine hardware in summer 1991 ("during the summer of 1991, this wish came true") and work was continuing (p. 128). Whether a machine of single-processor nodes counts as a many-core processor is for the synthesizer (inferred). | pp. 2, 4, 51, 56, 128 |
| SQ14 | Finding (analytical, first-order model, for a J-Machine running Cosmos): the network "should not become a critical resource until a J-Machine with over 7³ = 343 nodes is built" (2744 if routing speed doubles); beyond that "either the network will have to be made faster, the program slower, or some means of exploiting locality invented" (p. 114). On a 65536-node machine, "if objects continue to be allocated randomly, the network will become hopelessly congested" (p. 121). Also a name-space limit of "about 32000 objects" per node (p. 123). Nothing on shared memory or coherence. | pp. 110, 114, 121, 123 |
| SQ15 | Findings (designer's arguments). Resource allocation: Cosmos "serializes the allocation of distributed objects at one node because of the need to give each distributed object a unique ID"; splitting the ID space is proposed as the decentralised alternative, at no stated cost (p. 120). Naming: the single home node forms a "fanout bottleneck" for popular immutable objects (p. 119). Garbage collection: a parallel algorithm needing each node to track every ID sent "would be unfeasible", and mark-and-sweep "has to stop the J-Machine" and may lack network bandwidth (p. 120). Load management: migration-based schemes cost decision overhead and congestion at home nodes (p. 121). | pp. 119–121 |

## Concepts
| Concept | What the paper says | Page |
|---|---|---|
| new: message-driven processor | "The MDP is message-based. In its normal mode of operation, the MDP listens on the network for messages ... dispatches on the address given in the first word of the message"; "almost completely message-driven". | pp. 2, 176 |
| new: grain size | "the average amount of time a method executes before suspending", measured at about 60 instructions, which the author found "surprising; it was expected to be much lower". | abstract (PDF p. 5), p. 7 |
| new: operating system overhead | About 70% of active time is in the OS. "operating system overhead time overwhelms the execution time in Concurrent Smalltalk methods". | pp. 104, 50 |
| new: cfuture (context future) | "a local future which cannot be passed outside the function without being touched". It is implemented with the CFUT hardware tag, "using much less overhead than cboxes in CONCURRENTSMALLTALK". | pp. 8, 11, 178 |
| new: distributed object | "an object that can process many methods at the same time without any serialization bottlenecks other than those required by the algorithm". The OS routes group-name messages to constituents. | pp. 2, 20 |
| new: home node and object migration | Each object has a home node, which tracks its location; migration uses RequestObject, MigrateObject, UpdateHome and Unlock messages. | pp. 68–72 |
| new: criticality | A number limiting what a system call may do (e.g. "No message sends"). It was introduced because "almost all of its routines are non-reentrant". | p. 58 |
| new: reduction of method calls to function calls | A compiler optimisation that removes method dispatch and often inlines the call, "highly successful". | pp. 4, 49 |
| new: tail forwarding | A tail-forwarded call is "one call and no return", about 36 instructions against about 100. | pp. 104, 106 |
| new: parallelism control | "a parallel computer can fail if a program exhibiting too much parallelism is run on it". A queue-threshold switch to sequential evaluation was explored. | pp. 121–124 |
| new: fanout bottleneck | Serialising copies of immutable objects through their single home node. | p. 119 |

## Reference
Henry M. Levy (1984). *The Intel iAPX 432*. Chapter 9 of *Capability-Based Computer Systems*, Digital Press (Elsevier eBooks), pp. 159–186. https://doi.org/10.1016/b978-0-932376-22-0.50014-4. Version read: the author's scan of the printed book (homes.cs.washington.edu/~levy/capabook/Chapter9.pdf, saved as `papers/P72.pdf`, 28 PDF pages). Pages cited are the printed pages 159–186, the same as the publisher's range (Crossref), so there is no offset (PDF page = printed page − 158). Criteria: screened I1; full text meets I1 (p. 159, p. 171) and also appears to meet I2 (pp. 185–186), see Notes.

## Deepest pass
2

## Serves
Every review question this paper serves, and what it contributes to that question's answer.
| SQ | What it contributes | Page |
|---|---|---|
| SQ1 | Kind: object-based processor (Intel 432, revision 3) whose instruction set has "instructions that send messages to and receive messages from port objects", with interprocess communication "in hardware and microcode"; message semantics hold at the instruction set only for interprocess communication (scalar, CALL/RETURN and fault paths are not messages). Same kind as the other 432 records (P10, P75); no path added later is described | 159, 162, 171 |
| SQ2 | Kept non-message mechanisms: "shared system memory" over the bus (no reason given); CALL/RETURN with hardware-built contexts, preallocated because per-call allocation "was time-consuming"; local stack SROs because garbage collection "is prohibitive for short-lived objects"; hardware branch to fault/trace handlers; I/O through attached processors (no reason given). Level written in its own objects: system type managers are "partially in hardware ... and partially in operating system software", and "There are no special privileges in the Intel 432 system" | 159–160, 168–169, 172–173, 180, 184–185 |
| SQ5 | Finding: CALL (a procedure call, not a message send) went "from 300 microseconds on early prototypes to under 100 microseconds on the current version", no workload or configuration given; Levy (third party) attributes the speedup to context preallocation and local stack SROs (implementation and revision changes); "The initial version of the Intel 432 had performance problems", "corrected to some extent by later versions". No cost of SEND/RECEIVE and no conventional baseline | 185–186 |
| SQ6 | Finding, third party (Levy, 1984): the 432 "has not been a commercial success" (over 100 systems by 1983, "a small number by microprocessor standards"), "probably due in part to premature (and somewhat overzealous) marketing of the product before its implementation and software were ready", and initial performance problems | 186 |
| SQ9 | Finding (argument): costs of the raised interface are each byte access "potentially requires four references" (reduced by on-chip caches), 64K-byte segments forcing "special code" from the compiler for large objects, explicit traversal to load ADs, and variable instruction size (10 to over 300 bits); none is said to concern the message send | 166, 184–186 |
| SQ16 | Finding (inferred relevance; the 432 is not presented as reflective): programmer-defined type managers use mechanisms "identical to those used by operating system type managers", but hardware-defined operations stay outside as a base ("Some objects have hardware-defined operations while others do not"); the cost of that base is not stated | 173, 184–185 |
| SQ18 | Finding, from an evaluator not among the 432's designers (inferred): object addressing makes each byte access "potentially" need four memory references, overhead called "comparable to the overhead required on any conventional virtual memory system" and reduced by caches; 64K-byte segments impose compiler work; attributed to the addressing design itself (inferred), with no measured size | 166, 185–186 |

## Concepts
| Concept | What the paper says | Page |
|---|---|---|
| new: object-based microprocessor | The 432 is "the first object-based microprocessor"; "Everything in the Intel 432 is an object" | 159, 184 |
| new: access descriptor (AD) | Intel's term for a capability: 32 bits, rights plus two 12-bit indices; "ADs can be freely copied" | 161, 165 |
| new: object descriptor / object table / Object Table Directory | One descriptor per object holds its physical location "so that objects can be easily relocated or synchronized"; per-process object tables under one system-wide directory | 163–165 |
| new: message port and carrier | MESSAGE PORT is the "interprocess communication object"; a CARRIER is an "extension of a message used to queue it to a port"; instructions send and receive messages; only RECEIVE MESSAGE is named | 162, 171 |
| new: type manager (system and programmer-defined) | Each type is controlled by a type manager, "implemented partially in hardware ... and partially in operating system software"; programmer-defined ones use "identical" mechanisms | 173, 184–185 |
| new: type control object (TCO) and rights amplification | Holding a TCO lets a type manager create objects of its type and "amplify the rights" in restricted ADs | 176–178 |
| new: type definition object (TDO) | The "representative 'type'" of a programmer-defined object; its AD is stored in each object's descriptor | 177–178 |
| new: domain refinement (protected subsystem) | A refinement exposes only a domain's public part; CALL always loads the full domain, so callees reach private objects | 175–176 |
| new: context object | Hardware-built procedure invocation record; "the root of all objects reachable by the procedure"; preallocated per process in revision 3 | 169, 172–173 |
| new: storage resource object (global heap vs local stack) | Memory is allocated from SROs; global heaps need garbage collection, local stack SROs allow LIFO deallocation | 179–181 |
| new: level number (lifetime check) | "The hardware prevents the storing of an AD into a segment whose lifetime is longer than the lifetime of the object addressed by that AD" | 181–182 |
| new: "no special privileges" | "There are no special privileges in the Intel 432 system" | 184 |

## Reference
Weinreb, D., Moon, D. (1981). *Lisp Machine Manual*, Fourth Edition, July 1981. Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Artificial Intelligence Laboratory. Read in place of the record screened as R0-127: Weinreb, D., Moon, D. (1981). *The Lisp Machine manual*. ACM SIGART Bulletin no. 78 (October 1981), p. 10. https://doi.org/10.1145/1056737.1056738, which is a one-page notice of the manual, not the manual (see Notes).

## Deepest pass
2 (first pass over title page, preface, both tables of contents and chapter 1; second pass over the sections that serve the form: 10.5.2–10.5.3, 10.10, 14 (pp. 172–183), 20.1–20.6, 20.13–20.14, 21.5.1, 25 (pp. 428–435), 27.1 and 27.3–27.6. The other chapters of the 532-page manual were not read.)

## Serves
Every review question this paper serves, and what it contributes to that question's answer.
| SQ | What it contributes | Page |
|---|---|---|
| SQ1 | Kind: a microcoded language machine whose send is a call of the receiving object, dispatched in microcode: "The microcode binds self to the object, binds the instance variables ... and calls a dtp-select-method associated with the flavor"; the manual itself calls it a convention, "no new features are added to Lisp for message sending" (p. 285); no separate send instruction in the sections read (inferred). Started message-based and later added other paths: not stated | pp. 285, 309 |
| SQ2 | Mechanisms kept that are not sends, with reasons: shared memory between processes, "Unlike other systems which have special restricted mechanisms for inter-process communication, the Lisp Machine allows processes to communicate in arbitrary ways through shared Lisp objects" (p. 429); locking (%store-conditional, without-interrupts, process-lock, p. 429); sequence breaks, "a kind of interrupt" (p. 429); hand-microcoded subprimitives that "take the place of machine language in other systems" (p. 172); unrestricted access to internal state because "the Lisp Machine is an interactive system" and there is "no strong distinction between the 'system' programs and the 'user' programs" (p. 282) | pp. 172, 282, 429 |
| SQ3 | Kind: redirection without changing sender or receiver, at two levels: encapsulations (trace, advise) wrap a function's basic definition and survive its redefinition (p. 153), and method function specs are understood by fdefine (p. 309), so a method can be wrapped (inferred); structure-forward "causes references to old-object to actually reference new-object" by invisible pointers (p. 175). Cost: not stated | pp. 153, 175, 309 |
| SQ5 | Finding, designers' causes with no measured baseline: "in many programs the execution time is determined by paging rather than by CPU run time" (p. 484); generic instructions mean "data dependencies that can have major effects on the speed of execution" (p. 484); function call cost "somewhat higher than it should be", improving it "might require incompatible system architecture changes" (p. 485), i.e. tied to the design (inferred). Figures are estimates that "may vary ... by as much as a factor of two" (p. 484) | pp. 484–485 |
| SQ10 | Finding: messages built as a calling convention inside one shared address space, beside shared-object communication between processes: "Buffers containing messages from one process to another can be implemented as lists or arrays" (p. 429); encapsulation is not enforced, "Zetalisp makes no attempt to have the language automatically forbid constructs that circumvent the contract. This is intentional" (p. 282). Performance kept or lost: not stated | pp. 282, 285, 429 |
| SQ11 | Finding, designers' reasons for shared state alongside messages: processes communicate "in arbitrary ways through shared Lisp objects" rather than "special restricted mechanisms" (p. 429); the contract is left unenforced because "it is important to be able to examine and alter internal state interactively (usually from a debugger)" (p. 282) | pp. 282, 429 |
| SQ16 | Finding on a self-hosted system and its base: "Everything on the Lisp Machine is written in Lisp, including all system programs" (p. 1), but subprimitives "are normally hand-coded in microcode" (p. 172); the base's cost: "Subprimitives by their very nature cannot do full checking. Improper use of subprimitives can destroy the environment" (p. 172) | pp. 1, 172 |

## Concepts
| Concept | What the paper says | Page |
|---|---|---|
| new: generic operation / sending a message | "performing a generic operation is called sending a message"; "This message passing is how generic operations are performed" | p. 283 |
| new: method | "a function that handles a specific kind of message to a specific kind of object" | p. 284 |
| new: flavor | "in its simplest form, is a definition of an abstract type"; defined by defflavor, methods by defmethod | p. 286 |
| new: instance ("active object") | dtp-instance: "an instance of a flavor, i.e. an 'active object'"; a structure whose header points to an "instance descriptor" holding the method table | pp. 173, 309 |
| new: combined method | automatically generated function that "calls the appropriate methods in the right order", incorporating wrappers | p. 309 |
| new: select-method | an a-list of symbols and functions; the first argument is looked up to find the function to call; may have a default handler | p. 144 |
| new: entity | a closure-like primitive datatype "assumed to be a message-receiving object" | p. 311 |
| new: message-receiving stream | "A stream is a message-receiving object"; first argument names the operation | p. 338 |
| new: subprimitive | functions "normally hand-coded in microcode" that "take the place of machine language in other systems" and "cannot do full checking" | p. 172 |
| new: invisible pointer / forwarding | pointer that "does not represent a Lisp object", followed automatically on memory read and write | p. 174 |
| new: encapsulation | addition made by trace or advise around a function spec's basic definition, kept when the basic definition is redefined | p. 153 |
| new: communication through shared Lisp objects | processes share one address space and communicate "in arbitrary ways through shared Lisp objects" instead of "special restricted mechanisms for inter-process communication" | p. 429 |
| new: sequence break | "a kind of interrupt" that resumes the scheduler | p. 429 |

- 16 are your seeds and 1 comes from the review's need statement. The other 263 came from the database search.
- 163 of those 263 came from five search blocks you chose to screen in full at the search gate, every result rather than the top 24. Those five blocks returned about 900 results.
- In all, 1110 candidates were screened, and 280 were let in.

**Why so many passed**
- **The rule for "systems where a message send is built in" (I1) let in 160.** Any operating system kernel whose parts talk by messages qualifies. That covers the whole microkernel world: the L4 family alone has about 7 papers, plus Mach, QNX, Chorus and others. The critic counted about 112 different systems.
- **The rule for "answers one of the skeptic's questions" (I4) let in 107.** That rule admits a paper on any topic if it answers one of the 12 counter-evidence questions, so it pulls in coherence, virtualisation, distributed consensus, reflection and more. The protocol critic flagged it this session as the rule that widens the scope.
- **130 of the 280 were let in with "the full text decides".** The title and abstract couldn't settle them, so the screening leaned toward including them. Some will turn out not to fit once read.
- **19 questions** is a broad protocol. Each counter-evidence question opens its own corner of the literature.

**What it costs now**
With the change you just made, 280 included no longer means 280 to read. Questions that ask for kinds stop at about 30–40 papers instead of 110–120. Papers on systems of a kind already covered get deferred, not read. So the size of round 0 mostly shows up as a long deferred list, not as reading.

**If you want to shrink it anyway**
That's a protocol change, recorded with your reason (`/sls-1-protocol change`), followed by a re-screen. The two options that would matter most:
- tighten the rule for built-in message systems (I1), for example to exclude ordinary microkernels whose messages are only a software library
- narrow the counter-evidence rule (I4) to the strongest papers per question

Either one trades breadth of evidence for less to manage. Given how the depth rules now work, I wouldn't change it unless the deferred list itself bothers you. The coverage report, still running, will show how many papers each question actually needs, which is the better number to judge by.
