## Serves
Every review question this paper serves, and what it contributes to that question's answer.
| SQ | What it contributes | Page |
|---|---|---|
| SQ5 | Causes only, no own measurement, and for language-directed machines rather than message- or object-based ones (scope fit inferred; it serves SQ5 mainly by its criterion, I2). Third-party causes: the B6700 and MU5 had "difficulty achieving comparable performance for FORTRAN programs", because machines tailored to one language had problems generating code for other languages (inherent, inferred). Direct execution must redo the binding "every time a source statement is executed", which loses execution time (inherent). Designer's cause (Ditzel): on SYMBOL, adding hardware does not make a system "run proportionally faster". | pp. 98, 100, 102 |
| SQ6 | Reasons for HLLCs not being adopted: "there are no commercial direct or indirect execution high-level language machines" (p. 98); justifications not examined, and the machines "ignored the view of the total system" (p. 103); poor support for other languages (pp. 98–99); hardware debugging cost, from SYMBOL's designer (p. 99); better compilers and cheaper memory removed the motivation (pp. 98, 99); and direct execution "will not become viable" (p. 100). Stated by third parties, except Ditzel on SYMBOL. | pp. 98–100, 103 |
| SQ8 | Argument, not measurement. Ease of programming: "there is no difference inherent in the machine organization itself", and differences come from "the efficiency and cost to implement a given language and given level of debugging tools", e.g. SYMBOL's crude hardwired diagnostics against its superior software ones (p. 98). Correctness: "one would expect" that a high HLLESF, meaning cheap error checking, gives more reliable software (p. 101). | pp. 98, 101 |
| SQ9 | Arguments against raising the interface, with no measurement of its own. Cost: more logic, and hardware bugs (pp. 98–99). Compilers: they are still needed and are not "greatly" simplified (p. 98). Generality: an instruction set tailored to one language is "constrictive" (p. 99). Compaction: it may not come from the high level, and a cited Interdata 8/32 experiment found <1% speed difference after 20–30% size reduction (p. 99). Direction proposed: raise the level "only when there are specific advantages", with a compiler-generated set that does not block pipelining (pp. 101–102). Whether this applies to a message send: not stated. | pp. 98–99, 101–102 |

## Concepts
| Concept | What the paper says | Page |
|---|---|---|
| High-level language computer (HLLC) | Machines "directed towards the execution of" particular high-level languages; "only a handful ... have actually been implemented". | p. 97 |
| High-Level Language Computer System (HLLCS) | A system that "(1) Uses high-level languages for all programming, debugging and other user/system interactions. (2) Discovers and reports syntax and execution time errors in terms of the high-level language source program. (3) Does not have any outward appearance of transformations from the user programming language to any internal languages". "This definition does not restrict the implementation to hardware or software". | p. 100 |
| Direct execution machine | Machines "defined to execute a source program without any form of translation to an intermediate language". The authors expect them not to "become viable". | p. 100 |
| High-Level Language Execution Support Factor (HLLESF) | "the ratio of T_L to T_H", where T_H is execution time on an HLLCS and T_L is the time on a fast system that is not constrained to check and report errors. It is "an indication of how well the architecture supports a HLLCS". | p. 101 |
| HLL Size Support Factor (HLLSSF), HLL Preparation time Support Factor (HLLPSF) | Ratios of program size and preparation time (compilation, linking, loading) between the same two cases; "less important than HLLESF". | p. 101 |
| Semantic gap | One of the commonly cited justifications: "Reduce the semantic gap between programming and machine languages". The paper lists it without defining it. | p. 97 |
| Transparent reversibility of compilation | Errors are reported at source level from three data structures stored with each load module: an address map, a copy of the source and a symbol table. A decompiled version of the failing statement is then pattern-matched against the original to find the operator or operand at fault. Decompiling the whole program is "not recommended", because "it is not possible to recreate the original source line exactly". Stack machines "offer instruction sets which are easiest to decompile". | pp. 102–103 |

## Notes
- **Source read:** `research/papers/P280.pdf`, 8 pages, a scanned reprint of the ISCA 1980 proceedings pages (IEEE line on p. 97; PDF metadata: Acrobat 4.05 Scan Plug-in, 2002). It is the right paper: the title, both authors and their affiliations (Bell Laboratories; University of California, Berkeley) match the reference line (p. 97). The scan has no text layer, so it was read as page images. Where it came from (a UW CSE548 course page) was reported by the caller and not checked in this run.
- **Pass:** second pass on every page (pp. 97–104), including the reference list, to check the authorship of the SYMBOL papers for Q9. There was no third pass; the paper has no data or experiments to reproduce.
- **Criterion:** I2 is confirmed (pp. 97, 98, 99, 103). I4 (follow-up pass, gate 3c 2026-10-13): SQ9, SQ8. SQ9: the paper argues costs of raising the hardware interface toward the language in performance, cost, generality and compiler optimisation, starting from the semantic-gap justification it lists (p. 97) and through Axioms 1–6 and Attributes 4–9 (pp. 98–102); it does not say whether the arguments apply to a message send. SQ8: it argues, without measurement, that ease of programming has "no difference inherent in the machine organization itself" (p. 98), and expects that a system whose error checking costs little (HLLESF near one) yields more reliable software (p. 101). SQ8 asks for empirical evidence; the paper gives argument only, so it serves SQ8 as argument, not evidence. No other SQ among SQ10–SQ19 is answered: the paper does not discuss message/shared-memory duality, actor programs, many-core processors, central coordination, reflection, virtualisation, capability hardware or post-Dennard specialisation (pp. 97–103). No exclusion criterion applies: it is an 8-page conference paper (X5), and it is not a survey because it states its own reasons (X9).
- **Messages:** The paper is about high-level-language architecture in general (ALGOL, FORTRAN, COBOL, LISP and others). It never mentions messages, objects, object orientation or actors, so it serves SQ6 and SQ9 only as a baseline for the language-directed architectures that came before message-based ones (inferred).
- **Cited numbers:** Both numeric results (p. 99, p. 102) are cited from other work ([35] private communication; [50] Shustek's thesis) and are not the authors' own measurements.
- **Follow-up pass (2026-10-13):** read SQ1–SQ19 and pp. 97–103 again as page images to check I4. Changed: frontmatter (`status`, and `inputs` now listing SQ1–SQ19; `by` was already `reader`); *Reference* field row (I4 proposed, pages); *What shapes programs* (was `n/a (I2)`, now two rows, pp. 98, 101, 102); *Hardware–language trade-off* (one row added on compiler optimisation, pp. 101–103); *Criterion* note (I4 decision replaces the earlier inference). Nothing else was changed.

## Decision card
Every question must make sense to someone who has never opened the research files and does not know the method's vocabulary. Each card has:

- **Situation** (in the text before the question, or in the question itself): what is being decided and why it comes up now, in one to three sentences. Name who raised it (the reader, the skeptic…) and on what grounds.
- **Why it matters:** what changes in the thesis depending on the answer, in one sentence. "This paper will be used as evidence when answering *does X cost performance*", not "R0-023 → I4".
- **Question:** the choice itself, ending with a question mark.
- **Options:**
  - *label*: the action in plain words, one to five words ("Count it for both", "Re-check later", "Exclude it"). Never an ID or a code alone.
  - *description*: what choosing it means and what follows from it: what the thesis gains or loses, what work it triggers, what it costs.

This applies to everything meant for me: cards, reports, progress notes, step introductions.

- **No internal codes** in what I read: no row numbers ("3a"), file names (`R0-023`), field names, or arrows (`→`, `->`) standing for edits. Say what they mean: "the paper's reading record", "the list of papers found in the first search".
- **Method terms** (criterion, review question, snowballing round, gate, baseline…): the first time one appears in a session, give its meaning in a few words, from `ai/glossary.md`.
- **Check before asking:** read the card as if you had never seen the files. If any word needs a file open to be understood, rewrite it.

### Example
An invented case, for illustration only.

Bad:
> P21: which criteria? — *I1 + I4*: "add I4 for SQ3. R0-023 and P21.md Reference -> 'I1, I4'".

Good:
> The reader found that Doe 2019, *Checklists on Night Shifts* (P21), in the review because it reports a checklist used in practice, also measures error rates before and after. That directly answers the question "do checklists reduce errors outside surgery" (SQ3).
> Why it matters: if counted, the paper's measurements are extracted and used as evidence when that question is answered.
> **Should this paper also count as evidence for that question?**
> - *Count it for both (Recommended)*: it stays in for its original reason, and the fields for that question get filled in its reading record. The reader quotes the passage on page 7.
> - *Original reason only*: no change; the passage stays in the record as a note.

# C1: Message-driven processing

## Definition
A processor whose control is driven by arriving messages: the hardware buffers each message and starts a task to handle it, so there is no receive instruction. Merges the records' "message-driven processor", "no receive instruction", "message dispatch as task creation", "message queue as activation stack", "direct execution of messages" and "message unit / instruction unit split".

## First found in
P12

## What the papers say, compared
- **The designers, across one machine line and six years, agree on the idea.** The 1987 design has a controller "driven by the incoming message stream", with "no instructions ... required to receive or buffer the message" and a separate message unit and instruction unit (P69, pp. 189, 191–192). The 1989 paper puts it as "There is no receive instruction. A task is created for each arriving message" and compares the message queue to a stack of method activations (P64, pp. 4, 8–9). The 1992 node creates a task in 3 cycles (P12, pp. 1, 9); the 1993 evaluation measures dispatch in four cycles, with two priority queues and a background level (P65, p. 2). The kernel and language on top are "almost completely message-driven" (P70, pp. 2, 176).
- **How far the claim reaches differs.** Within a node the MDP still has ordinary local loads, stores and traps (P69, pp. 189, 194; P12, p. 8), so message semantics hold fully only between nodes.
- **A third party disagrees on whether hardware support pays.** The Active Messages authors say message-driven hardware lacks locality: a context lasts one handler, so large register sets cannot be used, making the support "partly counter-productive" (P33, pp. 435–437). They add that the J-Machine "does not actually support the message driven programming model fully" (P33, p. 437). The designers instead credit message-driven control for their low overhead (P69, pp. 195–196; P12, pp. 10–11). Culler co-designed Monsoon, a competing message-driven machine (P33, record Serves SQ5).
- **The measured overhead sits above the hardware.** On the J-Machine, about 70% of active time goes to the operating system (P70, p. 104), so a fast hardware dispatch does not make the whole send cheap (see C12).
- **Other machines that receive messages are not message-driven.** The M-Machine handles arrivals in a dedicated event thread, with no new task per message (P66, pp. 4–7). On the Lisp Machine a send is a function call (P73, p. 285). Machines that treat the network "essentially as a fast I/O device" are the contrast case the Active Messages paper names (P33, p. 431).

# C2: Handler address carried in the message

## Definition
Each message names, in its first word, the code the receiver runs when it arrives, so dispatch needs no lookup at the receiver. Merges "Active Messages", "dispatch instruction pointer (DIP)" and the MDP's header-as-instruction-pointer.

## First found in
P33

## What the papers say, compared
- **The same idea appears in software and in hardware.** Active Messages put the address of a user-level handler at the head of each message; the handler runs to completion on arrival (P33, p. 431). On the MDP the instruction pointer comes from the message header (P65, p. 2), and the processor "dispatches on the address given in the first word of the message" (P70, p. 2); the 1987 design encodes it as EXECUTE with a priority and an opcode (P69, p. 191). The M-Machine's first word is a DIP that the handler jumps to (P66, p. 7).
- **Where it runs differs.** Active Messages are a convention on conventional nodes (nCUBE/2, CM-5), carried by a user-level layer over a network interface (P33, pp. 431–433); the MDP and the M-Machine dispatch in hardware (P65, p. 2; P66, p. 7).
- **Protection is handled differently, or not at all.** The M-Machine restricts which DIPs a program may use (P66, pp. 3, 7). On the nCUBE/2 the kernel checks the destination and length of each send (P33, p. 433). On the 1987 MDP, READ and WRITE messages from any sender reach physical memory (P69, pp. 189–194). Whether a message that names its own handler can be made safe without a check on every message is not settled by these papers.

# C3: General mechanisms, not a hardwired model or policy

## Definition
The machine or kernel provides a few primitive mechanisms from which several programming models or policies are built, instead of building one model or one policy in. Merges "primitive mechanisms vs programming models", "general mechanisms rather than a hardwired model", "single primitive message (EXECUTE)", "policy inside the microkernel / mechanism, not policy" and the "microkernel minimality principle".

## First found in
P12

## What the papers say, compared
- **Processor designers argue for general mechanisms.** The MDP gives general mechanisms for communication, synchronisation and naming instead of specialising for one model, and is claimed "competitive with processing nodes specialized to a single model of computation such as iWARP" and the Transputer (P12, pp. 1–2, 23); it supports actors, dataflow and communicating processes (P64, pp. 1–2, 13). Only one message, EXECUTE, is hard-wired; richer messages run "almost as efficiently" as ROM macrocode (P69, p. 191). These claims are argued, not measured.
- **A third party goes further.** One fast primitive is "more versatile than supporting a single paradigm with special hardware", and software handlers "can exploit and optimize special cases" (P33, pp. 431, 437).
- **Kernel designers say the same of policy.** The weakness of first-generation microkernels "is the policy inside the microkernel"; L4 "provides a pure mechanism interface" and leaves policies to user-level servers (P46, pp. 74–76). Twenty years on, the minimality principle is "Retained" (P48, p. 136).
- **Where the principle stops.** L4 kept a fixed-policy scheduler in the kernel, because "All past attempts to export scheduling policy to user level have failed, generally due to intolerable overheads" (P48, p. 138). So the papers agree on the principle but report at least one function where it has not held.

# C4: Fine-grain concurrency and grain size

## Definition
Programs split into many short tasks on many small, cheap nodes; the grain size is the average work a task does before it suspends. Merges "fine-grain multicomputer / jellybean node", "fine-grain concurrent computer (grain size)", "physically fine-grain machines", "fine-grained communication" and "grain size".

## First found in
P12

## What the papers say, compared
- **The design target was very small.** The 1987 MDP aims at about 10 instructions per task, against a "natural grain" of about 20 instruction times and several hundred on existing machines (P69, pp. 190, 195). The 1989 and 1992 papers keep tasks of about 20 instructions, objects of about 8 words and nodes with about 10^4 bytes, as cheap "jellybean" parts (P64, pp. 2, 13; P12, pp. 1–2, 23).
- **Measurement found a larger grain.** On the simulated J-Machine the measured grain is about 60 instructions, which the author found "surprising; it was expected to be much lower" (P70, abstract, p. 7). The 1993 evaluation describes threads of 50 to 150 instructions (P65, p. 1).
- **The economic argument is the designers'.** Physically fine-grain machines give "proportionally better cost/performance while retaining the same total memory capacity" (P65, p. 12), and small messages are cheap enough that data need not be sent in large blocks (P65, pp. 5, 9).
- **A third party names a cost.** Short contexts leave no locality to exploit, which limits processing performance (P33, p. 435).

# C5: Presence tags and futures

## Definition
Memory words tagged as "not yet computed"; reading one traps and suspends the task until a value is written, which synchronises on data arrival without locks. Merges "presence tags / futures (FUT, CFUT)", "c-future / future tags", "futures via tags" and "cfuture (context future)".

## First found in
P12

## What the papers say, compared
- **All MDP papers keep the mechanism.** The 1987 design tags a reply target as a "context future" (P69, pp. 190, 194–195); later papers distinguish c-futures, cheaper and local, from copyable futures (P64, p. 12; P12, pp. 6–7; P65, pp. 2, 5). # C1: Message-driven processing

## Definition
A processor whose control is driven by arriving messages: the hardware buffers each message and starts a task to handle it, so there is no receive instruction. Merges the records' "message-driven processor", "no receive instruction", "message dispatch as task creation", "message queue as activation stack", "direct execution of messages" and "message unit / instruction unit split".

## First found in
P12

## What the papers say, compared
- **The designers, across one machine line and six years, agree on the idea.** The 1987 design has a controller "driven by the incoming message stream", with "no instructions ... required to receive or buffer the message" and a separate message unit and instruction unit (P69, pp. 189, 191–192). The 1989 paper puts it as "There is no receive instruction. A task is created for each arriving message" and compares the message queue to a stack of method activations (P64, pp. 4, 8–9). The 1992 node creates a task in 3 cycles (P12, pp. 1, 9); the 1993 evaluation measures dispatch in four cycles, with two priority queues and a background level (P65, p. 2). The kernel and language on top are "almost completely message-driven" (P70, pp. 2, 176).
- **How far the claim reaches differs.** Within a node the MDP still has ordinary local loads, stores and traps (P69, pp. 189, 194; P12, p. 8), so message semantics hold fully only between nodes.
- **A third party disagrees on whether hardware support pays.** The Active Messages authors say message-driven hardware lacks locality: a context lasts one handler, so large register sets cannot be used, making the support "partly counter-productive" (P33, pp. 435–437). They add that the J-Machine "does not actually support the message driven programming model fully" (P33, p. 437). The designers instead credit message-driven control for their low overhead (P69, pp. 195–196; P12, pp. 10–11).
- **The measured overhead sits above the hardware.** On the J-Machine, about 70% of active time goes to the operating system (P70, p. 104), so a fast hardware dispatch does not make the whole send cheap (see C12).
- **Other machines that receive messages are not message-driven.** The M-Machine handles arrivals in a dedicated event thread, with no new task per message (P66, pp. 4–7). On the Lisp Machine a send is a function call (P73, p. 285). Machines that treat the network "essentially as a fast I/O device" are the contrast case the Active Messages paper names (P33, p. 431).

# C6: Naming in message-based systems

## Definition
How a sender names a receiver or an object on another node or core: hardware translation tables, global object identifiers with a home node, name servers, or capabilities used as the only names. Merges "name translation (XLATE/ENTER)", "exposed translation cache", "global name translation", "global name space / object identifiers", "home node and object migration", "fanout bottleneck", "Global Translation Lookaside Buffer / Global Destination Table" and "centralised namespace".

## First found in
P8

## What the papers say, compared
- **Hardware translation on each node.** The MDP translates global object identifiers in an associative on-chip memory that also serves as a method cache (P69, pp. 189, 193); later versions expose it as ENTER/XLATE instructions "a systems programmer can use for any translation" (P64, pp. 12–13; P12, p. 7). The M-Machine caches a software Global Destination Table in a GTLB per node (P66, p. 7).
- **The MDP's own evaluators judge its naming insufficient.** The translation tables are "inadequate to transparently and inexpensively provide a global name space" (P65, p. 11). In the kernel above, each object has a home node that tracks it, and that node becomes a "fanout bottleneck" for popular immutable objects (P70, pp. 63–64, 68, 119).
- **Operating systems use name services, central or replicated.** Barrelfish maps service names to references through a name service, without saying whether it is one instance (P8, p. 10). fos holds the directory in a fleet of name servers cached by each microkernel (P102, pp. 5–7). Helios keeps the namespace in one coordinator kernel, "the only component of Helios that relies on centralized control", at the cost of two remote channels to set up a connection on the same kernel (P45, pp. 6, 8). Minix 3 uses one data-store name server and Singularity one root name server (P49, pp. 47–50).
- **Capabilities avoid a name service.** In KeyKOS naming is "intrinsically decentralized" because capabilities are the only names (P53, pp. 3–6). L4 moved from global thread identifiers, which leaked covert channels and pushed servers onto a "gateway thread, which could become a bottleneck", to capability-named endpoints (P48, pp. 137–138, 143).
- **Comparison.** Every non-capability scheme read has a central point or a bottleneck the authors name (P45, P49, P65, P70); only Helios gives a cost, and none measures a decentralised alternative.

# C7: Messages and communication in registers

## Definition
Message contents, the head of a message queue, or communication between execution units mapped onto processor registers, so a send or receive avoids memory. Merges "virtual message registers", "register-mapped message queue", "H-Thread" (register communication), "priority register sets" and "memory-based architecture for fast context switches".

## First found in
P33

## What the papers say, compared
- **Hardware designs map the queue onto registers.** The M-Machine makes the head of the message queue a register, so messages are not copied to or from memory (P66, pp. 7–8); its H-threads also communicate and synchronise "via registers" (P66, pp. 3–4). The Active Messages authors propose message registers, PC injection and user-level interrupts, and expect such support to cut handling to "a handful of instructions, but not to one" (P33, pp. 438–439).
- **A kernel does the same in software.** L4 uses 16–64 virtual message registers, some physical and the rest in pinned memory (P48, p. 137); in-register transfer is 10% faster than passing on the kernel stack on ARM11 and 4% on Cortex A9 (P48, pp. 137–138).
- **The MDP chose few registers on purpose.** It keeps one small register set per priority so a low-priority message is preempted "without saving state", and a memory-based instruction set so a context switches in under 10 cycles (P69, pp. 189, 191, 196). Its evaluators later name the "paucity of registers" as a limit (P65, p. 11).
- **The 432 had none.** It is a memory-to-memory machine with no data registers, for chip size and faster process swaps (P10, pp. 302, 318).
- **Tension.** Registers make sends cheap, but message-driven handlers are too short to use many registers (C1, C38).

# C8: Message buffering, queues and flow control

## Definition
Where messages wait between send and receipt, and what happens when buffers fill. Merges "return-to-sender flow control / throttling", "congestion as governor (no send queue)", "receive mailbox", "message port and carrier", "IPC endpoint", "message class (network)", "message priorities" and "parallelism control".

## First found in
P8

## What the papers say, compared
- **Kernels avoid buffering.** L4's synchronous IPC avoids kernel buffering; endpoints hold queues of waiting senders, not messages (P48, pp. 136–138). KeyKOS has no kernel buffering; a buffering domain can be placed in the path when needed (P53, p. 7). Minix 3 copies messages only when both sides are ready (P49, p. 48).
- **Machines buffer in hardware and push back.** The MDP has two hardware priority queues and a queue-overflow fault (P65, pp. 2, 10–11); the 1987 design has no send queue, so network congestion blocks the sending object (P69, p. 191). The M-Machine returns unconsumed messages to a buffer reserved at the sender, and SEND stalls when none is reserved (P66, p. 7); the J-Machine's evaluators propose the same "return-to-sender" scheme (P65, p. 11). The SCC's network uses two message classes and reserved virtual channels to keep routing free of deadlock (P21, pp. 175–176).
- **Overflow becomes a rule for programs.** On the J-Machine, Concurrent Smalltalk methods may not loop without a message send, so queues do not overflow (P70, p. 12, footnote), and a switch to sequential evaluation above a queue threshold was explored (P70, pp. 121–124).
- **Operating systems leave it to the sender or to tuning.** In fos a send to a full mailbox returns an error (P102, pp. 6, 8). Barrelfish tests with a 16-message queue, does not state full-queue behaviour, and names "extreme sensitivity to message queue lengths" as a limit (P8, pp. 10, 17).
- **The 432 queues at ports.** Messages are queued to a port object by a carrier (P72, pp. 162, 171).
- **Comparison.** No two designs read handle a full buffer the same way, and only the J-Machine papers report the effect on programs.

# C9: Synchronous (rendezvous) IPC

## Definition
Sender and receiver meet: the message is copied directly when both are ready, and the caller blocks until the reply. Merges "synchronous (rendezvous-style) IPC", "rendezvous message passing", "direct process switch", "resume key", "entry capability / resume capability" and "protected control transfer (Exokernel)".

## First found in
P46

## What the papers say, compared
- **Several kernel lines chose it.** In the original L4 it was "the only communication, synchronisation, and signalling mechanism" (P48, pp. 136–137); on IPC the kernel switches straight to the partner on the caller's time slice (P48, p. 145). Minix 3 passes "fixed-length messages using the rendezvous principle" (P49, p. 48). KeyKOS invokes keys by call, fork and return, with the kernel building a resume key for the reply (P53, pp. 3, 7); EROS consumes every copy of a resume capability on use, "ensuring an 'at most once' reply" (P77, p. 173). Exokernel's protected control transfer "crosses address spaces but does not transfer arguments" (P46, p. 74).
- **The 432's procedure call behaves the same way** by call and return semantics, though the paper does not use the word (P10, p. 321).
- **L4 found limits after 20 years.** Synchronous-only IPC "forces a multi-threaded design onto otherwise simple systems" and RPC-style IPC "sequentialises client and server" across cores, so asynchronous notifications were added (P48, pp. 136–139; see C10, C15).
- **Comparison.** The single-core kernels read (L4, Minix 3, KeyKOS, EROS) agree on synchronous IPC; the only paper with experience on multicore (P48) reports it as a limit there.

# C6: Naming in message-based systems

## Definition
How a sender names a receiver or an object on another node or core: hardware translation tables, global object identifiers with a home node, name servers, or capabilities used as the only names. Merges "name translation (XLATE/ENTER)", "exposed translation cache", "global name translation", "global name space / object identifiers", "home node and object migration", "fanout bottleneck", "Global Translation Lookaside Buffer / Global Destination Table" and "centralised namespace".

## First found in
P12

## What the papers say, compared
- **Hardware translation on each node.** The MDP translates global object identifiers in an associative on-chip memory that also serves as a method cache (P69, pp. 189, 193); later versions expose it as ENTER/XLATE instructions "a systems programmer can use for any translation" (P64, pp. 12–13; P12, p. 7). The M-Machine caches a software Global Destination Table in a GTLB per node (P66, p. 7).
- **The MDP's own evaluators judge its naming insufficient.** The translation tables are "inadequate to transparently and inexpensively provide a global name space" (P65, p. 11). In the kernel above, each object has a home node that tracks it, and that node becomes a "fanout bottleneck" for popular immutable objects (P70, pp. 63–64, 68, 119).
- **Operating systems use name services, central or replicated.** Barrelfish maps service names to references through a name service, without saying whether it is one instance (P8, p. 10). fos holds the directory in a fleet of name servers cached by each microkernel (P102, pp. 5–7). Helios keeps the namespace in one coordinator kernel, "the only component of Helios that relies on centralized control", at the cost of two remote channels to set up a connection on the same kernel (P45, pp. 6, 8). Minix 3 uses one data-store name server and Singularity one root name server (P49, pp. 47–50).
- **Capabilities avoid a name service.** In KeyKOS naming is "intrinsically decentralized" because capabilities are the only names (P53, pp. 3–6). L4 moved from global thread identifiers, which leaked covert channels and pushed servers onto a "gateway thread, which could become a bottleneck", to capability-named endpoints (P48, pp. 137–138, 143).
- **Comparison.** Every non-capability scheme read has a central point or a bottleneck the authors name (P45, P49, P65, P70); only Helios gives a cost, and none measures a decentralised alternative.

# C7: Messages and communication in registers

## Definition
Message contents, the head of a message queue, or communication between execution units mapped onto processor registers, so a send or receive avoids memory. Merges "virtual message registers", "register-mapped message queue", "H-Thread" (register communication), "priority register sets" and "memory-based architecture for fast context switches".

## First found in
P48

## What the papers say, compared
- **Hardware designs map the queue onto registers.** The M-Machine makes the head of the message queue a register, so messages are not copied to or from memory (P66, pp. 7–8); its H-threads also communicate and synchronise "via registers" (P66, pp. 3–4). The Active Messages authors propose message registers, PC injection and user-level interrupts, and expect such support to cut handling to "a handful of instructions, but not to one" (P33, pp. 438–439).
- **A kernel does the same in software.** L4 uses 16–64 virtual message registers, some physical and the rest in pinned memory (P48, p. 137); in-register transfer is 10% faster than passing on the kernel stack on ARM11 and 4% on Cortex A9 (P48, pp. 137–138).
- **The MDP chose few registers on purpose.** It keeps one small register set per priority so a low-priority message is preempted "without saving state", and a memory-based instruction set so a context switches in under 10 cycles (P69, pp. 189, 191, 196). - **The 432 had none.** It is a memory-to-memory machine with no data registers, for chip size and faster process swaps (P10, pp. 302, 318).

# C8: Message buffering, queues and flow control

## Definition
Where messages wait between send and receipt, and what happens when buffers fill. Merges "return-to-sender flow control / throttling", "congestion as governor (no send queue)", "receive mailbox", "message port and carrier", "IPC endpoint", "message class (network)", "message priorities" and "parallelism control".

## First found in
P21

## What the papers say, compared
- **Kernels avoid buffering.** L4's synchronous IPC avoids kernel buffering; endpoints hold queues of waiting senders, not messages (P48, pp. 136–138). KeyKOS has no kernel buffering; a buffering domain can be placed in the path when needed (P53, p. 7). Minix 3 copies messages only when both sides are ready (P49, p. 48).
- **Machines buffer in hardware and push back.** The MDP has two hardware priority queues and a queue-overflow fault (P65, pp. 2, 10–11); the 1987 design has no send queue, so network congestion blocks the sending object (P69, p. 191). The M-Machine returns unconsumed messages to a buffer reserved at the sender, and SEND stalls when none is reserved (P66, p. 7); the J-Machine's evaluators propose the same "return-to-sender" scheme (P65, p. 11). The SCC's network uses two message classes and reserved virtual channels to keep routing free of deadlock (P21, pp. 175–176).
- **Overflow becomes a rule for programs.** On the J-Machine, Concurrent Smalltalk methods may not loop without a message send, so queues do not overflow (P70, p. 12, footnote), and a switch to sequential evaluation above a queue threshold was explored (P70, pp. 121–124).
- **Operating systems leave it to the sender or to tuning.** In fos a send to a full mailbox returns an error (P102, pp. 6, 8). Barrelfish tests with a 16-message queue, does not state full-queue behaviour, and names "extreme sensitivity to message queue lengths" as a limit (P8, pp. 10, 17).
- **The 432 queues at ports.** Messages are queued to a port object by a carrier (P72, pp. 162, 171).
- **Comparison.** No two designs read handle a full buffer the same way, and only the J-Machine papers report the effect on programs.

# C10: Asynchronous and split-phase communication

## Definition
The sender continues after sending; the reply or completion arrives later, signalled by a flag, a message or a stored continuation. Merges "split-phase operation" (two records), "pipelining and batching of messages", "overlap of communication and computation", "asynchronous endpoint / notification" and "stateless, transaction-oriented server with continuations".

## First found in
P8

## What the papers say, compared
- **Designs for many cores start asynchronous.** In the multikernel an operation sends a request and continues, with several requests in flight or batched in one message for throughput (P8, pp. 2, 6). fos sends asynchronously to named mailboxes, and its servers store a continuation for long operations instead of blocking or locking (P102, pp. 6–7).
- **On multicomputers it is the "real architectural issue".** Active Messages replace "latency tolerance" with overlap of communication and computation; Split-C's remote PUT and GET return at once and signal completion by a flag (P33, pp. 431, 434).
- **A synchronous kernel had to add it.** L4 added a single-word asynchronous notification, where a send ORs a bit mask into the word and the receiver blocks or polls (P48, pp. 136–137), because synchronous-only IPC forced multithreaded designs (P48, pp. 136–139).
- **Hardware futures are the same idea at the word level** (C5).
- **Comparison.** No paper read argues for synchronous messages across cores; the one kernel that began synchronous moved partly away from it (P48), which matches the multicore designs (P8, P102).

# C11: One channel abstraction over several transports

## Definition
One message interface for the program, whatever carries the message (same core, another core, another kernel or a device of another instruction set); the transport is chosen per channel. Merges "late binding of protocol and transport" and "remote message passing (RMP) vs local message passing (LMP)".

## First found in
P8

## What the papers say, compared
- **Barrelfish binds transport late.** Protocol and transport are chosen at run time to fit the hardware or workload; all transports sit behind a common interface with marshalling generated by a stub compiler (P8, pp. 6, 10). Same-core LRPC and inter-core URPC are both offered (P8, pp. 8–10).
- **Helios keeps the interface and changes the cost.** Local message passing is zero-copy within a kernel; remote message passing marshals and copies once between kernels, beneath the same IPC abstraction (P45, pp. 3, 6–7). A local send takes about 10 µs and a remote one about 11–128 µs by size, read off its Fig. 5 (P45, p. 10).
- **fos leaves the transport open** ("via on-chip networks or shared memory") and turns system calls into messages through a proxy library (P102, pp. 5–8).
- **Comparison.** All three keep one interface; Helios measures the cost difference, Barrelfish does not claim that swapping transports is interposition (P8, pp. 6, 10), and Helios is the one that uses it to move a component without changing the program (C25).

# C12: Cost of one message send

## Definition
The time for one send and receive, or one IPC round trip, and what it is attributed to. Merges "RPC granularity / relative RPC overhead", "IPC fast path", "one-way message overhead (Ts, Tb)", "operating system overhead", "tail forwarding" and "small spaces".

## First found in
P46

## What the papers say, compared
- **Hardware message mechanisms: a few to about ten cycles, by their designers.** The 1987 MDP design handles a message in "less than ten clock cycles" against "about 300µs" on the Cosmic Cube, iPSC and S-NET (P69, pp. 190, 195–196); later papers give delivery plus dispatch "< 3µs" or "< 2 µs" against 5 ms on an iPSC (P64, p. 3; P12, p. 2), with iPSC configurations not given. The 1993 evaluation measures 11 cycles per message plus 0.5 cycles per byte, against 109–3200 cycles on the CM-5, nCUBE/2, DELTA and Active Messages (P65, p. 4). The M-Machine delivers a one-hop message in 5 cycles in simulation, with a 48-cycle software send path inside a remote read (P66, pp. 8–9).
- **Kernel IPC: from about 190 cycles to over 100 µs.** Mach IPC took 115 µs against 5 µs for L4 on a 486-DX50 (P46, pp. 73–75); seL4 reaches 188 cycles one way on ARM11 with a hand-optimised fast path (P48, pp. 135, 146). Barrelfish's URPC costs 450 cycles against 424 for L4 IPC on the same machine (P8, p. 10). A KeyKOS send costs "less than 500 cycles" on the 88x00 (P53, pp. 7, 13–16); an EROS round trip 2.38–3.21 µs on a 400 MHz Pentium II, where small address spaces have "a disproportionate impact" (P77, pp. 177–178, 180–183). Helios: about 10 µs locally (P45, p. 10).
- **Software layers over the hardware add most of the cost.** On the J-Machine a Concurrent Smalltalk call takes about 100 instructions (81–162 simulated), a tail-forwarded call about 36, and about 70% of active time is in the operating system (P70, pp. 104–108). Active Messages cut start-up from 160 to 30 µs on the nCUBE/2 by removing buffer management from the vendor library (P33, pp. 432–434).
- **Causes.** Liedtke puts "at least 73%" of the microkernel penalty on IPC, with hardware switching "only 3%–7%", and blames kernel structure and implementation (P46, pp. 74–75). Finer-grained objects and distribution will make calls between address spaces more frequent, so their cost matters more over time (P46, p. 73). The 432's procedure call, measured instead of its Send, costs 982 cycles, about 10 times a call on a 68010 or VAX (P10, pp. 308–310).
- **Comparison.** Hardware sends are one to two orders of magnitude cheaper than kernel IPC, but the J-Machine shows the gain can be lost in the software above it. Units (cycles or µs), clock rates and baselines differ across papers, and most figures are the designers' own.

# C13: Inherent versus implementation causes of performance

## Definition
Whether a measured slowness is attributed to the concept of the design or to how it was built (compiler, chip technology, code), and how that attribution is made. Merges "cycle sink", "synthetic 432", "inherent cost of object orientation", "artifacts vs concepts", "high-level language system = compiler + machine", "wait states", "normalized performance" and "time and space cost of the 432 approach".

## First found in
P10

## What the papers say, compared
- **Two third-party evaluations of the 432 isolate causes, and frame them differently.** Hansen et al. measure the 432 at about 1/20 of a VAX-11/780 and isolate the loss to parameter and global access in release 2 by modified programs (P29, pp. 18, 20, 23), but warn that "a high-level language system consists of the compiler and the machine, so we are not measuring just the architecture" (P29, p. 17). Colwell et al. separate the two: by simulator logs they attribute 25–35% to the Ada compiler and 5–10% to bit alignment and missing literals, build a "synthetic 432" with these fixed, and call the remaining 2–3x "our estimate for the inherent cost of the 432's style of object orientation" (P10, pp. 312–337). That inherent part is a residual, not isolated, and their summary percentages do not all match their tables (P10, pp. 329, 336–337). Their verdict: performance "dominated, in large part, by artifacts and not by concepts" (P10, p. 338).
- **Comparing machines is itself hard.** Wait states and normalisation to one clock rate change the ranking (P29, pp. 18–19, 22); cross-machine comparisons with different languages are a "rough estimate" (P10, pp. 309, 336).
- **Designers mostly attribute without isolating.** Liedtke blames the "basic architecture" and implementation of first-generation kernels, not microkernels as such (P46, pp. 73–75, 77). KeyKOS's designers call one cost a mistake of implementation ("we were mistaken") and another "a direct result of the underlying KeyKOS I/O design" (P53, pp. 13–16). The MDP's designers attribute a 3–4x area and 2–3x speed loss to standard cells (P12, p. 16). Barrelfish's authors call some overheads implementation (dispatch loop, threads library) and some design (avoiding kernel crossings) (P8, pp. 13, 15–16). Minix 3's call their slightly lower performance inherent to the design and also say the system "has not been optimized" (P49, pp. 47, 49–50).
- **A third party calls one cost inherent to message-driven hardware**: lack of locality, argued not measured (P33, p. 435).
- **Comparison.** Only the 432 has been through an independent cause-by-cause analysis; everywhere else the attribution is the designers' and unmeasured, which limits what can be said about whether a message machine's losses are avoidable.

# C14: Microkernels and multiserver operating systems

## Definition
A kernel reduced to address spaces, IPC and basic scheduling, with operating system services and drivers running as isolated user-level servers that communicate by messages. Merges "microkernel", "first-generation vs second-generation microkernels", "conservative and progressive criteria", "processor-dependent microkernel", "trusted computing base", "multiserver operating system", "multikernel vs microkernel" and "wheel of reincarnation".

## First found in
P46

## What the papers say, compared
- **Definition and its generations.** Liedtke defines the microkernel as "minimizing the kernel and implementing servers outside the kernel" (P46, p. 70). First-generation kernels "evolved step by step from monolithic kernels" and were "inefficient and inflexible"; the second generation is designed "from scratch" (P46, pp. 70, 74). He also holds that microkernels are "inherently not portable" (P46, p. 74) and sets two tests: applications must not be degraded, and new kinds must be supported (P46, pp. 72–73).
- **Why they were rejected, and why they might return.** Liedtke calls "the pure microkernel approach of the first generation ... a failure" for its measured penalty (P46, pp. 73, 77). Tanenbaum et al. agree they were "long discarded as unacceptable because of their lower performance", and see a comeback for reliability: "The wheel of reincarnation has turned" (P49, pp. 47, 50). They differ on the cause: Liedtke blames the first generation's design, while Minix 3's designers call a small loss (under 10% for user-mode drivers) inherent (P49, p. 47).
- **Durability.** The minimality principle is "Retained" after 20 years of L4 (P48, p. 136).
- **A multicore objection.** Barrelfish's authors say a microkernel "remains a shared-memory, multithreaded system in the kernel", which their multikernel avoids (P8, p. 17; see C16).

# C15: Non-message paths added later

## Definition
Mechanisms that are not message sends, added to a system that began message-based, usually for performance, convenience or compatibility. Merges "reintegration into the kernel", "long IPC" (abandoned for shared buffers), "selector-object dispatch" (bypass), "reduction of method calls to function calls" and "criticality".

## First found in
P12

## What the papers say, compared
- **Kernels moved servers back in, or added calls.** Chorus's "supervisor actors" and Mach's "kernel-loaded tasks" "reintegrated the most critical servers and drivers into the kernel", which "weakens the microkernel approach" (P46, p. 73). Mach "originally started with a single mach_msg system call, additional system calls were later added for performance" (P77, p. 182).
- **L4 added non-message primitives beside IPC.** Asynchronous notifications, counting semaphores and virtual IRQs were added, and long IPC was abandoned for shared buffers because it was complex, "rarely used" and hard to verify (P48, pp. 136–139).
- **An emulated system kept a shared table.** KeyNIX, a UNIX built on KeyKOS's messages, shares the process and open-file tables in a segment, which its designers call "the primary impediment to distribution" (P53, pp. 11, 17).
- **Compilers turn sends into calls.** On the MDP, a Concurrent Smalltalk call whose receiver type is known "is optimized directly to the correct function invocation" (P12, p. 20); the "reduction of method calls to function calls" was "added and found to be highly successful" (P70, pp. 4, 49). The kernel also has system calls that may send no messages, because "almost all of its routines are non-reentrant" (P70, p. 58).
- **Allowed by design, not built.** The multikernel model allows a replica shared under spinlocks by closely coupled cores, which the authors call "a next step" (P8, pp. 7, 18).
- **Comparison.** Reasons given: performance (P46, P77, P12, P70), simplicity and verification (P48), compatibility with an existing system (P53). In every case the message interface stayed and the new path went beside or below it.

# C16: Multikernel: the operating system as a distributed system of cores

## Definition
One kernel instance per core or per memory domain, sharing no kernel state, with all coordination between cores by explicit messages. Merges "multikernel", "explicit inter-core communication", "hardware-neutral OS structure", "CPU driver", "monitor", "dispatcher", "system knowledge base", "spectrum of sharing and locking", "satellite kernel", "NUMA as a shared-nothing multiprocessor", "affinity", "two-phase compilation", "factored operating system", "space multiplexing replaces time multiplexing", "fleet", "fos client", "OS-application locality aliasing" and "clustered multikernel".

## First found in
P8

## What the papers say, compared
- **Three designs from 2009, three motivations.** Barrelfish structures the OS "as a distributed system of cores that communicate using messages and share no memory", placing itself at the far end of a spectrum from shared and locked to fully replicated state (P8, p. 5); it argues from coherence costs and hardware diversity (P8, pp. 3–5). Helios runs a satellite microkernel per NUMA domain and per programmable device of another instruction set, and places processes by affinity hints at start (P45, pp. 1–8). fos factors the OS into services run by fleets of servers on their own cores, so "Scheduling becomes a layout problem not a time multiplexing problem" (P102, pp. 5–6), arguing from cache interference between OS and applications (P102, p. 4).
- **A kernel line that went part of the way.** L4's clustered multikernel uses a big-lock kernel across cores that share an L2 cache, and a restricted multikernel between clusters with "no memory migration" (P48, p. 143).
- **None is free of shared memory.** Barrelfish's channels and applications share memory (P8, pp. 5, 11); Helios carries remote messages over shared FIFOs (P45, pp. 6–7); fos may use shared memory as transport and for small applications (P102, pp. 2, 5).
- **Costs of not sharing.** Helios processes may not span domains, which "could hamper large, multi-threaded processes" (P45, pp. 5, 13); L4's restricted multikernel gives up memory migration (P48, p. 143); Barrelfish's split between CPU driver and monitors costs "several thousand cycles" per OS call (P8, pp. 11–12).
- **Evidence differs.** Barrelfish is measured up to 32 cores, but its authors warn against "quantitative conclusions from our large-scale benchmarks" (P8, p. 16); Helios is measured on 4 cores and an I/O card (P45, pp. 9–11); fos is a design under development (P102, p. 8).

# C17: Replicated state kept by agreement

## Definition
State that a shared-memory operating system would share is kept as a replica on each core, made consistent by message protocols between them. Merges "replicated (not shared) state", the multikernel "monitor" role, "microkernel to OS layer delegation" (cached answers) and "best-effort OS interfaces".

## First found in
P8

## What the papers say, compared
- **Barrelfish is the measured case.** Potentially shared state is a local replica kept consistent by agreement among per-core monitors (P8, pp. 6–7, 9). Unmap uses a one-phase commit and retype a two-phase commit among all monitors (P8, p. 11); the two-phase commit takes about 14k to 28k cycles over 2 to 32 cores and "serializes more messages" than a TLB shootdown (P8, p. 14). All cores must keep their capability lists consistent (P8, p. 10).
- **Its own authors list the costs.** Replica consistency adds latency and burden on developers (P8, p. 7), and in hindsight the decentralised capability scheme "was a mistake ... unnecessarily complex, and no more efficient than scalable per-processor memory managers" (P8, p. 10).
- **fos caches instead of agreeing.** Microkernels cache name and privilege answers from server fleets and invalidate them by message (P102, pp. 5–7); some interfaces return information "which may be slightly out of date" for speed (P102, p. 2).
- **Others avoid replication.** Helios keeps naming central rather than replicated (P45, p. 6; see C18). On the J-Machine, kernel data structures are replicated on every node (P70, pp. 2, 56), but objects keep one home node (C6).
- **Comparison.** Only Barrelfish measures agreement, and its authors judge one of their replicated designs not worth its cost; no paper read compares a replicated and a central version of the same function.

# C18: Central components in systems of message-passing parts

## Definition
Functions that stay with one coordinator (a node, a kernel, a server or a root object) in a system otherwise made of parts that share no state. Merges "coordinator kernel", "centralised namespace", "meter" (prime meter), "space bank" (master), "notional lock / lock server", "distributed object" and "fanout bottleneck".

## First found in
P45

## What the papers say, compared
- **Naming.** Helios keeps its namespace in the coordinator kernel "for the sake of simplicity", since it is used only at process start and connection setup (P45, pp. 5–6); Minix 3 and Singularity each have one name server (P49, pp. 47–50).
- **Resources.** KeyKOS subdivides CPU time from one kernel "prime meter" and storage from a master space bank, though "multiple master space banks" are possible (P53, pp. 4, 6); EROS's single space bank "owns all system storage" (P77, p. 179). The J-Machine kernel "serializes the allocation of distributed objects at one node because of the need to give each distributed object a unique ID" (P70, p. 120).
- **Failure handling.** KeyKOS checkpoints the whole system while "all processes are briefly suspended" (P53, pp. 4, 8); EROS halts all processes for a whole-machine snapshot, under 50 ms for 256 MB (P77, p. 174).
- **Atomicity and scheduling.** fos still needs "synchronization points", met by a lock server or a core acting as a transaction server, and warns "the cost of software-based lock management may dwarf the performance wins" (P102, pp. 5, 8). L4's designers think "a global scheduler makes more sense" on embedded multicores with cheap migration (P48, p. 138).
- **Interrupts.** Helios steers all interrupts to the coordinator, which "restricts the location of device drivers" (P45, pp. 6, 13).
- **Named costs.** Bottlenecks at a home node (P70, p. 119) or a gateway thread (P48, p. 143), and restricted placement (P45, p. 13); none is measured.
- **Comparison.** Reasons for keeping a centre: simplicity (P45), uniqueness of names (P70), a consistent snapshot (P53, P77), atomicity (P102) and cheap migration (P48). No paper read shows a decentralised version of these functions working with a measured cost, apart from Barrelfish's capability scheme, which its authors regret (C17).

# C19: User-level resource allocation

## Definition
Memory and other resources are allocated by user-level servers through kernel mechanisms (mappings, capabilities to untyped memory, space banks), not by policy inside the kernel. Merges "external pager", "recursive address spaces: grant, map, demap", "recursive page mappings / mapping database", "Untyped memory and retype", "space bank" (two records) and "meter".

## First found in
P46

## What the papers say, compared
- **L4's path.** Mach's external pager, which forwards page faults to user-level tasks, was "the first conceptual breakthrough toward real microkernels" (P46, p. 71). L4 builds address spaces outside the kernel by grant, map and demap, with coexisting memory servers that must "cooperate" (P46, pp. 75–76). This needed a mapping database, and seL4 replaced it with Untyped memory and retype, "seL4's main contribution to OS design": "by limiting access to Untyped memory, a system can control resource allocation" (P48, pp. 140–142).
- **KeyKOS and EROS use banks.** Space banks allocate disk and memory from a master bank, and meters convey the right to run for a time (P53, p. 6); EROS calls its space bank "uniquely as far as we know, user-level storage allocation" (P77, pp. 179, 183).
- **Multicore designs.** Barrelfish manages virtual memory at user level through capabilities and judges its scheme unnecessarily complex (P8, p. 10); fos allocates physical memory through a fleet (P102, p. 6).
- **Comparison.** All agree allocation can leave the kernel; they differ on whether the root is one object (KeyKOS, EROS) or capabilities to raw memory (seL4), and only Barrelfish reports regretting its design (C18).

# C20: Interrupts, exceptions and system calls turned into messages

## Definition
Hardware events, faults and traditional system calls are converted, by the kernel or the hardware, into messages to a handler that runs as an ordinary program. Merges "interrupts as IPC messages", "user-level device drivers" (two records), "interrupts integrated with message passing", "keeper", "event V-Thread", "message proxy library" and "sequence break".

## First found in
P46

## What the papers say, compared
- **Kernels convert interrupts.** In L4 "The kernel captures the interrupt but does not handle it, instead generating a message" for the associated user process, so drivers run in user mode and can be "replaced, removed, or added dynamically" (P46, p. 72); the practice is "Retained" after 20 years (P48, p. 139). Minix 3's handlers set a pending bit that "the kernel turns ... into a normal message" (P49, p. 48). Barrelfish's CPU driver demultiplexes device interrupts into messages (P8, p. 8).
- **Exceptions and system calls too.** KeyKOS delivers exceptions as messages to keeper domains (P53, p. 9). fos turns a traditional system call into a message to an OS server through a proxy library (P102, pp. 6–7).
- **Hardware can do it without a kernel.** The M-Machine handles translation misses, faults and message arrivals in a dedicated event thread "without stopping the thread" (P66, pp. 4–6).
- **Where it is not done.** On conventional microprocessors interrupts are "the only way to signal an asynchronous event", and the CM-5 polls because interrupts cost too much (P33, pp. 433–434, 439). The Lisp Machine keeps sequence breaks, "a kind of interrupt" (P73, p. 429). EROS enters the kernel per trap because of the Pentium's "irregular" saved state (P77, p. 178). Helios steers every interrupt to one coordinator (P45, pp. 5–6).
- **Comparison.** In every kernel read the trap or interrupt is first taken by privileged code and only then becomes a message, so the conversion sits on a base that is not a message (C42); only the M-Machine moves it into hardware.

# C21: Single-stack, event-driven kernel

## Definition
The kernel runs on one stack with no per-thread kernel state, handling each event to completion. Merges "CPU driver" (as an event-driven kernel), "event-based (single-stack) kernel", "lazy scheduling / Benno scheduling" and "interrupt-style kernel".

## First found in
P8

## What the papers say, compared
- **Three lineages converge.** Barrelfish's per-core CPU driver is "privileged, event-driven, single-threaded, nonpreemptable" (P8, p. 8). L4's newer kernels replaced the process kernel by an event kernel with continuations ("Replaced: Process kernel by event kernel in seL4, OKL4 and NOVA") (P48, p. 144). EROS has "no per-process kernel stack": a suspended process restarts at the trap instruction (P77, p. 178).
- **Above the kernel, the same idea.** fos servers run each transaction to completion and store a continuation instead of blocking (P102, p. 7).
- **Scheduling follows.** L4 moved from lazy scheduling to "Benno" scheduling for a bounded worst-case execution time (P48, pp. 144–145).
- **Comparison.** The papers agree on the structure but give different reasons: verification and bounded timing (P48), per-core independence (P8), the processor's trap format (P77). None measures it against a kernel with per-thread stacks.

# C22: Capabilities

## Definition
Unforgeable references that both name an object and carry the rights to use it. Merges "protected pointer (capability, Access Descriptor)", "access descriptor (AD)", "level number (lifetime check)", "guarded pointers", "key (capability)", "principle of least privilege", "capability", "protection domain", "weak access right" and "IPC capabilities".

## First found in
P10

## What the papers say, compared
- **In hardware and microcode.** On the 432 only microcode creates and changes Access Descriptors, which carry the bearer's rights; every reference is checked for rights and bounds (P10, pp. 302–306). ADs are 32 bits and "can be freely copied", and the hardware refuses to store an AD where it would outlive its object (P72, pp. 161, 165, 181–182). The M-Machine uses guarded pointers as a light-weight capability system (P66, pp. 2–3).
- **In software kernels on ordinary processors.** In KeyKOS "Every object in the system is exclusively referred to by one or more associated keys", and objects have "no intrinsic authority" beyond their keys (P53, pp. 3–4). EROS defines a capability as "an unforgeable pair made up of an object identifier and a set of authorized operations"; a weak capability gives transitive read-only access (P77, pp. 171, 174). seL4 puts all kernel objects and memory under capabilities (P48, pp. 137–142); Barrelfish models its capabilities on seL4's (P8, p. 10). Minix 3 restricts which IPC primitives and destinations a process may use with bitmaps, called IPC capabilities (P49, p. 48).
- **As a property of messages.** Hewitt and Smith, quoted, claim "Every actor transmission is in effect an inter-domain call efficiently providing an intrinsic protection on actor machines" (P15, p. 62); no system is given.
- **Cost.** On the 432 a byte access "potentially requires four references", which Levy calls comparable to conventional virtual memory and reduced by caches (P72, pp. 166, 185–186). The CAP computer's language-grain capabilities caused "higher-frequency dereferencing of capabilities than the hardware can effectively support", while "capability systems can perform well without resorting to specialized hardware assists" (P77, p. 182).
- **Comparison.** The papers agree on what a capability is; they disagree on where to check it. The software kernels (KeyKOS, EROS, seL4) report good performance on commodity hardware; the hardware designs (432, CAP) report costs, but only Levy's is attributed to the addressing itself and none is measured here (C31).

# C23: Invocation as the only system call

## Definition
The kernel offers one operation, sending a message by invoking a capability or port, and every other action is reached through it. Merges "key invocation", "domain", "capability invocation as the only system call", "actor transmission" and the 432's "message port" as an instruction-set operation.

## First found in
P53

## What the papers say, compared
- **Two capability kernels make it total.** KeyKOS relies "totally" on capabilities, "without any other mechanisms"; "Sending a message is sometimes referred to as key invocation", by call, fork or return (P53, pp. 3, 7). In EROS "capability invocation is the only 'system call' implemented by the kernel", so "all actions taken by a process are implicitly access checked" (P77, pp. 173–174).
- **A processor makes it partial.** The 432 has instructions that send messages to and receive messages from port objects, but procedure calls, scalar operations and faults are not messages (P72, pp. 159, 162, 171).
- **The actor version is a claim.** Hewitt and Smith's "universal communication mechanism", quoted by Steele and Gabriel, generalises Smalltalk's and Simula's messages (P15, pp. 61–62).
- **Where each kernel stops.** KeyKOS keeps the trap instruction for binary compatibility and treats loads and stores as "isomorphic to read and write messages on the page key" (P53, pp. 9–11). EROS has a per-process mode bit that disables capability invocation "For emulation of other operating systems", and keeps loads and stores (P77, p. 173). Mach started with one message call and added others (P77, p. 182).
- **Comparison.** The papers agree one invocation can carry all kernel services; both kernels read still keep memory access and a compatibility trap outside it.

# C25: Transparent interposition

## Definition
Placing a component (monitor, filter, buffer, proxy) between two communicating parties without changing either. Merges "transparent interposition", "access indirection / forwarding objects", "shadow endpoint", "clans and chiefs" (as redirection), "interposition (wrappers)", "lightweight protection domain (sandboxing)", "shadow driver", "paravirtualization", "encapsulation" and "invisible pointer / forwarding".

## First found in
P45

## What the papers say, compared
- **On messages, from a uniform interface.** In EROS "All capabilities take the same arguments at the trap interface", so a filter process or the kernel's indirector "can be transparently interposed in front of most objects"; a trivial invocation costs 1.6 µs against 0.7 µs for Linux getppid, and "function was favored over performance" (P77, pp. 174, 180). In KeyKOS an intervening domain can add message buffering transparently, and keepers run unmodified BSD binaries; queue domains impose "considerable context switch overhead" (pipe at 0.56 of Mach 2.5), and routing every trap to the keeper "severely penalizes all trivial system calls" (P53, pp. 7, 9–10, 12, 14, 16).
- **On messages, inserted by the system.** Helios inserts shadow endpoints on every remote channel "while preserving the original Singularity channel programming interface", and a process can be moved by editing its manifest "without any changes to the program binary"; the cost is the remote message's latency (P45, pp. 2, 6–7, 10). The M-Machine's trap handlers let "a variety of coherence policies and protocols" be placed under unmodified programs (P66, p. 6).
- **On messages, abandoned.** L4's kernel redirection to clan chiefs added two messages per round trip and was dropped; a more general IPC redirection "failed to gain traction" (P48, p. 139).
- **Not on messages: per-interface wrappers.** Nooks wraps each kernel–driver call in "a wrapper that checks the parameters for validity", catching 99% of fatal and 55% of non-fatal driver errors with 455 hand-written wrappers; drivers in paravirtualized Linux VMs on L4 cost 3–8% but need the guest kernel changed (P49, pp. 45–47). The Lisp Machine wraps function definitions with trace and advise and redirects references with invisible pointers (P73, pp. 153, 174–175).
- **Comparison.** Where every interaction is a uniform message (EROS, KeyKOS, Helios), interposition needs no per-interface code and its cost is one extra hop; where it is not (Nooks), it needs a wrapper per interface. L4 is the counter-case: a message kernel that found kernel-level redirection too costly.

# C26: Language-based protection

## Definition
Isolation between processes enforced by a type-safe language and its compiler or verifier instead of hardware address spaces. Merges "software isolation (from Singularity)" and "language-based protection".

## First found in
P45

## What the papers say, compared
- **Singularity and its descendant.** Singularity protects by language safety and verification rather than the MMU, as the Burroughs B5000 did (P49, p. 49). Helios inherits this: processes are isolated by type and memory safety, all in one address space at ring 0, so no MMU is required (P45, pp. 4, 6), and remote channels keep isolation by type safety, not hardware (P45, pp. 4, 6–7, 10).
- **The opposite choice in a language machine.** The Lisp Machine deliberately makes "no attempt to have the language automatically forbid constructs that circumvent the contract", so internal state can be inspected from a debugger (P73, p. 282).
- **Comparison.** Both language-protected systems read rest on a trusted part outside the language (C42); no paper read measures the cost of language protection against hardware protection.

# C27: Ownership transfer of message data

## Definition
A message's payload passes from sender to receiver so that only one party can reach it at a time, which avoids copying without creating shared state. Merges "single-owner shared heap", "channel contract and exchange heap" (ownership part) and "data race through a message-passed reference".

## First found in
P9

## What the papers say, compared
- **Enforced by the language.** In Singularity "at each instant every object on the heap belongs to a single process. However, ownership of an object can be passed over a channel", allowing zero-copy I/O (P49, p. 50). Helios keeps message data in an exchange heap whose ownership is checked at compile time (P45, p. 5); between kernels it copies once (P45, pp. 6–7).
- **Not enforced: races follow.** In Go, sending a reference to a shared variable over a channel lets both goroutines reach it, and real bugs result (Docker#22985, CockroachDB#6111) (P9, p. 9).
- **Copying instead.** Barrelfish copies cache-line-sized messages through URPC channels (P8, p. 9).
- **Comparison.** The only empirical evidence (P9) shows what happens without enforcement; no paper read measures defects or costs with enforced ownership transfer.

# C29: Failure isolation and recovery

## Definition
How a message-based system contains a failed part and restores it. Merges "fault isolation", "reincarnation server (self-healing)", "shadow driver" and "checkpoint with consistency check".

## First found in
P49

## What the papers say, compared
- **Per component.** Minix 3's reincarnation server is the parent of all servers and drivers and restarts one that crashes or "fails to respond to the periodic pings" (P49, p. 48); Nooks' shadow drivers log and replay a driver's communication after a restart (P49, p. 46). The motivation: in current kernels "Every single one of the millions of lines of kernel code can overwrite key data structures" (P49, pp. 44–45).
- **Whole machine.** KeyKOS takes system-wide checkpoints with all processes briefly suspended (P53, pp. 4, 8); EROS checks each whole-machine snapshot for consistency before commit, since "Once committed, an inconsistent checkpoint lives forever" (P77, p. 174).
- **None.** In Barrelfish "the complete system is a failure unit" (P8, p. 17).
- **Comparison.** Isolation by messages makes per-component restart possible (Minix 3), but the two persistent capability systems recover centrally (C18), and the multikernel does not attempt it.

# C30: Stateless kernel and single-level store

## Definition
The kernel holds no critical state of its own; all state lives in persistent objects, and kernel data is only a cache of them. Merges "stateless kernel", "single-level store" (two records), "the kernel owns no state" and "software caching of objects".

## First found in
P53

## What the papers say, compared
- **KeyKOS.** The kernel holds "no critical state"; its private storage "is merely a cache of the persistent state"; "all data lives in persistent virtual memory" and only the nanokernel knows main memory from disk (P53, pp. 2–3).
- **EROS, its successor.** "With the sole exception of the list of stalled processes ... the EROS kernel owns no state"; even the process table "is a cache", and persistence is transparent to applications (P77, pp. 170, 175–178).
- **Comparison.** Both papers come from one lineage and agree; no independent paper read evaluates the idea.

# C31: Object-based processor and object addressing

## Definition
A processor in which all information is held in protected objects, reached through capabilities and object tables, with a check on every reference. Merges "object model", "two-level addressing", "entered environment and object qualification", "transparent multiprocessing", "object-based microprocessor", "object descriptor / object table / Object Table Directory", "type manager", "type control object and rights amplification", "type definition object", "object-oriented architecture with software-transparent multiprocessing and fault tolerance", "segmentation structure" and "instruction set design".

## First found in
P10

## What the papers say, compared
- **What it is.** In the 432 all information is encapsulated in protected objects (P10, p. 297); "Everything in the Intel 432 is an object", the "first object-based microprocessor" (P72, pp. 159, 184). Access Descriptors lead through an Object Table Directory and object tables to physical addresses, separating location from rights (P10, pp. 304–305; P72, pp. 163–165); an object must be "entered" and "qualified" before use (P10, pp. 303–304). The object model lets the same software run on a variable number of processors (P10, p. 297). Witten and Cleary's abstract places the 432's novelty in its "sophisticated segmentation structure" and instruction set (P74, abstract; abstract only).
- **Cost, as each evaluator frames it.** Levy says a byte access "potentially requires four references", an overhead "comparable to the overhead required on any conventional virtual memory system", reduced by caches (P72, pp. 166, 185–186). Colwell et al. put the inherent cost of the 432's object orientation at 2–3x as a residual, and say flushing the data-segment cache on every protected call could be fixed by an AD cache "without violating any of the fundamental principles of object orientation" (P10, pp. 325, 336–337). Hansen et al. ask "how much performance is degraded because of the object-oriented architecture" but do not isolate it (P29, pp. 17–18, 23).
- **Comparison.** All three evaluators are independent of the designers; they agree the 432 was slow and disagree on how much is due to object addressing (P72: like virtual memory; P10: 2–3x residual; P29: not separable).

# C32: Message send and procedure call as one mechanism

## Definition
A message send and a procedure or method call are carried by the same machinery, or shown to be interchangeable. Merges "refinement (Message object)", "domain refinement", "context object", "generic operation / sending a message", "method", "flavor", "instance", "combined method", "select-method", "entity", "message-receiving stream", "Flavors", "actors and closures are the same concept", "selector-object dispatch" and "tail forwarding".

## First found in
P10

## What the papers say, compared
- **The 432 passes call parameters in a message.** A procedure call puts parameters in a Message object that is a refinement of the caller's context, saving the caller a cache miss but costing the callee 148 cycles to traverse (P10, pp. 306–307, 323); contexts are built by hardware (P72, pp. 169, 172–173).
- **The Lisp Machine makes a send a call.** "performing a generic operation is called sending a message"; microcode binds self and calls the flavor's select-method, and "no new features are added to Lisp for message sending" (P73, pp. 283–285, 309); Flavors is "a ... message-passing system" (P15, p. 26).
- **Equivalence, with exceptions.** Sussman and Steele found "the codes in apply for function application and for actor invocation were identical", so "actors and closures were the same concept"; Hewitt's exceptions were cells (state) and synchronizers (exclusive access) (P15, p. 17); the lambda calculus captures actors "excepting only side effects and synchronization" (P15, p. 63).
- **SOAR has no send instruction.** A send compiles to a call plus software lookup with an in-line cache (P11, pp. 37, 46–47; P261, p. 8).
- **A message machine whose compiler turns sends into calls.** On the MDP a method invocation is a message to its first argument, dispatched through a selector object, but known types bypass it with a direct call (P12, pp. 20–21); tail forwarding makes a call "one call and no return" (P70, pp. 104, 106).
- **Comparison.** Where the receiver is in the same address space, every system read treats send as a call; the equivalence fails exactly on state and synchronisation (P15), which is what separate message machines add.

# C33: Functional migration

## Definition
Moving a function (an operating system service, a language operation, a check) between software, microcode and hardware. Merges "functional migration" and "migrating functionality between levels of abstraction".

## First found in
P10

## What the papers say, compared
- **Upward, in the 432.** OS functions, language operations, object addressing and fault handling were migrated into microcode and hardware (P10, pp. 296, 298–299); type managers are "partially in hardware ... and partially in operating system software" (P72, pp. 173, 184–185). Colwell et al. find that even if IPC and procedure calls "were free, executing in zero time", the 432 would still be slow (P10, pp. 301, 309).
- **Both ways, in SOAR.** "the key to good performance is a willingness to migrate functionality from one level of abstraction to another"; SOAR replaced microcoded instructions with software trap handlers (P11, p. 126).
- **Minimal hard-wiring in the MDP.** Only one message is hard-wired and the rest are ROM code (P69, p. 191).
- **Comparison.** The papers agree migration should follow measurement, not the level's prestige; the 432 is the cautionary case and SOAR the counter-example (C35, C36).

# C33: Functional migration

## Definition
Moving a function (an operating system service, a language operation, a check) between software, microcode and hardware. Merges "functional migration" and "migrating functionality between levels of abstraction".

## First found in
P10

## What the papers say, compared
- **Upward, in the 432.** OS functions, language operations, object addressing and fault handling were migrated into microcode and hardware (P10, pp. 296, 298–299); type managers are "partially in hardware ... and partially in operating system software" (P72, pp. 173, 184–185). Colwell et al. find that even if IPC and procedure calls "were free, executing in zero time", the 432 would still be slow (P10, pp. 301, 309).
- **Both ways, in SOAR.** "the key to good performance is a willingness to migrate functionality from one level of abstraction to another"; SOAR replaced microcoded instructions with software trap handlers (P11, p. 126).
- **Minimal hard-wiring in the MDP.** Only one message is hard-wired and the rest are ROM code (P69, p. 191).
- **Comparison.** The papers agree migration should follow measurement, not the level's prestige; the 432 is the cautionary case and SOAR the counter-example (C35, C36).
