# C34: High-level-language computer architecture and the semantic gap

## Definition
Machines directed at executing particular high-level languages, usually justified as narrowing the "semantic gap" between programming and machine languages. Merges "high-level language computer (HLLC)", "HLL computer system (HLLCS)", "direct execution machine", "HLLESF", "HLLSSF / HLLPSF", "semantic gap" (two records), "transparent reversibility of compilation", "Lisp machine", "emulation machine", "CDR-coding", "generic instructions" and "high-level language uniprocessor".

## First found in
P15

## What the papers say, compared
- **The 1980 retrospective.** Ditzel and Patterson list "Reduce the semantic gap" among the common justifications without defining it (P280, p. 97), note that "only a handful" of HLLCs were built and none is commercial (P280, pp. 97–98), and expect direct execution machines not to "become viable" (P280, p. 100). They define a high-level-language computer system by its behaviour to the user, which "does not restrict the implementation to hardware or software" (P280, p. 100), and propose measuring support by the ratio of a fast unchecked system's time to the checked system's (HLLESF) (P280, p. 101).
- **Language machines built.** The Lisp machine was "specially microcoded to run Lisp" (P15, p. 12); the Dorado was "basically an emulation machine" for byte codes (P15, p. 14); Lisp Machine instructions are generic, typing operands at run time (P73, p. 484). The 432 is tested "as a high-level language uniprocessor" (P29, pp. 17, 23).
- **Judgements.** Ungar: earlier language machines "closely coupled the source language semantics to the hardware ... this approach has usually resulted in increased cost and poor performance" (P11, p. 14). The EROS authors use the term the other way: their kernel is fast partly because the "semantic gap" between its abstractions and the hardware is "minimal" (P77, p. 183).
- **Comparison.** The papers that judge the approach (P280, P11, P15) agree it did not pay; none of them discusses messages or objects as the raised interface (P280's record notes it never mentions messages).

# C35: Language support moved from hardware to the compiler

## Definition
Compilation and runtime techniques that obtain on simpler hardware the performance special hardware promised. Merges "compiler-protected intra-module call", "in-line caching", "compilation to a low-level instruction set", "Smalltalk On A RISC (SOAR)", "compiling all methods", "bytecodes as the semantic definition" (compiler side), "in-line method cache", "sufficiently smart compiler", "reduction of method calls to function calls" and "Threaded Abstract Machine".

## First found in
P10

## What the papers say, compared
- **SOAR's measurements.** Compiling Smalltalk to a low-level instruction set instead of bytecodes gives "an approximate doubling in speed" for about 500 KB more memory (P11, pp. 34–35, 68); in-line caching replaces lookup hardware, and instantaneous lookup hardware would gain at most 23% (P11, pp. 13, 45–47, 68). In-line caches work because "96% of the time the method invoked does not change" (P261, p. 8). Several SOAR features "could easily be performed by the compiler at marginal increased time and space costs" (1–3%), but software tag tests would cost an estimated 26% in speed (P261, pp. 6–7, 10).
- **The 432's compiler.** Moving intra-module call protection from hardware to the compiler would save up to 20.5% on Dhrystone (P10, pp. 315–316).
- **Lisp.** The "sufficiently smart compiler" was a recurring hope for stock hardware (P15, p. 23); stock-hardware Lisps did match Lisp machines on garbage collection (P15, pp. 34–35).
- **Message machines.** On the J-Machine, reducing method calls to function calls was "highly successful" (P70, pp. 4, 49). The Threaded Abstract Machine runs the message-driven model in compiler-managed software handlers, which "does not necessarily result in lower performance than a direct hardware implementation" (P33, p. 437).
- **Disagreement.** Ditzel and Patterson say special hardware does not "greatly" simplify compilers (P280, p. 98), while the J-Machine's hardware tags free the compiler from type analysis (P70, p. 11), and SOAR's hardware "in the main simplified" its compiler (P261, p. 10). The papers agree compilers recover most of the gain and disagree on whether tags still pay.

# C36: Architect's trap

## Definition
Specialised hardware features that speed one operation and add design time without improving overall performance.

## First found in
P11

## What the papers say, compared
- **Named by Ungar.** Four of SOAR's specialised features were "mistakes"; the garbage-collection hardware "probably did not speed up SOAR" (P11, pp. 70, 72, 126).
- **The same lesson in 1980.** On SYMBOL, adding hardware did not make the system "run proportionally faster" (P280, p. 102); HLLC designers "ignored the view of the total system" (P280, p. 103), and hardware is costly to debug (P280, p. 99).
- **In the 432.** Bit-aligned instructions did not make code much smaller than VAX or 68000 code, and the value of a complete instruction set is doubted because high-level-language users never see it (P10, pp. 298–299, 301).
- **In message-driven hardware.** Its support is "partly counter-productive" for processing performance (P33, p. 435).
- **Comparison.** The papers agree across language machines; P33 extends the warning to message-driven processors, the closest case to this thesis.

# C37: Hardware type tags and traps

## Definition
Data words carry type tags checked in parallel with the operation; a mismatch traps to software. Merges "tags trap bad guesses", "integer tags and traps" and "generic instructions".

## First found in
P11

## What the papers say, compared
- **SOAR guesses and traps.** "SOAR assumes that the operands are integers ... simultaneously checking the tags", trapping if wrong (P11, p. 31); on a non-integer "the hardware will trap and transfer to a handler that will look up the correct method" (P261, p. 6). Doing the tests in software would cost an estimated 26% in speed and 15% in image size (P261, pp. 6–7).
- **The MDP keeps tags for synchronisation and typing.** Tags make the no-fault case faster than "test and branch instructions" (P12, p. 7); traps on type errors serve dynamic typing and uniform local and remote access (P69, pp. 189, 194). Tags free the compiler from type analysis, "even if Optimist II cannot determine the type of some expression, performance does not suffer too much" (P70, p. 11), but there are only 16 tags (P70, p. 125).
- **The Lisp Machine makes every instruction generic,** which brings "data dependencies that can have major effects on the speed of execution" (P73, p. 484).
- **Comparison.** Three independent designs keep tags; the only quantified benefit is SOAR's estimate (P261), and nobody reads it against a compiler with type inference.

# C38: Register windows

## Definition
Overlapping register sets used as activation frames, so calls need not save registers to memory. Merges "register windows for frequent calls", "overlapping register windows", "spilling rules" and "pointer to register".

## First found in
P11

## What the papers say, compared
- **SOAR depends on them.** "SOAR would run 46% slower without them", because Smalltalk compiles to many calls (P11, pp. 43, 67, 70); it uses 16-register fully overlapped windows with simple spilling rules and hardware mapping registers to memory addresses (P261, pp. 3–4, 7, 10).
- **The contrast cases.** The 432 has no data registers, to save chip space and speed process swaps (P10, pp. 302, 318); the J-Machine's evaluators name the "paucity of registers" as a limit (P65, p. 11); and in message-driven processors a context lasts only one handler, so "large register sets cannot be used" (P33, pp. 435–437).
- **Comparison.** Call-heavy language machines gain from many registers, while message-driven ones cannot keep them busy; this is a design tension for any machine whose primitive is a send (C1, C7).

- **The contrast cases.** The 432 has no data registers, to save chip space and speed process swaps (P10, pp. 302, 318); the J-Machine's evaluators name the "paucity of registers" as a limit (P65, p. 11); and in message-driven processors a context lasts only one handler, so "large register sets cannot be used" (P33, pp. 435–437).
- **Comparison.** Call-heavy language machines gain from many registers, while message-driven ones cannot keep them busy; this is a design tension for any machine whose primitive is a send (C1, C7).

# C39: Garbage collection and memory reclamation support

## Definition
How objects are reclaimed, and whether hardware helps. Merges "Generation Scavenging", "ephemeral garbage collection", "generation tags (hardware write barrier)" and "storage resource object (global heap vs local stack)".

## First found in
P11

## What the papers say, compared
- **Software collectors won.** Generation Scavenging uses about 3% of CPU time with "no hardware support" (P11, pp. 50, 86, 110, 126), and SOAR's GC hardware "probably did not speed up SOAR" (P11, p. 72); its generation tags could be done by the compiler for about 1–2% (P261, p. 7). Moon's ephemeral collector for Lisp machines was "subsequently adapted for use on stock hardware", and the belief that stock Lisps could never match GC performance was "proven wrong" (P15, pp. 13, 27, 34–35).
- **The 432 avoided it for short-lived objects.** Global heaps need garbage collection, so local stack storage objects were added because collection "is prohibitive for short-lived objects" (P72, pp. 179–181).
- **In a message machine, global collection is hard.** The J-Machine kernel had none; a parallel algorithm tracking every sent ID "would be unfeasible", and mark-and-sweep "has to stop the J-Machine" (P70, pp. 58, 120).
- **Comparison.** On one processor, hardware GC support did not pay; on a machine of message-passing nodes, no collector was found that avoids a global stop.

# C40: Stock hardware good enough

## Definition
General-purpose processors, with better compilers, reach the performance that once justified special-purpose machines. Merges "stock hardware", "value lay in the software, not the hardware" and "general-purpose hardware good enough".

## First found in
P15

## What the papers say, compared
- **Lisp.** Stock hardware means "commercially available, general-purpose, 'off-the-shelf' computers" (P15, p. 23); "General-purpose hardware eventually became good enough to support Lisp once again", largely through fast RISC processors, and "the value lay ultimately in the software and not in its enabling hardware technology" (P15, pp. 15, 35).
- **Smalltalk.** A RISC with a few additions (SOAR) runs Smalltalk at about the speed of the Dorado (P11, p. 66); a specialised machine "must also exploit compilation to attain high performance" (P11, p. 17).
- **High-level-language machines.** Better compilers and cheaper memory removed their motivation (P280, pp. 98–99).
- **Capability kernels.** "capability systems can perform well without resorting to specialized hardware assists" (P77, p. 182).
- **Message machines, from their own designers.** The J-Machine's evaluators propose folding its mechanisms "into a conventional RISC processor core without affecting sequential performance" (P65, p. 12).
- **The other side.** Barrelfish's authors expect hardware may "drop [cache coherence] entirely in favor of a message-passing model" (P8, p. 5), and the SCC's designers argue coherence overhead will outgrow the value of more cores (P21, p. 173). Both are arguments, not measurements.
- **Comparison.** Every retrospective read agrees the stock-hardware argument won in the past; the only counter-arguments concern many-core chips and are unmeasured.

# C41: Adoption factors: compatibility, market and price

## Definition
Reasons other than raw performance why a machine or operating system is or is not adopted. Merges "cachet", "dedicated computers", "AI winter" and "compatibility as reason for coherence".

## First found in
P15

## What the papers say, compared
- **Market and marketing (third parties on the 432).** It "tried to do too many new things all at once", and its market "may still not be large enough or defined well enough" (P10, p. 337); its failure was "probably due in part to premature (and somewhat overzealous) marketing" (P72, p. 186).
- **Price and dedicated machines.** Customers "were not willing to buy expensive 'dedicated' computers and then spend money maintaining them" (P15, p. 35); adoption was driven partly by "cachet", and the "AI winter" hurt Lisp companies (P15, pp. 15, 29–30). Smalltalk environments "suffer from poor cost-performance" (P11, p. 10) and "require such expensive computers that few programmers can afford them" (P13, abstract; abstract only).
- **Compatibility and existing investment.** Systems "tend not to abandon compatibility to eliminate small costs" (P22, p. 1); there is "enormous investment" in Linux and Windows, and a scalability problem "must affect a substantial group of users" before it gets attention (P8, pp. 1, 16). HLLCs supported other languages poorly (P280, pp. 98–99).
- **Designers' view of their own machine.** The MDP's designers name the lack of well-established parallel benchmarks and programs "biased by the mechanisms ... of the machines for which they were initially written" (P12, pp. 23–24).
- **Business.** KeyKOS development "ceased in 1991 when the company closed" (P77, p. 170).
- **Comparison.** Third parties stress market, price and compatibility; designers stress benchmarks and implementation. Compatibility (P22, P8) is the factor that applies unchanged to any new machine today.

# C42: The base outside a self-defining system

## Definition
The level that a system written in its own terms still rests on and does not express in those terms: microcode subprimitives, a privileged kernel, a hand-built initial image. Merges "CPU driver" (as the base), "subprimitive", "no special privileges", "type manager" (hardware part), "bytecodes as the semantic definition", "constructor" (initial image) and "criticality".

## First found in
P8

## What the papers say, compared
- **Language machines.** "Everything on the Lisp Machine is written in Lisp, including all system programs", but subprimitives are "hand-coded in microcode", "cannot do full checking", and misused "can destroy the environment" (P73, pp. 1, 172). On the 3600 the OS, editor, compiler and collector were all Zetalisp, on a base "specially microcoded to run Lisp" (P15, pp. 12, 26); a new dialect can be bootstrapped inside a host providing "primitive operations such as arithmetic and I/O" (P15, p. 65). For SOAR "the virtual machine is the semantic definition of the language" (P261, p. 2).
- **Object processors.** On the 432, addressing, rights checks, IPC and scheduling stay in microcode and hardware, outside the object model, and that base fills chips (P10, pp. 298–299, 302, 305, 316). Programmer-defined type managers use mechanisms "identical" to the system's, yet hardware-defined operations remain (P72, pp. 173, 184–185).
- **Message machines.** On the MDP only EXECUTE is hard-wired and every other message is ROM code a user can redefine (P69, p. 191); but the kernel above is "hand-optimized assembly language" and the runtime is assembly because it implements "functionality that cannot be easily expressed in Concurrent Smalltalk" (P70, pp. 51–52).
- **Kernels.** Barrelfish's CPU driver, in C and assembly, lies outside the message model (P8, p. 8); L4 is written in assembler, C and C++, not in its own messages (P48, pp. 142–147); Singularity is "almost entirely in Sing#" except a trusted part (P49, pp. 49–50); EROS defines allocation and process construction in its own processes, but the kernel and "the hand-constructed initial system image" stay outside (P77, pp. 179–180).
- **Comparison.** Every system read keeps a base; its size ranges from one hard-wired message (P69) to large microcode (P10, P73). Only the 432 papers state what the base costs (chip space), and only the Lisp Machine manual states what it prevents (full checking).

# C37: Hardware type tags and traps

## Definition
Data words carry type tags checked in parallel with the operation; a mismatch traps to software. Merges "tags trap bad guesses", "integer tags and traps" and "generic instructions".

## First found in
P11

## What the papers say, compared
- **SOAR guesses and traps.** "SOAR assumes that the operands are integers ... simultaneously checking the tags", trapping if wrong (P11, p. 31); on a non-integer "the hardware will trap and transfer to a handler that will look up the correct method" (P261, p. 6). # C43: Shared memory built on messages

## Definition
A shared address space or coherent memory implemented by messages between nodes, kernels or caches. Merges "global virtual address space over message passing", "unifying shared memory and message passing", "shared memory layered on message passing", "incremental parallelization", "block status bits" (use), "coherence messages implement shared memory" and Split-C's PUT/GET.

## First found in
P12

## What the papers say, compared
- **Measured on two message machines.** The M-Machine layers "a coherent shared memory system ... on the message-passing substrate" in trap handlers, so unmodified sequential programs run and are parallelised step by step; a remote read costs 138 cycles against 3 for a local cache hit, a remote write 74 against 2 (simulated) (P66, pp. 1–2, 6, 8–10). On the J-Machine a remote read is a three-word request message costing 60 cycles to a neighbour and 98 across 512 nodes (P65, pp. 3, 11).
- **Claimed without measurement.** The MDP can "build a shared memory model that gives the application programmer a single, shared address space" (P12, pp. 3, 5); it is "an experiment in unifying shared-memory and message-passing parallel computers" (P64, p. 12) and offers "many of the advantages of both" (P69, p. 196).
- **In software layers and kernels.** Split-C gives a "familiar shared-memory style" of PUT and GET over Active Messages (P33, p. 434). Barrelfish builds a shared virtual address space from replicated page tables kept consistent by messages (P8, p. 11). KeyNIX builds a binary-compatible UNIX on KeyKOS's messages, at a cost for trivial calls (getpid at 0.4 of Mach 2.5) (P53, pp. 10–11, 14–15).
- **Every coherent chip already does it.** Coherence is carried by point-to-point request, forward, invalidation and acknowledgement messages between cache controllers (P22, pp. 2–3).
- **Comparison.** Where measured, remote shared access costs 20–50 times a local hit; properties kept: transparency (P66), failure isolation per process (P53); lost: encapsulation, since any program can load and store remote data (P66, record's inference). P22's point reframes the question: the choice is which level exposes the messages, not whether they exist.

# C44: Messages built on shared memory

## Definition
Message passing implemented over shared or coherent memory. Merges "URPC", "one-sided put and get" and the "Message Passing Buffer" as a message transport.

## First found in
P8

## What the papers say, compared
- **On coherent memory, at kernel level.** Barrelfish's URPC is a shared-memory, cache-line, point-to-point channel received by polling, tuned to the coherence protocol at two interconnect round trips per message, and costs 450 cycles against 424 for L4 IPC (P8, pp. 9–10). Helios carries remote messages over shared FIFOs, at 11–128 µs by size (P45, pp. 4, 6–7, 10). fos may use shared memory as its transport (P102, pp. 5, 8).
- **On non-coherent on-chip memory.** The SCC's messages are a software protocol of one-sided put and get over 16 KB per-tile buffers; messages under 16 KB are 15 times faster than through DDR3 (P21, pp. 173–177).
- **Inside one address space.** The 432's call message is an object in shared memory (P10, pp. 297, 306–307); Lisp Machine processes pass messages as lists or arrays in shared objects (P73, p. 429); Go's channels live in a language that also shares memory (P9, pp. 2–3).
- **What is lost.** Freedom from data races, when references pass through channels (P9, p. 9); encapsulation, unless a language or capabilities enforce it (P45, P10), and the Lisp Machine deliberately does not (P73, p. 282).
- **Comparison.** On current coherent hardware messages on shared memory cost about as much as kernel IPC (P8); which properties survive depends on enforcement above the memory, not on the memory.

# C45: Duality of message passing and shared memory

## Definition
The claim that message-based and shared-memory structures are equivalent, or each can be built from the other. Merges "message-passing/shared-memory duality", "actors and closures are the same concept" (as equivalence) and "coexistence of communication paradigms".

## First found in
P8

## What the papers say, compared
- **Cited, not tested.** Barrelfish cites Lauer and Needham: the two OS models are duals, and the machine architecture decides between them (P8, p. 3). The original paper (P18) is unread.
- **Each side claims the other maps onto it.** "any program that works for ... message passing systems (e.g., MPI cluster) can easily map to a shared memory system with caches" (P22, p. 8). Active Messages are "more primitive" than send/receive and shared memory and implement both (P33, p. 431). EROS models a load or store as "an efficiently cached capability invocation" (P77, p. 173). The MDP claims the advantages of both (P69, p. 196; P64, p. 12).
- **Equivalence with exceptions.** Actors equal closures except for state and synchronisation (P15, pp. 17, 63).
- **Swapping is used to fix bugs, not shown equivalent.** Go developers fix shared-memory bugs with channels and channel bugs with shared variables (P9, pp. 8, 11).
- **Coexistence in practice.** Message passing and scratchpads persist in niches beside dominant coherent shared memory (P22, pp. 1, 8).
- **Comparison.** Every statement read is an argument; none measures whether encapsulation, freedom from races or interposition survive the translation, which is what the duality question needs (see C43, C44).

# C46: Mixing messages with shared state

## Definition
Systems and programs that use shared memory, locks or direct calls alongside messages, and the reasons given. Merges "mixing message passing with other synchronization", "communication through shared Lisp objects" and the shared-state parts of "notional lock / lock server" and "single-owner shared heap".

## First found in
P9

## What the papers say, compared
- **Measured frequency (programs).** In six Go applications, shared-memory primitives are used more than channels (Mutex 45.01–70.34% against chan 18.48–42.99% of uses), stable from 2015 to 2018, and 16 blocking bugs mix a channel with a lock or wait; no developer reason is recorded (P9, pp. 4, 6–7, 11).
- **Reasons from system designers.**
  - Existing programs: Barrelfish supports threads sharing an address space because "most current programs" need it (P8, pp. 11, 15).
  - Performance: Singularity keeps a shared object heap, since if all data "had to go over channels, the system would be very slow" (P49, p. 50); L4 prefers shared buffers for bulk data (P48, pp. 136–138).

# C47: Kinds of concurrency defect

## Definition
Taxonomies of real concurrency bugs by pattern and by behaviour. Merges "atomicity violation", "order violation", "manifestation condition", "multi-variable concurrency bug", "data race (not a bug pattern)", "deadlock", "order intention", "blocking bug", "non-blocking bug" and "Go's new implementation of existing primitives".

## First found in
P5

## What the papers say, compared
- **By pattern (C/C++, shared variables and locks).** Of 105 bugs in four applications, 74 are non-deadlock (51 atomicity violations, 24 order violations, 2 other, 3 counted twice) and 31 deadlocks; 25 of 74 involve several variables; 101 of 105 need at most two threads (P5, pp. 331–336). Data races are left out as a category because "data-race free does not mean concurrency bug free" (P5, pp. 329, 332). Order intentions "cannot be easily enforced by the basic TM design or locks" (P5, p. 338).
- **By behaviour and cause (Go).** Of 171 bugs in six applications, 85 are blocking, a category broader than deadlock, and 86 non-blocking; 105 come from shared memory and 66 from message passing (P9, p. 5). Go's own versions of familiar primitives (RWMutex giving writers priority) cause new bugs (P9, p. 6).
- **Comparison.** P5 classifies by what went wrong in memory, P9 by how goroutines communicate; P9's "blocking" includes waits that P5 would not call deadlock. Different languages and populations prevent direct comparison of counts.

# C48: Is message passing less error-prone?

## Definition
The belief, tested empirically, that communicating by messages causes fewer concurrency bugs than sharing memory. Merges "cause dimension (shared memory vs. message passing)" and "message passing is less error-prone (common belief, refuted for blocking bugs)".

## First found in
P9

## What the papers say, compared
- **Tested in Go.** "Contrary to the common belief", message passing causes 49 of 85 blocking bugs (about 58%) although shared-memory primitives are used more; shared memory causes 69 of 86 non-blocking bugs (about 80%), so "When used correctly, message passing can be less prone to non-blocking bugs" (P9, pp. 2, 5–6, 9–12). The ratio divides bug counts by static counts of primitive use, not by how often each runs (P9 record, Correctness; pp. 4, 6).
- **Scope limit.** Go programs mix both models; none is a system where each piece of state has one owner (P9, pp. 2–3).
- **The shared-memory side, without a comparison.** Order intentions are hard to express or enforce with locks or transactional memory (P5, p. 338); P5 has no message-passing counts.
- **An argument.** Shared data has "correctness and performance pitfalls" (P8, p. 4).
- **Comparison.** The only direct test refutes the belief for blocking bugs and supports it for non-blocking ones, within a language that does not enforce ownership; evidence for systems that do is absent from the papers read (P78, P79 unread).

# C49: Scalability of cache coherence

## Definition
Whether the cost of keeping caches coherent grows slowly enough with the number of cores. Merges "single-writer, multiple-reader invariant", "scalable coherence", "amortized coherence traffic", "exact vs inexact encoding of sharers", "hierarchical inclusive coherence", "explicit eviction notifications", "recall (back-invalidation)", "direct vs indirect miss" and "complexity shifting".

## First found in
P22

## What the papers say, compared
- **It scales, analytically.** With exact sharer tracking, coherence traffic per miss does not depend on core count and is at most 20% above caches without coherence; hierarchical storage grows as the square or cube root of core count (5% or 2% of cache at 512 cores); recalls stay below 0.1% of misses; indirect misses cost 1.5–2 times a non-coherent miss (P22, pp. 3–7). These are analytical results on one chip, with no queuing modelled, and interconnect and "software non-scalability" left out (P22, pp. 3–9). Removing coherence "shifts the complexity from hardware to software" (P22, p. 9).
- **It may not, by argument.** The SCC's designers say "the computational value gained through additional cores will at some point be exceeded by the protocol overhead" (P21, p. 173). fos says "It is also unclear whether cache coherent shared memory will scale to large core counts", without a cited source (P102, pp. 2–5). Barrelfish cites a limit "to even 80 cores" (P8, p. 4).
- **Measured costs are at kernel and lock level.** Updating shared state costs about 12,000 extra cycles per update at 16 cores, "stalled on cache misses" (P8, p. 3); Linux and Windows unmap scale worse from serial IPIs (P8, p. 13); Linux's page allocator "does not scale beyond 8 cores under heavy load" (P102, pp. 3–4, 8–9); Helios's single dispatcher lock limits scaling on 4 cores (P45, pp. 9, 11).
- **Comparison.** The pro side is analysis of the protocol; the con side is argument plus measurements of software bottlenecks, which P22 explicitly sets outside coherence. The two sides do not yet meet on the same evidence (P23, P24, P98 unread).

# C50: Software-managed coherence and non-coherent on-chip memory

## Definition
On-chip memory shared by cores without hardware coherence, with software invalidating or tracking cached lines. Merges "Message Passing Buffer (MPB)", "Message Passing Memory Type (MPMT)", "INVDMB instruction", "software-maintained coherency" and "block status bits".

## First found in
P21

## What the papers say, compared
- **The SCC.** Each tile has 16 KB of on-die shared memory; cache lines marked MPMT can all be invalidated in one cycle by a new instruction, and "Shared memory coherency is maintained through software in an effort to eliminate the communication and hardware overhead required for a memory coherent 2D-mesh" (P21, pp. 173–177).
- **The M-Machine** caches remote data in local memory under software control with two status bits per 8-word block (P66, p. 9).
- **The analysts' reply.** Removing coherence moves complexity into software, and incoherent scratchpads persist only in real-time niches (P22, pp. 1, 8–9).
- **Comparison.** The designers (P21) give no measurement of the saving; the analysts (P22) give no measurement of the software cost. Both are open.

# C51: Network bandwidth as the scaling limit

## Definition
For machines of message-passing nodes, interconnect bandwidth and topology bound the number of nodes and how finely programs can communicate. Merges "terminal network bandwidth" and the network limits stated in the J-Machine papers.

## First found in
P65

## What the papers say, compared
- **Design.** The number of nodes is limited "by the addressability of the router and the bandwidth of the network", and a 3-D mesh is said to give "the lowest latency and highest throughput" (P64, pp. 2, 5).
- **Measured.** "global bandwidth is a critical resource that limits the computation to communication ratio"; under random traffic the network saturates at 6 of 14.4 Gbit/s bisection, and terminal bandwidth "often becomes the limiting factor" for neighbour communication (P65, pp. 2, 4–6, 11).
- **Projected.** The network "should not become a critical resource until a J-Machine with over 7³ = 343 nodes is built"; with random allocation on 65,536 nodes "the network will become hopelessly congested" unless locality is exploited (P70, pp. 110, 114, 121).
- **On a multiprocessor.** Barrelfish's NUMA-aware multicast stays near 3k cycles while broadcast and unicast grow linearly to about 13–14k at 32 cores (P8, p. 13).
- **Comparison.** The J-Machine papers agree the network is the limit and locality the cure; none of them shows how to get locality, which P70 leaves open.

# C53: Exploratory programming environments and their cost

## Definition
Environments such as Smalltalk-80 and the Lisp Machine, built for programmer productivity, which needed expensive machines. Merges "exploratory programming environment" (two records), "demands of Smalltalk-80 on traditional computer systems" and "price of Smalltalk".

## First found in
P11

## What the papers say, compared
- **Smalltalk.** Exploratory environments "remain largely experimental" because "They suffer from poor cost-performance"; the Dorado cost $120,000 (P11, pp. 6, 10–11). Ungar and Patterson's abstract lists Smalltalk-80's demands on traditional systems and says SOAR lets them estimate its performance cost (P13, abstract; abstract only).
- **Lisp.** The Lisp machine was meant to "support a Lisp development environment" (P15, p. 12); it is "an interactive system" with "no strong distinction between the 'system' programs and the 'user' programs" (P73, p. 282). Customers would not buy "expensive 'dedicated' computers" (P15, p. 35).
- **Comparison.** Both lines tried special hardware to make such environments affordable; both were overtaken by stock hardware (C40). The full text of P13 would show whether SOAR's authors agree.

# Coverage of SQ1

Saved as `sls/4-synthesis/SQ1.coverage.md`. Which papers serve this question, what each added, and whether the question has what it needs (`research/sls/4-synthesis/step.md`).

## Rule
- **Kind:** kinds.
- **Unit:** a kind of message-based system: the level where the send is a primitive (an instruction, a hardware or microcode mechanism, or the kernel's own means of communication), combined with how the mechanism works. A paper also adds a new unit if it shows a new kind of path, added later, that is not a message.
- **Enough when:** at least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 5 in a row add nothing new (10 + 5).
- **From the reading order:** several papers on one system count as one reading; only the strongest is read for it. Abstract-only records (P74) are linked but do not count (gate 3c).

## Read
Papers with an accepted record that serve this question, in the reading order of SQ1.md (records on the same system are grouped and counted as one reading).
| # | Paper | Contributes | New? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | P10 | Object-based processor (Intel 432): Send is an "interprocess communication primitive" in the instruction set, with IPC, scheduling and dispatching in microcode and hardware, beside memory-to-memory data instructions (pp. 297–298, 306–307) | new (reading 1: Intel 432) |
| – | P72 | Same system: instructions send to and receive from port objects, IPC "in hardware and microcode"; calls, scalar and fault paths are not messages (pp. 159, 162, 171) | covered by P10 (same system, counted with it) |
| – | P74 | Abstract only: names only the 432's segmentation and instruction set (abstract) | not counted (abstract only, gate 3c) |
| 2 | P12 | Message-driven multicomputer node: SEND in the instruction set, hardware buffering and dispatch, "There is no receive instruction" (pp. 1, 6, 9); later non-message path at language level: calls of known type compiled to direct function invocation (p. 20) | new (reading 2: MDP/J-Machine; a kind and a later-path kind) |
| – | P65 | Same system: send instructions, hardware task creation on arrival, dispatch in four cycles (p. 2) | covered by P12 (same system) |
| – | P64 | Same system, 1989 design: SEND instructions, two hardware priority queues, task per message (pp. 7–9, 13) | covered by P12 (same system) |
| – | P69 | Same system, 1987 design: transmit instruction, message unit with hard-wired EXECUTE (pp. 189, 191–192, 194) | covered by P12 (same system) |

| 3 | P8 | Multikernel: the kernel's inter-core communication is "explicit messages" over URPC on coherent memory with polling; a replica shared under spinlocks allowed by the model, not built (pp. 5, 7, 9, 18) | new (reading 3) |

| 8 | P66 | Multicomputer node with a user-level protected SEND instruction, hardware destination translation (GTLB), register-mapped receive queue and dispatch via DIP to an event thread; messages between nodes only (pp. 3–7) | new (reading 8) |
| 9 | P73 | Microcoded language machine whose send is a microcode-dispatched call of the receiving object; "no new features are added to Lisp for message sending" (pp. 285, 309) | new (reading 9) |
| 10 | P102 | Factored OS: microkernel messaging among server fleets on separate cores, asynchronous sends to named mailboxes (pp. 5–6, 8) | covered by P8 (same level and mechanism: kernel messages between cores of one chip; fleets are OS structure) |
| 11 | P45 | Satellite kernels per NUMA domain and per programmable device of another instruction set, talking by contract-typed channels with software isolation (pp. 1–3, 6–7) | new (reading 11): heterogeneous satellite kernels with language-isolated channels |
| 12 | P33 | Message-driven nodes (J-Machine, Monsoon) with SEND in the execution unit; a design-only proposal of processor support for user-level handlers; Active Messages themselves a user-level layer (pp. 431, 436, 438–439) | covered by P12 (the built kinds are P12's; the proposal is not a built system) |
| 13 | P49 | Minix 3 multiserver OS with rendezvous fixed-length messages and interrupts as messages; Singularity, a language-protected microkernel with typed channels (pp. 47–50) | covered by P46 and P45 |

# Coverage of SQ2

Saved as `sls/4-synthesis/SQ2.coverage.md`. Which papers serve this question, what each added, and whether the question has what it needs (`research/sls/4-synthesis/step.md`).

## Rule
- **Kind:** kinds.
- **Unit:** a kind of mechanism kept below the language that is not a message send (e.g. shared memory, interrupts, traps, privileged instructions, microcode, global registers), together with the reason given for keeping it; or a kind of level found to be written in the system's own objects and messages. A mechanism already recorded counts as new again only with a reason not yet recorded.
- **Enough when:** at least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 5 in a row add nothing new (10 + 5). Abstract-only records (P74) do not count (gate 3c).

## Read
In the reading order of SQ2.md: the named lessons paper first, then processors alternating with kernels, then the papers the order does not name.
| # | Paper | Contributes | New? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | P48 | Shared buffers (long IPC complex, "rarely used"), kernel–user shared message registers (portability, cost), in-kernel fixed-policy scheduler (no user-level scheduler "without imposing high overhead"), in-kernel timer and interrupt-controller drivers, interrupts disabled in the kernel and a big lock (simplicity, verification); kernel in assembler/C/C++ (pp. 136–139, 142–147) | new |
| 2 | P10 | Shared memory in a "pure memory-to-memory architecture" (chip size, faster process swap, "conceptual unity and simplicity"); microcode as sole creator of protected pointers (unforgeable); I/O only through the Interface Processor; unprotected branch instructions never generated (pp. 302, 311, 315–317) | new (new reasons for shared memory; microcode and I/O kinds) |
| 3 | P8 | Coherent shared memory under every message ("the only inter-core communication mechanism available"); traps and system calls into the CPU driver; hardware-routed interrupts; IPIs and MONITOR/MWAIT to wake a receiver; application shared memory because "most current programs" need it; CPU driver outside the message model (pp. 8–11, 14) | new |
| 4 | P12 | Presence and type tags with fault handlers ("makes software more efficient and robust"), segment descriptors (relocation, protection), translation table (global naming), diagnostic port (supervisory commands), local READ/WRITE (pp. 3, 5–8) | new |
| 5 | P53 | Privileged in-kernel low-level drivers ("Except where performance compels otherwise"), shared segments in KeyNIX (state shared between UNIX keepers), loads and stores as "isomorphic to read and write messages", trap instruction kept for binary compatibility (pp. 4–5, 9–11) | new |
| 6 | P21 | On-die shared memory (MPB) "to increase performance of a message passing programming model"; cache management (MPMT, INVDMB) for software coherency; off-chip memory via LUT (pp. 174–176) | new |
| 7 | P77 | Per-trap kernel entry (Pentium's "irregular" saved state); drivers and store in the kernel "To simplify security assurance"; mode bit disabling invocation "For emulation"; levels in its own processes: storage allocation, virtual copy, process construction (pp. 170, 173, 178–180) | new |
| 8 | P66 | Shared memory over a global address space because it "simplifies programming"; register writes across clusters and global condition-code registers for parallelism and barriers; traps in a dedicated thread to avoid cancelling issued operations; sync bit per word (pp. 3–6) | new (global registers first recorded) |

# Coverage of SQ2

Saved as `sls/4-synthesis/SQ2.coverage.md`. Which papers serve this question, what each added, and whether the question has what it needs (`research/sls/4-synthesis/step.md`).

## Rule
- **Kind:** kinds.
- **Unit:** a kind of mechanism kept below the language that is not a message send (e.g. shared memory, interrupts, traps, privileged instructions, microcode, global registers), together with the reason given for keeping it; or a kind of level found to be written in the system's own objects and messages. A mechanism already recorded counts as new again only with a reason not yet recorded.
- **Enough when:** at least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 5 in a row add nothing new (10 + 5). Abstract-only records (P74) do not count (gate 3c).

## Read
In the reading order of SQ2.md: the named lessons paper first, then processors alternating with kernels, then the papers the order does not name.
| # | Paper | Contributes | New? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | P48 | Shared buffers (long IPC complex, "rarely used"), kernel–user shared message registers (portability, cost), in-kernel fixed-policy scheduler (no user-level scheduler "without imposing high overhead"), in-kernel timer and interrupt-controller drivers, interrupts disabled in the kernel and a big lock (simplicity, verification); kernel in assembler/C/C++ (pp. 136–139, 142–147) | new |
| 2 | P10 | Shared memory in a "pure memory-to-memory architecture" (chip size, faster process swap, "conceptual unity and simplicity"); microcode as sole creator of protected pointers (unforgeable); I/O only through the Interface Processor; unprotected branch instructions never generated (pp. 302, 311, 315–317) | new (new reasons for shared memory; microcode and I/O kinds) |
| 3 | P8 | Coherent shared memory under every message ("the only inter-core communication mechanism available"); traps and system calls into the CPU driver; hardware-routed interrupts; IPIs and MONITOR/MWAIT to wake a receiver; application shared memory because "most current programs" need it; CPU driver outside the message model (pp. 8–11, 14) | new |
| 4 | P12 | Presence and type tags with fault handlers ("makes software more efficient and robust"), segment descriptors (relocation, protection), translation table (global naming), diagnostic port (supervisory commands), local READ/WRITE (pp. 3, 5–8) | new |
| 5 | P53 | Privileged in-kernel low-level drivers ("Except where performance compels otherwise"), shared segments in KeyNIX (state shared between UNIX keepers), loads and stores as "isomorphic to read and write messages", trap instruction kept for binary compatibility (pp. 4–5, 9–11) | new |
| 6 | P21 | On-die shared memory (MPB) "to increase performance of a message passing programming model"; cache management (MPMT, INVDMB) for software coherency; off-chip memory via LUT (pp. 174–176) | new |
| 7 | P77 | Per-trap kernel entry (Pentium's "irregular" saved state); drivers and store in the kernel "To simplify security assurance"; mode bit disabling invocation "For emulation"; levels in its own processes: storage allocation, virtual copy, process construction (pp. 170, 173, 178–180) | new |
| 8 | P66 | Shared memory over a global address space because it "simplifies programming"; register writes across clusters and global condition-code registers for parallelism and barriers; traps in a dedicated thread to avoid cancelling issued operations; sync bit per word (pp. 3–6) | new (global registers first recorded) |
| 9 | P73 | Shared Lisp objects instead of "special restricted mechanisms for inter-process communication"; locking; sequence breaks; hand-microcoded subprimitives; unrestricted access to internal state because "the Lisp Machine is an interactive system" (pp. 172, 282, 429) | new |
| 10 | P65 | Presence tags ("natural to associate the synchronization tag with the data"), priority interrupts with separate register sets for "Fast interrupt processing", name translation, send faults; no hardware barrier because software suffices (pp. 2, 5–6, 9–10) | new (new reasons for tags and interrupts) |
| 11 | P46 | I/O ports in driver address spaces; grant/map/demap kept in the kernel ("required to implement memory managers and pagers"); shared memory between the Unix server and its clients; DMA as a path no kernel can stop; kernel-mode extensions to save switches (pp. 72–73, 75–76) | new |
| 12 | P72 | Shared system memory (no reason); CALL/RETURN with preallocated hardware contexts (per-call allocation "was time-consuming"); local stack storage objects (garbage collection "prohibitive for short-lived objects"); hardware branch to fault handlers; type managers partly in hardware; "There are no special privileges" (pp. 159–160, 168–169, 172–173, 180, 184–185) | new |
| 13 | P64 | Tags for "synchronization on data availability"; ENTER/XLATE for a global address space and "the freedom to experiment with different address translation mechanisms"; segmented memory for relocation and protection (pp. 7, 9–10, 12–13) | new (minor: new reasons for tags and translation) |
| 14 | P69 | Memory-based instructions (fast context switches); type, overflow and translation traps (dynamic typing, uniform local and remote access); associative table (global names, one-cycle method lookup); level in its own terms: every message above EXECUTE is ROM code the user can redefine (pp. 189, 191–192, 194, 196) | new |
| 15 | P70 | System calls for Cosmos utilities (function-call overhead); fixed MDP code; per-node globals "because of flaws in the MDP architecture"; CST locks; CST runtime written in CST, Cosmos and MDP runtime in assembly (pp. 51–52, 54, 57, 60–61, 74–75, 180) | new |
| 16 | P33 | Interrupts as "the only way to signal an asynchronous event"; polling on the CM-5 because interrupts cost too much; kernel traps where there is no user-level network access; DMA for large messages; memory-mapped FIFOs; busy-wait flags (pp. 432–439) | new |
| 17 | P45 | System calls for process-private resources because "Local message-passing is slower than a system call"; timer, interrupt controller and traps for scheduling; shared memory and DMA under remote messages (PCI-E accesses "stall the initiating CPU"); interrupts steered to one kernel; kernel in Sing# except per-device assembly (pp. 2, 4–7) | new |
| 18 | P49 | Kernel calls for privileged operations, since user-mode drivers "cannot execute privileged instructions"; clock driver in the microkernel; Singularity's shared object heap ("the system would be very slow" otherwise); mutexes in the microkernel; Singularity "almost entirely in Sing#" (pp. 47–50) | new |
| 19 | P102 | Application shared memory ("in a small application, it can be quite useful"); microkernel name and privilege caches (fast lookups); static privileges as a "privilege fixed point" to prevent dependency cycles; OS services written as message servers, microkernel outside (pp. 2, 5–7) | new |
| – | P74 | Abstract only: names no escape route (abstract) | not counted (abstract only, gate 3c) |

## Rule
- **Kind:** evidence.
- **Unit:** a finding: a measurement or argument that the hardware's execution model, or the language, libraries, tools or training, shapes how programs are designed or how correct they are.
- **Enough when:** at least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 3 in a row add nothing new (10 + 3).

## Read
The named paper read first, then the others with measurements first and the language and hardware sides alternating.
| # | Paper | Contributes | New? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | P280 | Argument: ease of programming has "no difference inherent in the machine organization itself"; differences come from the cost of implementing a language and its tools; cheap error checking is expected ("one would expect") to give more reliable software (pp. 98, 101) | new |
| 2 | P9 | Language side, from 171 bugs: causes traced to Go's features and libraries and to "the lack of a clear understanding in new Go features"; no hardware factor examined (pp. 2, 6, 9–10, 12) | new |
| 3 | P8 | Hardware side, argument: in a shared-memory OS the knowledge for efficient sharing "is encoded implicitly in its implementation", tying it to one hardware design; programmers reason about "messages sent by the cache-coherence protocol" (pp. 2, 4) | new |
| 4 | P5 | Language and primitive side: order intentions not easily expressed or enforced by locks or transactional memory; "Most programmers think sequentially"; 29 of 57 Mozilla reports mention no tool (pp. 329, 333, 338) | new |
| 5 | P22 | Hardware side, argument: with coherence "programmers can concentrate on choreographing independent work"; removing it "shifts the complexity from hardware to software" (pp. 1, 9) | new |
| 6 | P70 | Hardware shapes language and code, designer's statement: target costs shaped CST's design, and MDP queues impose a rule that methods may not loop without a send (p. 12) | new |
| 7 | P12 | Designers' assertion: "most parallel programs are very biased by the mechanisms (or lack thereof) of the machines for which they were initially written"; fine-grain parallelism hard to extract from C or FORTRAN (pp. 18, 24) | new |
| 8 | P65 | Designers' argument: "Requiring coarse-grain communication complicates programming"; data placement costs programming effort (pp. 5, 7) | covered by P12 |

# Coverage of SQ11

Saved as `sls/4-synthesis/SQ11.coverage.md`. Which papers serve this question, what each added, and whether the question has what it needs (`research/sls/4-synthesis/step.md`).

## Rule
- **Kind:** evidence.
- **Unit:** a finding: a reason developers give or a study reports for using shared state, locks or other mechanisms alongside messages, or a thing the pure message model is reported unable to express or too costly for.
- **Enough when:** at least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 3 in a row add nothing new (10 + 3).

## Read
Empirical studies of real programs first, then the named L4 lessons, then the others.
| # | Paper | Contributes | New? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | P9 | Six Go applications use shared memory more than channels (Mutex 45.01–70.34% vs chan 18.48–42.99%, stable 2015–2018); 16 blocking bugs mix a channel with a lock or wait; no developer reason recorded, the authors only "suspect" (pp. 4, 6–7, 11) | new |
| 2 | P48 | Kernel designers: shared buffers "generally preferred for bulk data transfer"; synchronous-only IPC "forces a multi-threaded design", so notifications and semaphores were added; RPC-style IPC "sequentialises client and server" (pp. 136–139) | new |
| 3 | P53 | KeyNIX's developers shared UNIX tables in a segment, "the primary impediment to distribution"; the developers are the kernel's designers (pp. 11, 17) | new |
| 4 | P73 | Designers: processes share Lisp objects instead of "special restricted mechanisms"; the contract is unenforced so state can be examined from a debugger (pp. 282, 429) | new |
| 5 | P8 | OS designers support threads sharing an address space because "most current programs" need it (pp. 11, 15) | new |
| 6 | P70 | The language provides locks "to synchronize computation" and build atomic transactions beside messages; no developer reports (pp. 11, 19–20, 54) | new |
| 7 | P12 | The compiler replaces sends with direct calls when the receiver's type is known, as an optimisation; frequency and cost not stated (p. 20) | new |

## Status

| 2 | P8 | Shared-state updates cost ~12,000 extra cycles each at 16 cores, "stalled on cache misses"; Linux and Windows unmap scale worse from serial IPIs; cites a coherence limit "to even 80 cores"; authors warn against quantitative conclusions (pp. 3–4, 13, 16) | new |
| 3 | P102 | Linux 2.6.24.7's page allocator "does not scale beyond 8 cores under heavy load" (16 cores); simulated OS/application cache interference; coherence scaling called "unclear" without a source (pp. 2–5, 8–9) | new |
| 4 | P21 | Argued by designers: coherence overhead will exceed the value of more cores; power density as a general limit; measured: memory controllers dominate power at low voltage because DDR3 I/O cannot scale (pp. 173, 180) | new |
| 5 | P45 | A shared-memory kernel on 4 cores: one dispatcher lock limits scaling, two kernels scale around it; IPIs for balancing "harm performance as the number of cores grows"; remote misses 38% slower (pp. 9, 11) | new |
| 6 | P64 | Design statement for a machine with no shared memory: node count limited by router addressability and network bandwidth; 3-D mesh chosen for latency and throughput (pp. 2, 5) | new |
| 7 | P65 | Measured: "global bandwidth is a critical resource"; the network saturates at 6 of 14.4 Gbit/s under random traffic (pp. 2, 4, 11) | new |
| 8 | P70 | Analytical: the network becomes critical above 343 nodes; random allocation would congest a 65,536-node machine; a name-space limit of about 32,000 objects per node (pp. 110, 114, 121, 123) | new |

- **Unit:** a finding: a measurement, projection or argument that hardware shared memory, cache coherence or a shared-memory kernel does or does not scale to many cores, or a limit reported on many-core scaling in general (power, communication, serial fractions).

| 2 | P8 | Shared-state updates cost ~12,000 extra cycles each at 16 cores, "stalled on cache misses"; Linux and Windows unmap scale worse from serial IPIs; cites a coherence limit "to even 80 cores"; authors warn against quantitative conclusions (pp. 3–4, 13, 16) | new |

## Rule
- **Kind:** evidence.
- **Unit:** a finding: a proof, measurement or argument that a system function needs global agreement or works better with central or logically central coordination, or what a decentralised version of it costs or gives up.

## Read
The operating system papers named last in SQ15.md's order (P46, P48, P70, P102), then the others.
| # | Paper | Contributes | New? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | P46 | Memory servers kept out of the one mandatory kernel ("alternative memory servers may coexist") for coexistence and machine dependence; an in-kernel memory policy gave up "complete main-memory control"; argued (pp. 74–76) | new |
| 2 | P48 | "a global scheduler makes more sense" on embedded multicores; the restricted multikernel gives up memory migration; "All past attempts to export scheduling policy to user level have failed"; thread-ID naming led to a bottleneck "gateway thread"; argued (pp. 138, 143) | new |
| 3 | P70 | Distributed-object allocation serialised at one node for unique IDs; the home node a "fanout bottleneck"; parallel garbage collection "unfeasible", mark-and-sweep stops the machine; migration costs decisions and congestion (pp. 119–121) | new |
| 4 | P102 | Atomicity needs "synchronization points": a lock or transaction server; "the cost of software-based lock management may dwarf the performance wins"; not certain all cases avoid local locks (pp. 5, 8) | new |
| 5 | P8 | The decentralised capability scheme "was a mistake ... no more efficient than scalable per-processor memory managers"; replica consistency costs latency and developer effort; two-phase commit "serializes more messages"; no failure handling (pp. 7, 10, 14, 17) | new |
| 6 | P45 | Naming kept central "for the sake of simplicity"; per-domain memory and scheduling give up processes spanning domains; interrupts centralised, restricting driver placement (pp. 5–6, 13) | new |
| 7 | P53 | Failure handling by a system-wide checkpoint suspending all processes; scheduling and storage from one prime meter and one master space bank; the shared KeyNIX tables block distribution; no cost of a decentralised version (pp. 4, 6, 8, 17) | new |
| 8 | P77 | Failure handling by a whole-machine snapshot with all processes halted (under 50 ms for 256 MB); storage through one space bank (pp. 174, 179) | covered by P53 |

# Coverage of SQ18

Saved as `sls/4-synthesis/SQ18.coverage.md`. Which papers serve this question, what each added, and whether the question has what it needs (`research/sls/4-synthesis/step.md`).

## Rule
- **Kind:** evidence.
- **Unit:** a finding: a cost of object-based or capability-based hardware, its size, and whether the evaluation attributes it to object orientation, fine-grained protection or object addressing themselves or to compilers or implementation, with whether the evaluator is independent of the designers.
- **Enough when:** at least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 3 in a row add nothing new (10 + 3).

## Read
Independent evaluations first, in SQ18.md's order, then the others.
| # | Paper | Contributes | New? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | P29 | Independent (Berkeley): asks "how much performance is degraded because of the object-oriented architecture" but does not isolate it; the costs it isolates are put on the release 2 implementation and compiler; "we are not measuring just the architecture" (pp. 17–18, 23) | new |
| 2 | P10 | Independent: the "synthetic 432" shows the wasted cycles were "not spent in pursuit of object orientation" (35–45% in the text, 2.2–93.7% by benchmark in the table); data-cache flushing on protected calls fixable by an AD cache; residual 2–3x the "rough estimate" of the inherent cost of the 432's style of object orientation (pp. 325, 329–330, 336–338) | new |
| 3 | P72 | Evaluator not among the designers (inferred): object addressing makes a byte access "potentially" need four references, "comparable to ... any conventional virtual memory system", reduced by caches; 64 KB segments add compiler work; attributed to the addressing design (inferred); size not measured (pp. 166, 185–186) | new |
| 4 | P77 | Third party, sizes not given: the i432's performance "suffers dramatically" from complexity (cited); CAP's capability cache adequate only for "large grain objects"; both attributed to design, not compilers (pp. 182–183) | new |
| 5 | P12 | Designers, not independent: a 3–4x area and 2–3x speed loss put on standard cells (implementation), not on tags or object addressing; the costs of tags and translation themselves not measured (pp. 7, 16) | new |

## Status
open: 5 read, fewer than 10; all 5 added a finding. Only the 432 has an independent, measured attribution, and its inherent part is a residual (P10). Modern capability hardware (P30 and the CHERI papers) is unread.

# Selection criteria

A paper is included if it meets at least one inclusion criterion and no exclusion criterion. Each verdict names the criterion that decided it. There is no restriction on publication date. "Message-based" in these criteria means: meets I1.

Terms used in the criteria and the SQs:
- **Below the programming language:** in the operating system kernel, the instruction set, microcode or hardware; not in a language runtime, library or virtual machine hosted on a conventional kernel (as in X2).
- **Written in its own objects and messages:** the level's code is objects receiving messages in the system's own model, not a lower language, microcode or hardware outside that model.
- **Without changing either:** neither the sender's nor the receiver's code, nor how they name each other, is modified to place the component between them.

| ID | Inclusion criterion |
|---|---|
| I1 | A paper is included if it describes, implements, simulates or evaluates a processor, instruction set, microarchitecture, multicomputer node or operating system kernel in which sending a message, invoking a method on an object, or delivering a message to an actor is a primitive of that level, i.e. one of: (a) an instruction of the instruction set; (b) a hardware or microcode mechanism; (c) for a kernel, the stated means by which the kernel and its system services, or the kernel's own parts, communicate (as in microkernels, multikernels, or operating systems written in an object or actor language that run without an underlying conventional kernel). The paper must name the mechanism with at least one of these terms: message, message passing, send, mailbox, actor, active message, inter-process communication (IPC), method invocation. (SQ1–SQ5) |
| I2 | A paper is included if it is a retrospective, evaluation or historical account of at least one computer architecture that its authors describe as directed at a high-level language, object-based, object-oriented or message-driven, and it reports either measured performance of that architecture or a stated reason for its performance, adoption, abandonment, or becoming unnecessary. (SQ5, SQ6) |
| I3 | A paper is included if it is an empirical study of concurrency defects (bugs) in real programs or systems (not only examples written by the authors) and it reports counts or proportions of defects either split by communication mechanism (shared memory versus message passing) or for programs or systems built on message passing only, or for programs or systems built on shared memory only, as the comparison baseline for SQ7. Programs whose defects are reported as accesses to shared variables count as shared-memory programs even if the paper does not use that term. (SQ7) |
| I4 | A paper is included if it reports evidence or an argument that directly answers one of SQ8–SQ19, whether or not it mentions messages or objects. (SQ8–SQ19) |

| ID | Exclusion criterion |
|---|---|
| X1 | A paper is excluded if it meets none of I1, I2, I3, I4. |
| X2 | A paper included only through I1 is excluded if message passing appears only at the application, library, language runtime, virtual machine or network-protocol level, running on a processor whose instruction set and hardware have no message mechanism and on a kernel that fails I1(c) (e.g. an actor library, the Erlang virtual machine, a Message Passing Interface library, a Smalltalk virtual machine hosted on Unix or Windows). Does not apply to papers that meet I2 or I3. |
| X3 | A paper is excluded if the system is a cluster or network of separate computers, each with a processor whose instruction set and hardware have no message mechanism and a kernel that fails I1(c), and the message mechanism lies only in the network interface or interconnect between them. |
| X4 | A paper is excluded if the hardware it presents is stated to serve only a fixed function or domain (e.g. neural-network inference, signal processing, packet switching, graphics) and is not stated to run general programs. Does not apply to papers included through I4. |
| X5 | A paper is excluded if it is not one of: journal article; conference or workshop paper longer than 2 pages; book or book chapter; doctoral or master's thesis; technical report of a university, company research laboratory or standards body; magazine article of a professional society (Association for Computing Machinery, Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, USENIX); architecture or system reference manual published by the system's manufacturer. Patents, slides, posters, extended abstracts of 2 pages or fewer, blog posts, forum posts, encyclopaedia entries and product brochures are excluded. |
| X6 | A paper is excluded if its full text is in neither English nor Spanish. |
| X7 | A paper is excluded if its full text cannot be obtained from the publisher, an author's or institution's web page, arXiv, Semantic Scholar, the Internet Archive, or the university library. The sources tried are recorded with the verdict. |
| X8 | A paper is excluded if it reports the same system and the same results as another included paper. The one with more pages is kept; the other is excluded unless it reports at least one measurement, design element or stated reason absent from the kept one. |
| X9 | A paper is excluded if its title or abstract presents it as a survey, review, overview or taxonomy of other work and it reports no measurement and states no reason under I2 of its own. Its reference list is still used for snowballing. |

questions.question: The re-screen covers 181 papers: each is checked against the rules from its abstract, introduction and conclusion, and the tightened counter-evidence rule applies. That's well beyond the 20-item limit for one agent, so it would run as about 9 screeners of 20 papers each. Each fetches papers online, so it's a sizeable share of a usage window, similar to the link batch that hit the limit earlier. You'd then decide the verdicts at a screening gate, grouped by reason, not one card per paper. How should I run it?

options.label: First 20, then the rest (Recommended)

options.label: All 181 at once
